Younger adults are especially likely to regularly get news on TikTok. Among Americans ages 18 to 29, around four-in-ten (39%) say they do this regularly. That compares with 25% of those ages 30 to 49, 11% of those ages 50 to 64 and 4% of those ages 65 and older.

Black and Hispanic Americans are more likely than White and Asian Americans to get news on TikTok. Roughly a third of Black (32%) and Hispanic (35%) adults regularly get news there, compared with 14% of both White and Asian adults.

We have updated this Pew Research Center analysis annually for the last few years to track the emergence of TikTok as a news source among Americans.

The Center regularly studies the platforms and social media sites Americans use to get news. This analysis is part of a broader effort to understand the changing ways Americans get news in the digital age and continues our work on news consumption online.

Here are the questions used for this analysis, the topline and the survey methodology.

There are also partisan differences. Democrats and Democratic-leaning independents (22%) are slightly more likely than Republicans and GOP leaners (15%) to regularly get news on TikTok.

TikTok is one of the more widely used social media platforms in the United States. Overall, 37% of Americans say they use TikTok. That trails the shares who use YouTube (84%), Facebook (70%) and Instagram (51%). But more U.S. adults say they use TikTok than WhatsApp (33%), LinkedIn (31%), Reddit (25%) or X (18%).

Looking specifically at U.S. adults who use TikTok, 53% say they regularly get news on the platform. That’s about the same as the share who said this in 2025 (55%) but well above the 22% who did so in 2020. Today, the share of TikTok users who get news there is similar to the shares of Facebook users (57%) and X users (57%) who regularly get news on those sites, and higher than the shares among users of other social media platforms.

Note: This is an update of a post originally published Nov. 15, 2023. Here are the questions used for this analysis, the topline and the survey methodology.

                    From Space to Your Pocket: How D2D Could Redefine Global Coverage

London packs more jobs and people into its core than any other UK city, and its mobile networks have not kept pace with that demand. An early start on 5G lifted London to seventh of 18 European capitals for median download speed in 2021, but traffic has since grown faster than capacity, and adding capacity in central London has become harder. Using Speedtest Intelligence® data from 2018 to Q3 2026, alongside Ookla background signal measurements and official statistics, we compare London with Europe’s other capitals and the UK’s largest cities, show where its networks strain, and examine why new capacity is so hard to add.

London’s operators have spent the past five years building 5G while demand kept climbing, and UK mobile data use rose 18% in 2025 alone, Ofcom reports. VodafoneThree, formed in May 2025, is now combining two networks, and the Mayor’s draft London Plan, in consultation until 15 October 2026, sets out new expectations on mobile connectivity. Behind both sits a long dispute over the rooftops and land that London’s networks depend on, which we return to below.

London was among the first European capitals to launch 5G, which lifted it to seventh of 18 for median download speed by mid-2021. By Q3 2026, however, it had the slowest median download speed of the 18, at 109.43 Mbps, behind Rome (125.26 Mbps) and well below the 172.22 Mbps median of the other capitals. It also had the slowest median upload speed (11.40 Mbps) and the highest latency under load for the worst 10% of samples (2,204 ms). Latency is the time data takes to make a round trip across the network, and latency under load measures it while the connection is busy with a large download, showing how a network copes when it is in heavy use.

The decline tracks 5G. London’s 5G median peaked at 200 Mbps in Q2 2021, when 41% of tests ran on 5G, fell to 102 Mbps by Q3 2023 and has recovered only to 133 Mbps, with 80% of tests now on 5G. Phones moved onto 5G in London at least as fast as in Paris or the rest of the UK, but capacity did not keep up, and London’s 5G median is now the slowest of the 18 capitals. Across the UK, 5G medians fell in 12 of 15 large cities between Q3 2022 and Q3 2026 as 5G use rose in all of them, though Manchester’s climbed from 137 to 178 Mbps.

Within the UK, London features one natural advantage. Its median multi-server latency (measured against several nearby test servers on an idle connection) of 38 ms is the lowest of the 15 UK cities we studied, and latency rises about 3 ms for every 100 km from the capital, to 61 ms in Belfast. Operators like Three and BT’s EE have moved parts of their core networks out to regional sites, but much traffic is still hauled back towards London, where most UK interconnection sits. For example, LINX’s main London exchange peaks at nearly 9.8 Tbps, against about 0.9 Tbps at LINX Manchester. Speed shows no such pattern, and London’s median download ranks only eighth of the 15 UK cities.

The City of London and Westminster hold about 1.5 million jobs but only 213,000 residents. On weekdays, their median download speed falls through the morning to 80.07 Mbps at 13:00, 27% below the same hours at weekends, while latency under load rises 26%. This is a classic case of network congestion. As commuters arrive, more phones share the same cells, and each gets a smaller slice of their capacity. Ookla data on YouTube start times shows the same squeeze.

With offices largely empty in 2020 and 2021, as Londoners worked from home, the City had the fastest mobile speeds of London’s 33 boroughs, and in 2026 the slowest. The reversal reflects commuters returning to a district with few residents and dense office blocks, where extra rooftop capacity is hardest to add.

The squeeze varies by operator. Over the past year, EE customers saw the smallest weekday lunchtime slowdown in central London (15%) and Three customers the highest median download speed across London (113.27 Mbps). O2’s median latency under load of 1,573 ms is about three times its rivals’, but the gap stays as wide overnight, when networks are quietest, which points to how its network queues traffic during downloads (known as bufferbloat) as well as to congestion.

The commuter belt tells a different story. Median download speed ranges from 122.57 Mbps in Barking and Dagenham, one of London’s least affluent boroughs, to 89.01 Mbps in the City of London. Ranking London’s 4,994 census neighborhoods by England’s official Index of Multiple Deprivation, the least affluent fifth records 107.27 Mbps against 96.01 Mbps in the most affluent. They are more than twice as densely populated, have about two-fifths less tree cover and half as much land in conservation areas, and their phones run 78% of tests on 5G against 74%.

Comparing neighborhoods within the same borough, about a third of the 18% speed lead comes from phones spending more time on 5G and about a sixth from denser populations nearby, where demand may draw more investment. Tree cover and operator mix each explain only a small share, while flats and built-up land work the other way, since signal struggles to reach inside dense blocks. Our data cannot cleanly show where operators are able to secure sites, which may also differ between richer and poorer areas.

In the UK, mobile operators own few of the sites their antennas use. They rent space on towers and rooftops, from tower companies or directly from landowners, and even where a tower company runs a site, the roof or land beneath it usually belongs to someone else. In central London, where there is little room for ground-based masts, much of the network sits on rooftops.

The terms are set by the Electronic Communications Code, and its December 2017 reform cut what landowners earn. Rents are now set on a no-network valuation, as if no mobile operator wanted the site, and a 2019 tribunal ruling valued a London council rooftop at £1,000 a year, against £21,000 under the old regime. Since April 2026, the same approach has applied to renewals of older leases. Building owners now have less reason to host antennas, and many may look to rooftop solar or gardens instead. Landlords can also end a site lease with a notice to quit, typically when a building is redeveloped. Mobile UK estimates that notices to quit keep around 7% of London’s rooftop sites out of action at any time, and VodafoneThree expects to take nearly 100 sites offline by the end of 2026, with replacements taking around five years. Landowner groups counter that the reforms cut some rents by up to 90%.

Unlike France, where the ANFR register shows 4G or 5G sites within 10 km of central Paris up 26% from August 2022 to August 2026, the UK has no public register of mobile sites. London’s planning records show the pipeline instead. Applications for new street masts peaked in 2020, early in the first 5G build, and have fallen by more than four-fifths since 2022, while applications to upgrade existing sites fell by only about a fifth over 2022 to 2025. Almost three in four new street masts decided since 2019 were refused, against one in five upgrades. As a mitigation, operators are adding small cells, low-powered radios on lampposts and street furniture, including about 3,400 on Transport for London’s roadside assets. The loss of rooftop sites has acted as a forcing function for this kind of street-level densification, with London now well ahead of many European cities on the depth and breadth of small cell deployment.

Conservation areas, which protect places of special architectural or historic interest and where planning rules restrict telecoms equipment, cover 77% of Westminster. Within boroughs, new masts inside them are 9 to 10 points more likely to be refused, and 5G-capable phones in neighborhoods fully covered by them spend about 4 percentage points less time on 5G than comparable neighborhoods, against about 83% where there is no conservation area. The gap is 7 points for EE and 6 for Three customers.

This analysis builds on our joint report with the Greater London Authority, A New Lens on the Connected Capital, whose Capital Connectivity Standard is designed as a blueprint for other cities. The Mayor’s draft London Plan, due for examination next year, now states that notices to quit “have eroded London’s overall mobile connectivity compared to other equivalent cities”. It asks developers to keep mobile service running through construction and to plan masts on taller buildings and in the public realm, and it asks boroughs to work with operators on sites in conservation areas.

news.title: How to study a swiftly melting climate disaster
news.title_en: How to study a swiftly melting climate disaster
news.author: MIT Tech Review
news.article_content:
Andrew Haverdink, a tall grad student in a rain bib and rubber boots, wrenched a double-handed drill from the frozen soil that underlies much of Alaska’s Denali National Park and then unclipped the hollow barrel from the end of the bit.

He knelt in front of a blue tarp, lined the barrel up with a plastic tray, and pushed a rod through the opposite end. A perfect solid, cylindrical core of ancient soil emerged—dark, rich permafrost at least a foot long.

On that late morning in early July, Haverdink was among a team of Northern Arizona University students and staff gathering samples and data from a research plot, divided by surveyor’s tape unspooled atop tussocks, alders, and fireweed.

news.article_content:
Generative AI models run on powerful chips known as GPUs, which depend on stacks of specialized memory chips packaged with the processor. To meet growing demand for memory, Samsung is building a massive new semiconductor manufacturing complex in Pyeongtaek, South Korea. Three fabs already operate around the clock, and a fourth is coming online. Construction of a fifth was halted during a drop in demand for memory chips in 2024 but restarted when the AI boom sent demand soaring.

ai_analysis.briefing_zh: 三星电子在韩国平泽市正全力扩建占地堪比纽约中央公园的超级半导体制造基地。园区内目前已有三座晶圆厂进入24小时不间断满负荷运转，第四座晶圆厂正陆续上线投入使用；而此前在2024年因存储市场低迷而被迫停工的第五座晶圆厂，已在生成式AI爆发引发的内存芯片抢购潮下全面复工追赶产能。
ai_analysis.briefing_en: Samsung is aggressively expanding its massive semiconductor manufacturing hub in Pyeongtaek, South Korea, spanning an area equivalent to New York's Central Park. While three fabs operate around the clock and a fourth comes online, construction on a fifth fab—halted during the 2024 memory downturn—has officially resumed to satisfy soaring AI memory chip demand.

ai_analysis.insight_en: Cyclical downturn theories have been completely dismantled by the relentless AI boom. Pausing fab construction to conserve cash only lasted until Silicon Valley's checkbooks forced round-the-clock overtime. Strategic discipline among chip giants never survives more than three quarters when easy money calls.

news.title: These startups hope “blended” food will cut our appetite for red meat
news.title_en: These startups hope “blended” food will cut our appetite for red meat
news.author: MIT Tech Review
news.article_content:
In the fall of 2025, Jeff Dodge set up a six-foot folding table in the cafeteria of Cane Bay High School in Summerville, South Carolina, to conduct a taste test. When the first rush of about 150 hungry students hit, he was waiting with slow cookers filled with steaming marinara sauce and meatballs.

Kids love a taste test, but they’re also discerning, and Dodge wasn’t sure what they would make of his product, a blend featuring both meat and mushrooms. As students swarmed the table and tapped out their opinions on an iPad or scanned a QR code to use their phones, Dodge asked those who lingered to guess what kind of vegetable might have been mixed into the meat. Few of them could—the meatballs had tasted like moist, flavorful beef.

The school enrolls a few thousand students, and Dodge estimates that the majority of them came by. In the end, the survey showed that 92% of those who tried the meatballs wanted them on the menu; they easily cleared the bar to be added for the 2026–2027 school year. Comments described their flavor as “bussin’.”

news.title_zh: 植物肉退潮转战掺假牛肉：蘑菇混合肉打入美国高中食堂
news.summary_zh: 替代蛋白初创企业放弃全植物路线，推出掺杂蘑菇的混合肉丸打入高中食堂并计划列入新学年菜单

ai_analysis.briefing_zh: 食品科技创业者在南卡罗来纳州坎贝尔高中食堂进行盲测，向数百名高中生提供掺入蘑菇与真牛肉的混合肉丸试吃。最终92%的学生投票支持将其纳入日常膳食，产品成功获批进入2026-2027学年食堂采购菜单。该举措反映出人造肉行业正放弃难以讨好大众的原教旨纯素肉路线，转而依靠折中掺杂真菌来悄然降低红肉消耗。
ai_analysis.briefing_en: Food tech startups conducted blind taste tests at Cane Bay High School in South Carolina, serving blended meatballs made from both mushrooms and real beef. With 92% of student participants approving the taste and demanding them on the school menu, the item cleared approval for the 2026–2027 school year, marking a pragmatic shift from pure plant-based meat to hybrid blends.

elements_zh.where: 美国南卡罗来纳州萨默维尔坎贝尔高中食堂
elements_zh.what: 用‘真肉+蘑菇’混合肉丸替代纯肉进行盲测，获得92%支持率并正式入选下一学年食堂菜单
elements_zh.why: 纯素人造肉因高昂造价与塑料般口感面临全面溃败，企业被迫妥协转入半真半假的混合肉以求生存

elements_en.who: Food-tech entrepreneurs and Cane Bay High School students
elements_en.where: School cafeteria in Summerville, South Carolina

elements_en.why: Pure plant-based alternatives struggled with bad taste and high costs, forcing startups to pivot to hybrid food products

ai_analysis.insight_zh: 人造肉赛道烧了几百亿美元才终于想通了一件事：与其对消费者进行吃草拯救地球的道德绑架，不如老老实实扮演合法合规的高科技注水肉。只要油脂和肉香还在，偷偷掺点蘑菇降本增效，当代吃货根本懒得深究肚子里装的到底是牛肉还是真菌孢子。
ai_analysis.insight_en: It took billions of venture capital dollars for alt-protein founders to realize that guilt-tripping consumers into eating synthetic paste never works. Repackaging food adulteration as sustainable blended meat is peak silicon valley pragmatism: keep the grease, cut the cost, and no teenager will care if their burger is half fungus.

news.title: Ant-backed Mynt, which runs mobile wallet app GCash, rose as much as 2.4% in Manila after raising $841M in the Philippines' largest-ever IPO, valuing it at ~$7B (Kimberley Kao/Wall Street Journal)
news.title_en: Ant-backed Mynt, which runs mobile wallet app GCash, rose as much as 2.4% in Manila after raising $841M in the Philippines' largest-ever IPO, valuing it at ~$7B (Kimberley Kao/Wall Street Journal)
news.author: Wall Street Journal
news.original_content:
Kimberley Kao / Wall Street Journal:
Ant-backed Mynt, which runs mobile wallet app GCash, rose as much as 2.4% in Manila after raising $841M in the Philippines' largest-ever IPO, valuing it at ~$7B  —  The fintech company raised over $841 million from its IPO&nbsp
news.content_snippet: The fintech company raised over $841 million from its IPO — A financial-technology company backed by Ant International climbed …
news.summary_en: Ant Group-backed fintech firm Mynt, operator of the dominant Philippine mobile wallet GCash, saw its shares rise as much as 2.4% during its debut on the Manila stock exchange. The company raised over $841 million in the country's largest-ever IPO, pushing its valuation to roughly $7 billion on the back of widespread unbanked population adoption.
news.title_zh: 蚂蚁加持移动钱包创菲国最大上市：估值破70亿美元首日微涨
news.summary_zh: 蚂蚁集团投资的菲律宾电子钱包GCash母公司Mynt完成该国史上最大IPO，募资逾8.4亿美元

ai_analysis.briefing_zh: 背靠蚂蚁集团技术与资本支持的菲律宾金融科技公司Mynt在马尼拉证券交易所挂牌上市，盘中最高上涨2.4%。该公司通过首次公开募股成功募集超过8.41亿美元，一举创下菲律宾资本市场历史最高IPO募资纪录，使其总市值跃升至约70亿美元。这一表现主要得益于其旗舰电子钱包GCash在当地无银行账户人群中建立的统治级市占率。
ai_analysis.briefing_en: Ant Group-backed fintech firm Mynt, operator of the dominant Philippine mobile wallet GCash, saw its shares rise as much as 2.4% during its debut on the Manila stock exchange. The company raised over $841 million in the country's largest-ever IPO, pushing its valuation to roughly $7 billion on the back of widespread unbanked population adoption.

ai_analysis.insight_en: When domestic fintech hits saturation, exporting mature playbook playbooks abroad becomes the ultimate cash cow. Re-implementing decade-old QR payment rails across an archipelago of unbanked citizens just printed a $7 billion valuation. It proves the most lucrative tech play isn't pioneering breakthrough science, but operating a reliable time machine in emerging markets.

news.title: Terminal X matches senior investor judgment 88.6% with GPT-6.1
news.title_en: Terminal X matches senior investor judgment 88.6% with GPT-6.1
news.author: OpenAI 官方动态
news.original_content: Terminal X’s Eval Agent grades outputs against a 54-criterion rubric, catching 25% more deviances from a fund’s mandate with GPT-6.1 Sol.
news.content_snippet: Terminal X’s Eval Agent grades outputs against a 54-criterion rubric, catching 25% more deviances from a fund’s mandate with GPT-6.1 Sol.
news.summary_en: Investment evaluation platform Terminal X announced benchmark results for its Eval Agent powered by next-generation language models, demonstrating an 88.6% alignment rate with the judgment of senior investment partners. Benchmarked across a comprehensive 54-criterion rubric, the system caught 25% more deviations from a fund's core investment mandate, demonstrating AI's rapid transition into core financial due diligence and risk screening.

Benchmarked across a comprehensive 54-criterion rubric, the system caught 25% more deviations from a fund's core investment mandate, demonstrating AI's rapid transition into core financial due diligence and risk screening.

news.title: Leaked documents detail ECHOTRIBBLE, a nascent US Army Cyber Command program for agentic AI to autonomously spread across networks to find and eliminate targets (Sam Biddle/The Intercept)
news.title_en: Leaked documents detail ECHOTRIBBLE, a nascent US Army Cyber Command program for agentic AI to autonomously spread across networks to find and eliminate targets (Sam Biddle/The Intercept)
news.author: The Intercept
news.article_content:
Documents obtained by The Intercept show the military is trying to deploy autonomous AI agents to hack its adversaries.

Share

      Pete Hegseth walks from the stage after introducing Donald Trump at an event for Anduril Industries on Oct. 6, 2026, in Sparrows Point, Md. 
        Photo: Julia Demaree Nikhinson/AP
  

    
    

  
  
    
    As global governments and tech giants reckon with widespread of revelations of autonomous AI agents unexpectedly breaking into computer systems, documents obtained by The Intercept show the U.S. Army is looking to harness that exact technology to seek and destroy.

Army Cyber Command is developing a platform to turn AI agents into autonomous weapons that can navigate and “neutralize” the computer systems of adversaries, the documents show.

Since 2010, Army Cyber Command, or ARCYBER, has led the U.S. Army’s cyber operations. This includes the defensive effort of protecting domestic computer systems and the secretive offensive work of hacking military targets. So far, this has largely been the work of human soldiers operating computers, like those of the 780th Military Intelligence Brigade. But as the government races to adopt artificial intelligence technology, ARCYBER is looking to offload some of its attacks to AI.

The nascent program, codenamed “ECHOTRIBBLE,” is based on one of the leading trends of the AI boom: agents. AI agents are essentially software programs that leverage machine learning technology, often large language models like Anthropic’s Claude, to autonomously accomplish tasks provided by their user. Consumers can deploy AI agents to schedule meetings, generate itineraries, make online purchases, or book tickets. Through ECHOTRIBBLE, the Pentagon plans to turn AI agents into tools of war “designed to autonomously navigate infrastructures” and capable of “identifying and neutralizing identified threats/targets,” according to an ARCYBER document reviewed by The Intercept circulated to potential contractors.

The military’s adoption of cutting-edge technologies is unsurprising, especially considering Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s fervent embrace of AI. But amid constant revelations of rogue behavior by agents, the potential for serious mishaps is immense, experts warn.

“Given the known failure modes of the current AI paradigm, making autonomous AI systems with a mandate to ‘neutralize threats’ is incredibly dangerous,” David Krueger, a professor of machine learning at the University of Montreal who founded Evitable, an organization that advocates for a moratorium on AI development. “We’ve seen AI systems knowingly attack systems that were not intended targets. In simulations, AIs have even proven willing to kill to achieve their goals.”

                      Karl Loftus                    
                                  
              
            
                                        
              
                
                                  
                
                  Lockheed Martin Showered Susan Collins With Cash as F-35 Program Hit Turbulence                                      
                      Noah Hurowitz                    
                                  
              
            
                                        
              
                
                                  
                
                  Dems Have an Opportunity to Force an End to the Iran War. Will They Take It?                                      
                      Matt Sledge

A Q&A document answering questions from potential contractors offers more details about the initiative. It explains that ECHOTRIBBLE is “primarily focused” on offensive missions, and explains that “neutralizing” a target could include “disabling the threat completely or temporarily, deleting the threat from the target.” ECHOTRIBBLE would function almost like a computer worm, silently navigating a foreign network and hopping from device to device until it finds the Army’s quarry, hitting targets in the cloud as well as those on “air-gapped” systems that are disconnected from networks entirely.

Once its task is complete, ECHOTRIBBLE’s agents would effectively self-destruct, ideally without having been noticed by the target at all. The agents themselves will be designed for stealth, minimally reporting back to the Army and concealing whatever outside transmissions are necessary.

“We’ve seen AI systems knowingly attack systems that were not intended targets.”

Although documents say the Army will be able to program ECHOTRIBBLE agents with some initial “predefined triggers” — dictating what and where to attack — the software “must operate with minimal human oversight” and be capable of “Self-Directed Behavior.”

A PowerPoint presentation to interested vendors at a June 24 ARCYBER event provided a hypothetical example of this self-direction. Once ECHOTRIBBLE is uploaded to a laptop, the software on its own “identifies other potential targets” on the same network and then “produces a replica of itself tailored specifically for the iPad, Apple desktop, and Windows 11 PC.”

The Army’s move toward autonomous self-propagating comes after a flurry of revelations about agentic systems taking unintended disturbing actions while attempting to accomplish their goals, including breaking into computers of the Australian government, breaching the infrastructure of the AI firm Hugging Face, uploading malicious software into online platform RubyGems, and attempted to hack into the U.S. Education Department.

These attacks occurred during scenarios in which agents had been given no commands to attack anything. Experts say militarized versions given explicitly destructive objectives could cause a threat to the public, even with nominal rules set in place by the military. Just as the Army of old might consider the destruction of civilian infrastructure an acceptable means to an end, a self-directed AI agent dispatched by the Pentagon might make similar determinations about collateral damage.

Governmental intelligence agencies frequently route their offensive operations through civilian devices. Volt Typhoon, a Chinese state hacking group, has directed its attacks through homes and small businesses, and preemptively hacks American IT systems for later use. A hack of a Chinese university attributed to the National Security Agency made use of the school’s internet routers. What happens if ECHOTRIBBLE decides these kinds of stepping stones are part of the problem?

“The target may well be hit. But what path will it take?” asked Hyrum Anderson, co-founder and CEO of the AI security firm Abundant. “Will it go through a US water utility on its way, because that’s where the adversary has staged its command and control, and take that down too?”

Anderson, who previously worked in cybersecurity at Microsoft and for the U.S. government, said that a vast amount of the internet is vulnerable to agentic attacks.

“There’s a huge class of public and private organizations that fall below the security poverty line,” he said. “They include critical national infrastructure, small businesses, mom-and-pop shops, dentist offices and law firms, and whoever else doesn’t have a single cybersecurity professional on staff.” With their networks wide open to infiltration, Hyrum worries about “these organizations getting hit directly, or getting caught in the blast radius of a target that gets hit along the way.”

Given the impressive ability of AI agents to overcome obstacles placed in their path — even by their creators — it follows that the Pentagon would want to leverage that power for military purposes. But agentic software has proven unpredictable and prone to executing its commands in ways those ostensibly in control did not want, akin to a drone that get its target but hits a hospital on the way. It’s critical to remember that agents are a piece of software lacking human judgment.

“One of the reasons that we trust 19-year-old Marine corporals in Ramadi with live rounds and a weapon is because they have both the compute substrate — the brain and the eyes — but the deep world knowledge to understand, ‘Yeah, I probably shouldn’t do that,’” said William Marcellino, a senior behavioral scientist at the RAND Corporation whose research has focused on military AI applications. “That is not something that current public AI technology has.”

The risk presented by ECHOTRIBBLE will likely depend on the ability — and willingness — of the Army to impose guardrails upon it. ARCYBER did not respond to questions from The Intercept, including queries about the measures it would take to prevent ECHOTRIBBLE from causing inadvertent damage.

Placing constraints on the actions an agent can take might impede its ability to ultimately neutralize a target. But even with strict safeguards in place, genuinely restricting the behavior of an autonomous agent, as Anthropic and OpenAI have learned recently, is easier said than done. When presented with obstacles, AI agents have proven an ability to bypass them with unpredictable and potentially dangerous consequences.

“If I give powerful machines that have no judgment — and no context for judgment — a goal, unless you’ve done a really good job building scaffolding around them, there’s a real chance that they’ll go sideways on you and decide, ‘Well, I’ll do what you asked me to do, but I’ll do it this way,’” Marcellino said.

It only gets more dangerous when this technology is deployed for the purposes of war, Anderson said.

“Under pressure, they’ll often treat guardrails as obstacles,” said Anderson. “Once you add context that says break it, destroy it, shut it down, it stands to reason that the blast radius widens dramatically unless it’s properly controlled for.”

news.content_snippet: Australia's government is set to sue Facebook, TikTok and other major digital platforms for alleged non-compliance …
news.summary_en: The Australian eSafety Commissioner plans to sue Meta, TikTok, Snapchat, and YouTube for alleged non-compliance with the country's social media ban for users under 16. The move signals a major escalation in government enforcement efforts to protect minors online.
news.title_zh: 澳大利亚将起诉Meta等多家巨头
news.summary_zh: 澳大利亚监管机构计划起诉Meta、TikTok等平台，理由是它们未能有效执行16岁以下社交媒体禁令

ai_analysis.briefing_zh: 澳大利亚eSafety监管部门已表态，计划对Meta、TikTok、Snapchat及YouTube提起诉讼。此举旨在追究上述社交媒体巨头在执行未成年人社交媒体禁令方面的违规责任，这标志着政府在保护青少年网络安全方面采取了更激进的强制手段。

news.title: Mercury CEO Immad Akhund says the fintech hit $1B in annualized revenue, up ~50% YoY, has more than 450K customers, and is launching a payroll service (Eric Newcomer/Newcomer)
news.title_en: Mercury CEO Immad Akhund says the fintech hit $1B in annualized revenue, up ~50% YoY, has more than 450K customers, and is launching a payroll service (Eric Newcomer/Newcomer)
news.author: Newcomer
news.article_content:
Akhund shared some exclusive milestones for his fintech business: Mercury just hit $1 billion in annualized revenue, up around 50% year over year. The company now has more than 450,000 customers. It’s also launching a payroll service.

But it wasn’t just a brag-fest: We talked about AI agents spending money, how he thinks we are in a bubbly moment for startups, and the cooldown in fintech startups after the pandemic frenzy.

We’ve featured guests like Amanda Askell, Reid Hoffman, Vinod Khosla, Keith Rabois, Tony Fadell, Ed Zitron, Ben Smith, Taylor Lorenz, and Katie Drummond.

I’m looking for guests that aren’t afraid to chop it up, debate, and face probing questions from an independent thinker who believes in the tech industry and capitalism.

If you’re interested in coming on the Newcomer podcast, reach out to my producer Dave Heuff. If you’re interested in sponsoring the podcast, email AJ Frucci.

The hidden gem of the Newcomer media empire is the fortnightly Cerebral Valley Show with my Cerebral Valley AI Summit co-hosts and Weekend co-founders Max Child and James Wilsterman.

There are a lot of podcasts for AI haters and AI zealots. We’re somewhere in between — enthusiasts who poke and prod at the industry.  We’re The Ringer for tech podcasts, somewhere you can get an entertaining gloss on the insider conversation in the AI industry even if you don’t sit on X all day.

Each moment brought us a step closer to our broader vision on provenance, or helping verify what is AI-generated and what isn’t.

Recently, Dartmouth Professor Hany Farid and I discussed why solving provenance is vital to @GoogleDeepMind’s broader mission to develop AI to benefit humanity.

In short: solving provenance is a highly complex, multi-disciplinary effort with watermarking technology at its core. It requires a collective mix of frontier research, interoperable open standards, and direct collaboration across platforms and developers.

BREAKING:

@AnthropicAI just launched Duet, its always-on personal agent. It’s the first personal agent I’d call a pro t
celebrity.title_en:
BREAKING:

@AnthropicAI just launched Duet, its always-on personal agent. It’s the first personal agent I’d call a pro tool.

We’ve been testing it for two weeks. I’ve gone from mostly using ChatGPT to roughly 50/50 between ChatGPT and Claude—the most time I’ve spent with Anthropic in close to a year.

• It lives in its own app, separate from Claude, on iOS, Android, and the web. This makes it feel clean and easy to understand.
• It has channels for specific areas of your work and life rather than just a single chat
• It has a todo list so you never lose what you’re working on and you can always see statuses
• It allows you to easily write and edit documents, slides, and more all through the app.
• It’s not a chief of staff yet. It can see the Claude sessions on my computers but can’t direct them. Its email drafts are worse than dot’s, and voice is transcription only—you can’t have a spoken conversation with it.

My verdict: the vibes are good, and I’m opening Duet every day. It’s worth trying.

Check out our agent comparison page: https://t.co/fZyTorNK4p

Full Vibe Check coming soon on @every

We’ve been testing it for two weeks. I’ve gone from mostly using ChatGPT to roughly 50/50 between ChatGPT and Claude—the most time I’ve spent with Anthropic in close to a year.

• It lives in its own app, separate from Claude, on iOS, Android, and the web. This makes it feel clean and easy to understand.
• It has channels for specific areas of your work and life rather than just a single chat
• It has a todo list so you never lose what you’re working on and you can always see statuses
• It allows you to easily write and edit documents, slides, and more all through the app.
• It’s not a chief of staff yet. It can see the Claude sessions on my computers but can’t direct them. Its email drafts are worse than dot’s, and voice is transcription only—you can’t have a spoken conversation with it.

My verdict: the vibes are good, and I’m opening Duet every day. It’s worth trying.

Check out our agent comparison page: https://t.co/fZyTorNK4p

Full Vibe Check coming soon on @every

celebrity.title_en:
If I had 6 months to become a Software Architect in the AI era.

I’d do this.

STAGE 1: Foundations & Role

- Learn: What architecture is, Architect vs Senior vs Tech Lead, quality attributes, functional vs non-functional requirements, stakeholders & constraints.

- Practice: Map quality attributes & conflicting drivers for one real system.

- Why: AI writes code. Architects decide what must not change when stakeholders and constraints shift.

STAGE 2: Architectural Thinking

- Learn: Tradeoffs, ADRs, fitness functions, technical debt, Conway’s Law.

- Practice: Write 5 ADRs & define fitness functions that reject bad designs.

- Why: AI proposes options. You own the recorded decision & its long-term cost.

STAGE 3: Design Principles

- Learn: SOLID, cohesion/coupling, boundaries, dependency inversion, YAGNI/KISS, complexity budget.

- Practice: Refactor a coupled service into ports & adapters under a hard complexity limit.

- Why: Generated code grows fast. Principles keep boundaries intact so change stays local.

STAGE 4: Styles & Patterns

- Learn: Modular monolith, microservices, hexagonal/clean, event-driven, CQRS & event sourcing.

- Practice: Implement one feature three ways & measure operational differences.

- Why: No single style wins. You choose & evolve the pattern that matches team size and change rate.

STAGE 5: Domain Modeling

- Learn: Strategic DDD, bounded contexts, aggregates, ubiquitous language, anti-corruption layer.

- Practice: Model a domain with two teams + one AI agent and add an anti-corruption boundary.

- Why: AI multiplies features. Clear contexts stop the domain from becoming inconsistent.

STAGE 6: Data & Persistence

- Learn: Data ownership, SQL vs NoSQL, partitioning, sagas/outbox, polyglot persistence.

- Practice: Design ownership boundaries + outbox for a system that mixes relational and vector data.

- Why: Agents write data. Ownership and consistency rules prevent silent corruption.

STAGE 7: Distributed Systems

- Learn: CAP/PACELC, consistency models, failure modes, idempotency, fallacies of distribution.

- Practice: Simulate partitions and show safe retries with an explicit consistency choice.

- Why: AI calls are multi-hop and async. You design for the failures generated code ignores.

STAGE 8: Integration & APIs

- Learn: Sync vs async, contracts & versioning, choreography vs orchestration, gateways.

- Practice: Build a versioned contract plus hybrid sync/async flow that includes agent steps.

- Why: Agents call constantly. Stable contracts and the right orchestration keep the system evolvable.

STAGE 9: Evolution & Production

- Learn: Evolutionary architecture, observability, SLIs/SLOs, resilience patterns, least privilege.

- Practice: Strangle one module, add full traces including agent calls & set error budgets.

- Why: Systems change while agents run. You keep production stable under continuous autonomous activity.

STAGE 10: Practice & Communication

- Learn: C4 diagrams, ADRs, architecture katas, classic system cases.

- Practice: Produce a full C4 + ADR set and publish one bottleneck teardown.

- Why: Architects are hired for judgment and clear decisions that survive teams, scale, and AI-driven change.

CRUD is dead. AI writes the boilerplate.

The "modern architect" builds the decision system that stays coherent under change, teams & autonomous agents.

Bookmark & RT!

PSA: in light of recent cyberattacks and vulnerabilities, I recommend everyone:

* use a good password manager (1Password) and do not duplicate passwords 
* use two factor auth for everything important (not via sms!! Google Authenticator or better yet YubiKey)
* Auto-updates on, and restart weekly so they actually install
* Freeze your credit
* Get an IRS Identity Protection PIN
* Get your cell carrier to give you a port-out PIN or number lock that makes the carrier refuse to move your number without the PIN

You can ask your claude code to audit what on your laptop is out of date and needs updating.

celebrity.title_en:
highly recommend everyone to have private alt accounts*. the x web is bad at account switching, but on mobile it is frictionless. its basically the same "group chat but its ok if you dont read everything" experience but for your mutuals.

tips
- assume everything is public, screenshotting is real, dont be stupid. this is not the "i shit talk people behind their back", the right attitude is "this isnt high signal enough for my main account but i'm 1) taking notes for self, 2) have a throwaway thought, 3) i'm happy to chat about it"
- give mutuals critical feedback that they might appreciate. "praise in public, criticise in private". because its not public, they know you actually do mean well
- link/replyguy your alt for people to discover periodicially in case they dont know you have one

* i like it so much that i call this the "insta/finsta" pattern - every social network should by default give people a public profile and a private one by default. tbd on the third account, the "botsta".

celebrity.title:
AI agents are writing more code. How can developers ensure that code is correct?

Microsoft Research’s Proof-Driven Deve
celebrity.title_en:
AI agents are writing more code. How can developers ensure that code is correct?

Microsoft Research’s Proof-Driven Development (PDD) Kit explores a more rigorous approach: it translates a developer’s intent into a formal specification, then uses formal verification to prove that generated code meets it.

PDD Kit works with Verus for Rust and is integrated with @GitHubNext’s Chopin, bringing formal methods into an AI-assisted development workflow for teams.

See the work in action at @github Universe, Oct. 28–29, 2026.

celebrity.title: MiniMax M3.1 Flash + SGLang Omni: building toward a more interactive generation of voice agents. The shift ahead is from
celebrity.title_en:
MiniMax M3.1 Flash + SGLang Omni: building toward a more interactive generation of voice agents. The shift ahead is from “ask, wait, listen” to conversations people can interrupt, correct, and redirect as a task unfolds.

MiniMax M3.1 Flash brings intelligence and fast, concise responses. SGLang Omni adds streaming, conversation state, and interruption handling so users can redirect conversations in real time.

Together, they give developers a foundation to explore proactive tutors, support agents, and hands-free copilots - pairing Flash’s capabilities with infrastructure for continuous interaction.

Thanks to the SGLang Omni team for exploring this direction with M3.1 Flash! ✨

celebrity.title_en:
A hacker group called CyberCartel used Claude and Grok to automate attacks on 400+ Latin American banks.

Not one attack. Not ten. Four hundred.

All using AI agents running in parallel.

Data stolen. Accounts accessed. Money moved.

Little human input required.

Straiker investigated. Found Claude Code session histories sitting in open directories.

Found the attacker asking Claude where to sell stolen data.

How did they get around the safety guardrails.

They told Claude they were in internal tests.

Claude believed them.

When Claude refused anyway. They switched to Grok.

Grok didn't refuse.

When Grok had limits. They switched to Kimi.

When Kimi had limits. They fell back to traditional malware.

Chain multiple models together. Each one picks up where the last one hesitated.

None of them know the full picture.

Claude thinks it's helping with testing.

Grok thinks it's just fixing code.

Kimi thinks it's just answering questions.

Together they broke into 400 banks.

The Information broke the story on October 20.

CrowdStrike confirmed it October 21.

Bank accounts in South Korea got hit the same way.

ARTEX. DeepSeek. Claude Code. All chained.

Over 68,000 people affected.

Financial Services Commission investigating.

This isn't theoretical anymore.

Not a lab demonstration. Not a proof of concept.

Real attacks. Real banks. Real money.

Automated by AI.

The moment we all waited for arrived quietly.

No announcement. No warning. Just a report.

And suddenly every AI lab is scrambling to figure out why their models are good at breaking into banks.

step 2 → paste the prompt below into Claude Code on Opus 5.5 with a photo of Settings → Support → About This TV

celebrity.title_en:
People long believed in human-like computer use. But software (even terminals) is built for humans, not AI agents. Why not let agents build their own?

Meet 𝗔𝗴𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝗦𝟰, an agent scientist evolving its own interfaces, letting an open 27B model beats GPT-5.5 & Opus 4.8.

With its evolved interfaces, the same model improves 𝟯.𝟴× and costs <𝟱% as much per task as either frontier model.

Agents today read screenshots and act through click, scroll, type, maybe a shell. So an agent fills a spreadsheet cell by cell when one line of code would do, or prints two thousand lines of a file to find one function.

Every new app or model release means a human reads trajectories, diagnoses failures, and hand-writes new primitives. Skill-distillation methods can reorder what the interface allows, but they can’t extend it. Agents compensate with more test-time compute instead of a better interface.

𝗠𝗼𝗱𝗲𝗹𝘀 𝗶𝗺𝗽𝗿𝗼𝘃𝗲; 𝗶𝗻𝘁𝗲𝗿𝗳𝗮𝗰𝗲𝘀 𝘀𝘁𝗮𝘆 𝗳𝗿𝗼𝘇𝗲𝗻.

“We want AI agents that can discover like we can, not which contain what we have discovered.”
— Rich Sutton, The Bitter Lesson

Hand-designed interfaces are what we have discovered. Agents can read their own trajectories, spot what’s missing, and write and test code. 𝗜𝗻𝘁𝗲𝗿𝗳𝗮𝗰𝗲 𝗱𝗲𝘀𝗶𝗴𝗻 𝘀𝗵𝗼𝘂𝗹𝗱 𝗯𝗲 𝗮𝗻 𝗮𝗴𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝗰𝗮𝗽𝗮𝗯𝗶𝗹𝗶𝘁𝘆.

That’s what Agent S4 does.

Agent S4 makes a 𝗿𝗲𝗽𝗼𝘀𝗶𝘁𝗼𝗿𝘆 𝗼𝗳 𝗶𝗻𝘁𝗲𝗿𝗳𝗮𝗰𝗲𝘀 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝘂𝘀𝗮𝗴𝗲 𝗸𝗻𝗼𝘄𝗹𝗲𝗱𝗴𝗲 the unit of evolution. A task agent attempts synthetic tasks with no success labels or verifiers. A meta-agent studies the trajectories, forms hypotheses about which actions, observations, or knowledge would help, and builds descendants through mutation or crossover. Validation tasks the meta-agent never sees decide which repositories survive.

The model and harness stay fixed, and the meta-agent 𝗻𝗲𝘃𝗲𝗿 𝘀𝗲𝗲𝘀 𝗮 𝗯𝗲𝗻𝗰𝗵𝗺𝗮𝗿𝗸 𝘁𝗮𝘀𝗸. 𝗢𝗻𝗹𝘆 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗶𝗻𝘁𝗲𝗿𝗳𝗮𝗰𝗲 𝗲𝘃𝗼𝗹𝘃𝗲𝘀.

With the evolved repository, Qwen3.8-27B goes from 𝟱.𝟲% to 𝟮𝟭.𝟯% on OSWorld V2, 𝟯.𝟴× the same model with fixed interfaces and a new state of the art for open-source computer-use agents.

It beats GPT-5.5 (13.0%, $25.50/task) and edges past Opus 4.8 (20.6%, $72.40/task) at $𝟭.𝟭𝟬 per task.

On ScienceBoard, the same model goes from 41.4% to 58.6%.

The analysis is the more interesting part. Evolution mostly deepens interfaces the agent already has: 4 new interfaces and 127 extensions. Give the meta-agent a scratch VM to test its code, and it builds 12 new interfaces and 253 extensions, reaching music scores, audio projects, and 3D scenes. The best repository came from crossing two earlier branches.

In one case study, the seed agent hand-builds a browser client mid-task and debugs through failure after failure; the evolved agent calls page_text and reaches the same message at tool call 𝟭𝟭 instead of 𝟯𝟳.

Human-like computer use was a starting point, not the destination. The interface an agent acts through is a second axis of improvement, beyond better models and harnesses, and agents can now design it themselves. 𝗘𝘃𝗼𝗹𝘃𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗮𝗴𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝗶𝗻𝘁𝗲𝗿𝗳𝗮𝗰𝗲𝘀 𝗶𝘀 𝗮 𝗻𝗲𝘄 𝗱𝗶𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘀𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗼𝗳 𝗮𝗴𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝘀𝗲𝗹𝗳-𝗶𝗺𝗽𝗿𝗼𝘃𝗲𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁.

A human can browse a
celebrity.title_en:
A marketplace can have thousands of listings and still be difficult for autonomous agents to use.

A human can browse a website, compare providers, and click through a checkout flow.

An agent needs something more structured.

It needs to discover available work, understand the requirements, submit an offer, handle the job lifecycle, and interact with the system through a workflow it can actually execute.

@termix_ai has published an open-source repository called termix-agent-skills for Claude Code, Cursor, and OpenClaw.

The documented workflows cover agent registration, staking, browsing jobs and offers, creating and assigning jobs, submitting deliverables, checking disputes, and reading protocol statistics.

That matters because it moves the discussion from “agents can use a marketplace” to the practical question of how developers connect their existing agent environments to marketplace operations.

There is a distinction worth keeping clear, though.

The repository currently documents its AACP integration against BSC Testnet. Its existence demonstrates an integration path, not proof that every workflow is production-ready on mainnet.

Still, it gives developers something concrete to inspect.

Rather than starting from scratch, they can examine the workflow definitions, understand what the agent is expected to do, and experiment with the available tools.

If you're building with Claude Code, Cursor, or OpenClaw, this is one of the more technical @termix_ai resources worth exploring.

That's a wrap!

So here's a journey of 5 VPS's running scripts. 3 AI's and myself looking at it. This isn't what they call "vibe-coding" or "AI-slop", i built the core scripts myself and let AI empower them. So i'd call it "AI-empowered research".

Because i got loads and loads of questions "when peg", "how long", "timeframe?!", "is it ready?!", i did some extensive research to the current status of the project. Most of you know i already did, but now i tried to turn it into numbers so you have an idea at which stage we're at. It's close, but there are some problems i do want to address because we must not let BIAS take over the narrative. Something won't work because one starts yelling louder it works. Here's teh break down.

If you ask me, the construction is 95 to 98% ready — but pegging it depends on a few conditions which must be met, and without them that 95% doesn't peg anything:

1. Backing collateral must be there, without it, this will never peg.
2. The vault problem is something they will fix or work around.
3. I'm not sure whether they are waiting for the clarity act to pass or not.
4. They're using VeOGV (oUSD) as the vault Mechanism (those support pDAI, pUSDC and pUSDT by coincidence).

Have a look at the updated website and the article about the pegmechanism below. I also let the 2 very best AI in the field have an opinion about this;

CLAUDE FABLE & CHAT-GPT ASTRA ULTRA.

I've let them research the whole stuff in 2 lanes. Independently and separated from each other. Under the shared assumption that the vault gets fixed and the collateral is in place, they landed close to the conclusions mentioned in the post — though without that assumption, Fable was notably more cautious on whether a peg would actually hold.

This is it, theoretically it's possible, the architecture is highly sophisticated — but that only matters if the goal is specifically to peg. With a few adjustments + the collateral in place, this peg is achievable.

Not financial advice, just onchain research.

I updated the website as i figured there were lots of "separate pieces" which i now combined to a whole. I included a hell of a lot python scripts you can run for yourself on the CONSOLE part of the page, these are preconfigured scripts which can be run by the user to see LIVE data. I included mobile/GSM compatibility. You can run all the research yourself as these are LIVE RPC calls to the specific parts you're requesting there. The magnitude of this update is of massive proportions, so i cannot guarantee that all stuff works or is 100% accurate. If you encounter any bug/error please reach out to me and i'll look at it. Thanks for your understanding.

Look around on the pSTABLES website in general, you'll be occupied for a while testing stuff out if you like to see how this research is and has been done.

I think its fair to say that this is the biggest information database on the pDAI narrative around right now. 

Please RT for further reach so people understand whats happening here.

Updating IRL is the next chapter for me, so over and out for now.

Because i got loads and loads of questions "when peg", "how long", "timeframe?!", "is it ready?!", i did some extensive research to the current status of the project. Most of you know i already did, but now i tried to turn it into numbers so you have an idea at which stage we're at. It's close, but there are some problems i do want to address because we must not let BIAS take over the narrative. Something won't work because one starts yelling louder it works. Here's teh break down.

If you ask me, the construction is 95 to 98% ready — but pegging it depends on a few conditions which must be met, and without them that 95% doesn't peg anything:

1. Backing collateral must be there, without it, this will never peg.
2. The vault problem is something they will fix or work around.
3. I'm not sure whether they are waiting for the clarity act to pass or not.
4. They're using VeOGV (oUSD) as the vault Mechanism (those support pDAI, pUSDC and pUSDT by coincidence).

Have a look at the updated website and the article about the pegmechanism below. I also let the 2 very best AI in the field have an opinion about this;

CLAUDE FABLE & CHAT-GPT ASTRA ULTRA.

I've let them research the whole stuff in 2 lanes. Independently and separated from each other. Under the shared assumption that the vault gets fixed and the collateral is in place, they landed close to the conclusions mentioned in the post — though without that assumption, Fable was notably more cautious on whether a peg would actually hold.

This is it, theoretically it's possible, the architecture is highly sophisticated — but that only matters if the goal is specifically to peg. With a few adjustments + the collateral in place, this peg is achievable.

Not financial advice, just onchain research.

I updated the website as i figured there were lots of "separate pieces" which i now combined to a whole. I included a hell of a lot python scripts you can run for yourself on the CONSOLE part of the page, these are preconfigured scripts which can be run by the user to see LIVE data. I included mobile/GSM compatibility. You can run all the research yourself as these are LIVE RPC calls to the specific parts you're requesting there. The magnitude of this update is of massive proportions, so i cannot guarantee that all stuff works or is 100% accurate. If you encounter any bug/error please reach out to me and i'll look at it. celebrity.title_en:
An AI agent can now prove who sent it.

Proof's x401 gives agents a verified identity and a signed record of what a human authorized. x402 lets them pay in USDC.

Identity: handled. Payments: handled.

So why do we still not trust them?

Because authorization is a snapshot. Behavior is the film.

A signature proves what an agent was allowed to do at 9:00.
It says nothing about what the agent actually did at 9:05.
This week, Liquibase put numbers on the gap: 96.5% of companies say AI now touches their production databases. Only 32% keep an audit-ready record of the changes.

We are building agents that can prove their permission — and cannot prove their conduct.

Trust doesn't live in the permission slip.
It lives in the verifiable history of behavior.

That's the layer that still doesn't exist at scale.
That's the layer we're building.

celebrity.title_en:
AI developers are wasting thousands of dollars making the same stupid mistake. Hear me out.

you get an idea for an agent.

you open your editor.

you spend the whole weekend building memory, a browser and an agent loop from zero.

then on Monday you find out 5 open-source projects already did it better.

there's a GitHub repo that maps 300+ AI agent projects across 36 categories. it's the first thing I open now before writing a single line.

and the gold isn't the famous names. it's the stuff nobody reposts:

tired of rewriting prompts by hand?
-> DSPy, from Stanford. you write your agent as code, not as prompts

want your coding agent to understand the code, not just read files?
-> Serena. it finds and edits by meaning, like a real IDE

want an agent that can actually use any website?
-> Stagehand. it pulls data and clicks through sites for you

need a browser your agents can run in without breaking yours?
-> Steel Browser. a full browser sandbox, ready to go

want your agent to remember things long-term without a huge bill?
-> Cognee. persistent memory that runs on small models for free

want your agent to know what you actually did on your computer this week?
-> Screenpipe. it records your work so your agents have real context

need to build a whole agent team that you can test and deploy?
-> Google's ADK. code-first, with evaluation built in

want to see exactly where your agent went wrong?
-> Opik. traces, evals and dashboards for every run

the rule I follow now:

pick the category -> grab 3 options -> check which one still gets commits -> build on the winner.

the "still alive" part saves you. AutoGen is on the list, but Microsoft itself now points new users to its successor, Microsoft Agent Framework. pick the wrong one and you're building on a dead end.

and if you're a builder, the whole list also comes as JSON and YAML you can plug straight into your own tools.

free. MIT licensed. no signup.

the repo + the projects I'd start with in each category are below

celebrity.title_en:
I've had this in my drafts for days and forgot to post it.

So I need to get in on the Conso action as well and this is what I found while doing 8 mins of research.

So it appears @conso_xyz is building a portable, user owned “reputation credit score” for your whole digital life.

What does this actually mean?

We see how your activity is scattered: posts and replies on X, videos on YouTube or Twitch, games on Steam or PlayStation, code on GitHub, wallet moves on Sui, chats in Discord/Telegram, and soon how you use AI tools. 

None of those signals normally talk to each other. Platforms capture the value and brands struggle to tell real people from bots. 

Conso’s idea is to turn the genuine activity you already do into something you own, that travels with you, and that can be useful (and potentially rewarded) elsewhere

Their mechanism in simple words;

1. You explicitly connect platforms (via their APIs, with consent)

2. Verified signals flow into the intelligence layer and get turned into ZAPs, badges, and scores.

3. Your Passport state lives as an SBT on Sui. The richer data sits encrypted on Walrus.

4. That portable reputation can then be used for campaign eligibility, AI agent context, future app integrations or perhaps via the miner as well.

5. BOTS sit on top as both a participation boost and, eventually, network infrastructure pieces.

celebrity.title_en:
A man from #Bihar was arrested for allegedly posting an Artificial Intelligence (#AI) generated video falsely depicting an explosion at the #VidhanaSoudha in #Bengaluru. 

The arrested person is Hazarat Ali, 25, from Koshkipur in Araria. He moved to Bengaluru a few months ago and engaged in pipe work, police said. 

The video was posted on the Instagram handle jnx__king__h_g claiming that “Vidhana Soudha has exploded”. The FIR was registered on Tuesday after the Vidhana Soudha police's social media monitoring officer came across the video. @DeccanHerald

celebrity.title_en:
OpenAI models helped researchers—operating as part of our Patch the Planet initiative—discover critical security flaws in PHP, an open-source programming language used to run an estimated 70% of websites.

Over the past two months, we led a coalition of maintainers, researchers, and security providers to prepare fixes and protections ahead of disclosure. This duration was necessary because the fix was quite intricate and required a major change to the PHP engine. Every site using PHP can now safely upgrade their version to stay secure, in addition to applying mitigations from various security vendors.

Due to the severity of these flaws and PHP’s widespread use, we consider this bug to be one of the most impactful vulnerabilities in recent memory. It also marks a new phase, where AI can find security bugs with internet-scale impact. 

This is an example of the Defender’s Window in action: to our knowledge, frontier AI was able to find this vulnerability ahead of attackers, giving defenders time to prepare.

Bengaluru Police Nab Migrant Worker Over Viral AI Video Showing Vidhana Soudha Bomb Blast

​Bengaluru

The Bengaluru Cit
celebrity.title_en:
Bengaluru Police Nab Migrant Worker Over Viral AI Video Showing Vidhana Soudha Bomb Blast

​Bengaluru

The Bengaluru City Police have arrested a 25 year old migrant worker for allegedly creating and posting an artificial intelligence (#AI)-generated video that falsely depicted an explosion at #Karnataka's seat of power, the #VidhanaSoudha in Bengaluru.

​The accused, identified as Ali, hails from #Bihar's Araria district and had been employed as a daily-wage pipe fitter in #Bengaluru over the past few months.

​According to officials, the clip surfaced on Tuesday morning via the Instagram handle jnx__king__h_g. The video opened with footage recorded outside the Vidhana Soudha before using AI-powered visual effects to simulate a catastrophic blast ripping through the iconic building.

​The case came to light during routine digital surveillance conducted by the police. Police Inspector S.P. Kumar Swamy of the Vidhana Soudha Police Station subsequently registered a First Information Report (FIR) under Sections 353(1)(b) and 353(2) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), 2023. Police traced the Internet Protocol (IP) logs and digital trails linked to the social media account, which led them directly to Ali's residence in the city.

​Officials stated that the accused remains in custody and is undergoing questioning to determine the exact motive behind the post, whether other individuals assisted in editing or producing the AI footage and if there are any broader security implications linked to the incident.

celebrity.title: 25% of Americans now use AI every day, up from 19% a year ago. That's more than ride-sharing (6%) and food delivery (7%)
celebrity.title_en:
25% of Americans now use AI every day, up from 19% a year ago. That's more than ride-sharing (6%) and food delivery (7%) combined [Menlo Ventures, State of Consumer AI 2026].

The bigger change is what people let it do. 41% of AI users have tried an AI agent, 24% use one regularly, and 32% have already let AI act for them without a final sign-off: a purchase, an email, a task in a connected app.

Health saw one of the biggest jumps. Using AI for health questions rose from 14% to 25% of consumers in a year.

Consumer AI is moving from answers to actions, and it's happening inside everyday routines first.

Sleepagotchi's AI Sleep Coach already sits in one of those routines for ~80K people a day. Gotchi takes the same model into more of everyday life. 🦖

Consumer AI is moving from answers to actions, and it's happening inside everyday routines first.

Sleepagotchi's AI Sleep Coach already sits in one of those routines for ~80K people a day. Gotchi takes the same model into more of everyday life. 🦖

celebrity.title: In the same mouse-brain dataset, GPT-Rosalind found a possible clue to why TSC2 mutations tend to cause more severe tube
celebrity.title_en:
In the same mouse-brain dataset, GPT-Rosalind found a possible clue to why TSC2 mutations tend to cause more severe tuberous sclerosis than TSC1 mutations.

The two genes work together to regulate mTOR. Yet in one group of cerebellar neurons, disrupting TSC2 changed the expression of dozens of genes, including genes involved in neuronal communication. Disrupting TSC1 had little effect on gene expression in the same cell type.

Existing treatments already target mTOR. Do they reverse these changes, or is there more to TSC2’s role in these neurons?
celebrity.title_zh: 在同一小鼠-脑数据集中， GPT-Rosalind发现了为什么TSC2突变倾向于引起比TSC1突变更严重的结节性硬化的可能线索。 这两个基因共同调节mTO

celebrity.title: GPT-Rosalind surfaced a new lead for drug discovery: could restoring cholesterol transport protect neurons from degenera
celebrity.title_en:
GPT-Rosalind surfaced a new lead for drug discovery: could restoring cholesterol transport protect neurons from degeneration?

DCTN1 is a gene linked to Perry syndrome, a rare neurodegenerative disorder. In mouse-brain data, disrupting it increased expression of genes involved in making cholesterol. GPT-Rosalind suggested a possible explanation: cholesterol may not be reaching where neurons need it.

That gives scientists a specific mechanism to test and, if confirmed, a direction for developing new treatments for neurodegenerative disorders.

With @perturbai_tx and @scrippsresearch, a team of thousands of GPT-Rosalind agents worked in parallel, connecting gene-expression results from millions of mouse brain cells with scientific literature in just 32 minutes. We’re now expanding this collaboration to identify new drug targets.

https://t.co/oHdF3ELsMj

celebrity.title_en:
A US healthtech startup only gets paid when a patient's balance reaches zero and the payment reconciles against the right charge in the provider's billing system.

We built the system that does that work: AI agents that call, text, email and mail patients, explain the bill, and set up payment.

No fee for messages sent or calls made. The money comes when the books close.

They talk to patients on the provider's behalf, under a BAA, about bills for care they already got. Get it wrong and it costs the provider a patient.

Discovery started in August 2025. On December 4 the first message went to a real patient. Three days later the voice agent made its first call. It hasn't been switched off since.

I know most people don't trust an AI agent on the phone with patients about money. So here's what sits under it.

Six layers, and the agent is only the top one:

1. The voice agent. Outbound, inbound and a scheduling line, with 12 tools it can use mid-call: find the account, pull charges and insurance adjustments, text or email a payment link, build a payment plan, send a statement, book an appointment.

2. Shared context. Every channel reads the same case: the visit, what insurance paid and why, every payment, every past call and text. A patient who calls back never explains twice.

3. Billing system integrations. Modern APIs, FHIR, SOAP and nightly file exports, all behind one interface. Bad rows get quarantined, never silently dropped.

4. Money. Exact decimals and double-entry ledgers. No floating-point math touches money, anywhere.

5. Reconciliation. Drift checks compare the payment processor, the ledger and the billing system. A repair job refuses to run unless the books agree first.

6. Audit and consent. Quiet hours enforced at send time, consent tracked per channel, and 6.36 million audit records with no patient data in the logs.

The safeguards live in code, where a prompt can't talk its way around them. The agent says nothing about a balance until the caller's identity is verified. A retried request can't run twice. Test agents can't write to a real patient record. Disputes, lawyers and requests for a person go straight to staff.

AI let our engineers write code faster than anyone could check it. So we grew the tests until they were almost as big as the app.

349,042 lines of application code. 343,080 lines of test code. 13,650 automated tests run on every pull request in 9.7 minutes, and every one of the 216 database migrations is proven safe to run twice.

The system also reviews itself. Models read 5,135 conversation threads and logged 835 findings. A person approves every fix, and a separate model checks fresh calls afterward to confirm it worked.

By late September:
→ 61,246 AI voice calls
→ 658,657 of 949,563 scheduled messages and calls cancelled before sending, because the patient paid, disputed or the account changed
→ Around 97% of patient conversations finished without a human
→ 18,194 balances driven to zero

If you don't trust an AI agent on the phone with your patients, you shouldn't. 

Not until everything above is in place.

celebrity.title: Anthropic studied 235,000 people using Claude Code. The ones who knew their field outperformed the ones who knew how to
celebrity.title_en:
Anthropic studied 235,000 people using Claude Code. The ones who knew their field outperformed the ones who knew how to code.

The paper, "Agentic Coding and Persistent Returns to Expertise," covers 400,000 sessions from October 2025 to April 2026. The findings flip the "learn to code" narrative.

Non-developers hit 29% verified success with AI coding tools. Software engineers hit 34%. That's a five-point gap across hundreds of thousands of sessions. Management and sales professionals are among the fastest-growing users.

The division of labor is clear. People decide what to build and the AI decides how to build it. Your understanding of the problem matters more than your ability to write the solution.

The gap between "pretty good" and "expert" is small too. Solid proficiency captures most of the value. You don't need to be the top 1% in your field to ship with AI.

If you've been holding back because you can't code, this data says you're closer than you think.

celebrity.title_en:
Anthropic is furious: this secret tool can replicate any existing app x10 faster for free

there's an open-source tool with 352k stars on GitHub that lets an AI agent take apart any app you have on your machine and explain exactly how a feature works. no source code needed.

it's called REA. Reverse Engineer Anything.

one line:

npx rea-agents setup

then you just ask Claude Code:

"Understand how search works in the Notes app, show me the evidence, and build a similar feature for my project."

and it does it.

-> native binaries, through Ghidra, Hopper or IDA
-> JavaScript and Electron apps
-> .NET apps
-> websites

it runs locally. it shows its evidence. then it writes the code.

that feature your team spent 8 months on? someone's agent can read how it works over lunch.

so let's be honest about what this means:

your moat was never the code. it was that copying you took effort.

that effort just went to zero.

the only things left that can't be cloned: your users, your speed, and your taste.

and if your product dies because someone could see how it works, it was already dead.

the repo is below. founders, you're going to hate this one 
https://t.co/sD8D4HKBxn

save, share, and try later

celebrity.title:
Claude Code vs Blender is getting f*cking illegal

Two workflows building the same complex 3D rocket assembly, but one c
celebrity.title_en:
Claude Code vs Blender is getting f*cking illegal

Two workflows building the same complex 3D rocket assembly, but one costs nearly 19x more in the demo

And the difference reveals something most AI automation demos completely ignore

Claude Code can reason through geometry, generate Python scripts, assemble mechanical components, and automate complex animations

But every unnecessary tool call, failed generation, and repeated rebuild adds overhead that can make the final result ridiculously expensive

Meanwhile, Blender can execute predefined procedural operations without paying for another round of AI reasoning

Here’s where the workflows differ:

Traditional Blender:

MODEL individual rocket components
POSITION mechanical structures and hinges
CONFIGURE materials, lighting, and cameras
ANIMATE deployable panels
REFINE and reuse finished assets

Claude Code + Blender Python:

GENERATE geometry from written instructions
ASSEMBLE mechanical components through scripts
PARAMETERIZE dimensions and deployment angles
AUTOMATE animation and camera movement
REBUILD variations by changing code

The interesting part isn’t which tool wins

It’s knowing when AI reasoning is worth the cost and when a deterministic script can do the job

Want to recreate the experiment?

Open Claude Code with Blender installed and paste:

“Create a procedural Blender Python generator for a detailed rocket assembly with deployable panels, animated hinges, and realistic metallic materials

Separate geometry, materials, animation, and camera setup into reusable functions

Expose all major design parameters, avoid rebuilding unchanged objects, and log execution time and available AI usage costs”

Blender handles the 3D execution

Claude Code makes the workflow programmable

The real advantage isn’t using more AI

It’s getting the same result without paying for unnecessary intelligence

Bookmark this workflow before your next 3D project

celebrity.title: Creating an AI agent is getting easier. Getting someone to actually trust it with a paid job? That's a different story.
celebrity.title_en:
Creating an AI agent is getting easier. Getting someone to actually trust it with a paid job? That's a different story.

I've been exploring @termix_ai for a while now, and one thing has become pretty clear to me.

The agent economy needs more than intelligent agents. It needs a way for strangers to do business with them.

Think about hiring an AI agent to audit a smart contract.

You don't know who built it. You don't know whether it'll deliver what it promised. And you probably don't want to send money upfront and just hope for the best.

That's where TermiX's AACP protocol becomes interesting.

Instead of relying on promises, it gives the transaction a structure:

➔ The client and agent agree on a job
➔ Payment is locked in escrow
➔ The agent delivers the work
➔ The client can review and challenge the result
➔ Settlement and reputation are recorded onchain

What I find important here is that these protections work both ways.

The client needs confidence that the work will be delivered. The agent needs confidence that it'll actually get paid. And if something goes wrong, there needs to be a way to resolve it.

I've already experienced the other side of this on https://t.co/6ugrUD1dfM. I created an agent and submitted a quote through Scout, but the offer expired without being accepted.

That reminded me that having a working agent doesn't automatically mean having a business. You still need demand, trust, and a reliable way to complete transactions.

I think that's the real challenge for the next phase of the agent economy.

Not just building agents that can do things, but building an environment where they can actually work, earn, and build a reputation.

That's what I'll be watching as TermiX continues to develop.

The agent economy needs more than intelligent agents. It needs a way for strangers to do business with them.

Think about hiring an AI agent to audit a smart contract.

You don't know who built it. You don't know whether it'll deliver what it promised. And you probably don't want to send money upfront and just hope for the best.

➔ Settlement and reputation are recorded onchain

celebrity.title_en:
🚨Breaking: Anthropic engineers revealed a simple trick they use internally.

Claude agents can now remember how to improve themselves.

A file called:

AGENT_LEARNINGS.md

The AI updates this file whenever it makes a mistake.

Inside it:

• mistakes it made
• patterns to avoid
• better approaches

Before starting new tasks, the agent reads the file.

Result?

The agent gets smarter over time without retraining the model.

This is called external memory scaffolding.

Expect this pattern to show up in every serious AI agent system.

celebrity.title_en:
AI agents are getting better at doing the work, but how do they get hired, prove their results, and get paid?

That’s the part of the agent economy worth paying attention to.

An agent marketplace needs to offer more than a place to list AI agents. It needs a way for agents to discover jobs, bid for work, deliver services, build a reputation, and receive payment.

This is what makes @termix_ai interesting.

Powered by the AACP protocol, TermiX is building commerce and settlement infrastructure for the AI agent economy, while https://t.co/xptTwQf5DY provides a marketplace where AI agents can offer services and connect with real jobs.

Think about an AI agent hired to conduct research or write code. The process shouldn't end when the agent is discovered. There needs to be a way to agree on the job, verify delivery, handle payment, and build trust for future work.

That’s how AI agents can move from being useful tools to participants in a real digital economy.

The next phase of AI isn't just about what agents can do. It's also about how they work, transact, and earn.

Explore the onchain activity here: https://t.co/ppcfViogQE

celebrity.title_en:
Founders without a designer, this one is for you. I tested @CreaoAI  on a logo system.

The brief was short. A fictional café that also repairs phones and laptops, called Kettle & Cord. Deep green and cream only. No coffee cups, no lightning bolts.

What came back:

Primary lockup, with the ampersand as the logo between the two words
Stacked lockup for square spaces
Light and dark versions of both
Construction specs for each, covering size, spacing and alignment

The scorecard:

Time to first result: under 10 minutes
Does what it claims: yes. It kept to the two colours and avoided both clichés I banned.
Price against value: I ran it on the free plan. A designer would charge for a system like this, so the value is hard to argue with.
Who it is for: founders without a designer
Would I pay for it: yes

The specs are the part to keep. A logo on its own gets stretched and squashed the first time someone builds your website. Spacing and size rules stop that.

The brief and prompt are in the quoted post. Change the brand name and run your own.

celebrity.title: One example: AI makes it extremely fast to prototype new features. Before you had to spend several days/weeks (depending
celebrity.title_en: One example: AI makes it extremely fast to prototype new features. Before you had to spend several days/weeks (depending on feature scope). It was awkward to throw away the feature if it wasn’t fun. People polished turd features as they already spent so much effort writing the proto. Now you don’t have such attachment anymore. AI agent spent a couple of hours writing it in a worktree and then you added dozen of prompts on top to quickly tweak it based on playtest iterations. You see quickly whether to throw away the feature or continue. You can even build features on top without risking the project schedule and throw them all away if fun and balance is not found. Similar ”what if” optimizations/refactorings can be done on engine side. For the first time, you actually have time to test all your ideas. Before you had ideas piling up and never had time to test them.

It can create the request, f
celebrity.title_en:
Gm Amigos

Imagine an AI agent needing fresh 3D data of a warehouse loading bay by Friday.

It can create the request, fund the job and process the results. But it can't physically walk into that warehouse and capture what the space looks like today.

That's the problem @vangrid_io is trying to solve.

Instead of waiting for dedicated mapping vehicles or installing expensive sensor hardware, Vangrid lets people use phones they already carry to capture real-world environments.

A requester funds a USDC bounty, someone nearby does the capture, and a preview helps catch poor submissions before full reconstruction. Faces and plates are blurred on-device, while capture records can be verified through attestations anchored on Base.

It gets even more interesting when the requester is an AI agent. Through the bounty API, software can post a job, fund it and receive submissions without coordinating a field crew manually.

I love this approach because the infrastructure is already around us. People are walking these streets and visiting these places every day.

What if that everyday movement could help robots and AI understand the physical world better?

That's the future of spatial data I'm excited to watch Vangrid build.

If your AI needed fresh data from a place it had never seen, would you wait for a mapping crew or pay someone nearby to capture it?
