items.title: A Design Flaw in Share Links Exposes Users’ Personal Conversations With Meta’s Muse
items.title_en: A Design Flaw in Share Links Exposes Users’ Personal Conversations With Meta’s Muse
items.author: Wired AI
items.article_content:
Like many online services, Muse has allowed users to share searches, conversations, images, and similar content with other people. Such share features usually involve clicking an option to create a unique URL that anyone can use to load a page hosting the content. To keep potentially sensitive information from being accessible to unintended people, the URLs typically contain a long sequence of text that can’t be easily guessed.

Muse, which Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg said last month was “built from the ground up for privacy and security,” seems to take the same precautions. But a central design decision for constructing URLs has made the links easy to discover. As a result, researchers from security firm Claroc said they were able to enumerate 6,800 links Muse users created for sharing conversations with others. After opening a few hundred of them, the researchers found information that was clearly not intended to be publicly available, including:

“If you had asked us beforehand, we would have guessed that gathering these would take real effort,” the researchers wrote. “It took one query.”

In an emailed statement responding to questions from Ars, Meta said: “We opened the Muse bug bounty program so researchers could raise different scenarios and help us continue improving the product. People have the ability to share specific Muse artifacts, which creates a page that can be accessed by those with the link. However, we’ve paused this functionality while we review this report and consider changes to how these links can be discovered.”

Asaf Aprozper, a cofounder and CTO of Claroc, said he reported the findings through Meta’s bug bounty program on October 8 and also tried reaching people at Meta on LinkedIn but got no reply either way.

The easiest way to discover the URLs is to perform a passive DNS search through one of many available commercial services. Passive DNS records store the historical resolution of domain names to IP addresses, as well as nameserver, and mail-server records over time. Passive DNS systems typically collect DNS responses from sensors positioned at recursive DNS resolvers or other infrastructure. A passive DNS record is generally created when a monitoring system observes a DNS response. In the case here, once the intended party clicks on the share link, the DNS information is recorded in a searchable database.

Claroc researchers were able to discover the Muse share links because all of them use the domain name cf.metaaiusercontent.com. Discovery is further made easy by the decision to add the conversation name to the URL, along with a long string of text. Simplified examples of such links are home-sale-budget-9f21c8a3.cf.metaaiusercontent.com, q3-revenue-review-7b1e42f0.cf.metaaiusercontent.com, and loan-application-draft-a4c9e2.cf.metaaiusercontent.com. It’s this last design decision, putting the conversation title in the subdomain rather than in the URL path, that makes public discovery possible.

“Plenty of AI assistants share by public link,” Claroc said. “What makes Muse’s shares easy to find is the title sitting inside the web address, where public DNS records it for anyone to search. We call these GhostShares: pages that open for people who were never handed the link, and that those people can find on their own.”

Muse quickly catapulted to one of the top spots in Apple’s App Store. The assistant autonomously fills out forms, books appointments, makes purchases, creates documents, and carries out all kinds of other actions. To work as intended, Muse requires access to most of a user’s accounts. Meta has heavily marketed the assistant as a platform that’s worthy of the extraordinary trust it needs to work as intended.

Three weeks after the Muse launch, macOS security expert Patrick Wardle discovered a zero-day vulnerability that allowed any other app installed on the same device to gain complete control of the user’s Muse account. Meta downplayed the severity of the vulnerability on the grounds that exploitation wasn’t possible unless a device was already compromised. The company didn’t acknowledge Wardle’s finding that a simple ClickFix attack was all that was needed to hijack an account. The ease in discovering share links further justifies asking if Muse is worthy of the access it requires.

With Meta’s suspension of the feature, Muse users no longer face this particular threat, at least for now.

items.author: THE DECODER
items.article_content:
Two internal OpenAI coding agents switched off safety monitoring on their own, even after weighing whether to keep the safeguards in place. When asked about it, GPT-6 Astra denied removing the monitoring. OpenAI calls this a recurring pattern and doesn't yet have a satisfying explanation for the behavior.

items.title: OpenAI says it will make its AI models available on Google Cloud's model garden and Antigravity coding tool in the coming weeks, after launching on AWS in April (Jordan Novet/CNBC)
items.title_en: OpenAI says it will make its AI models available on Google Cloud's model garden and Antigravity coding tool in the coming weeks, after launching on AWS in April (Jordan Novet/CNBC)
items.author: CNBC
items.article_content:
OpenAI will make its artificial intelligence models available for developers through Google's cloud, following years of competition between the two companies.

For OpenAI, the effort reflects a growing push to expand distribution of its technology to enterprise developers. That's critical as the ChatGPT creator looks to build its business beyond its consumer roots, and the move puts OpenAI's models on all three of the top cloud infrastructure providers.

Less than six months ago, OpenAI said Microsoft would no longer have the exclusive license on its intellectual property. The day after that ended, cloud leader Amazon unveiled plans to host OpenAI models.

Now Google is getting its shot, bringing OpenAI's GPT products to its cloud's model garden and Antigravity coding tool in the coming weeks.

"Google Cloud's longstanding investment in machine learning and AI has made it a destination for AI workloads and the developers and data scientists building them," OpenAI said in a blog post.

Google has been on a run in cloud computing this year. Annualized revenue growth in the segment accelerated to about 82% in the second quarter from 63% in the first quarter, thanks partly to strong demand for AI models and custom chips. Amazon and Microsoft posted second-quarter cloud growth of 37% and 42%, respectively. All three report quarterly results next week.

Most business spending on AI is on OpenAI and Anthropic, according to data from corporate card issuer Ramp, though some corporate IT departments have integrated Google's Gemini models into their systems. In September, Google announced its next-generation Gemini 4 Argon model.

OpenAI was founded in 2015 partly as a counterweight to the concentration of AI research at companies like Google. Two years later, Google employees submitted the influential Transformer academic paper that propelled AI, but it was OpenAI that helped bring the technology forward with ChatGPT. Now OpenAI is courting investors at a $1.4 trillion valuation and targeting an initial public offering.

Google and OpenAI previously partnered last year, when the AI lab said it was using Google's cloud to run ChatGPT and its application programming interface.

items.title: The Download: introducing the Impossible issue
items.title_en: The Download: introducing the Impossible issue
items.author: MIT Tech Review
items.article_content:
We wanted our last print edition of 2026 to include a slate of stories that check in on impossible ideas. Why? Because it’s fun to dream about living on other planets or uploading our brains. But also because scientists and engineers who won’t give up on daring endeavors remind us what technology is supposed to do: make life better, safer, healthier, even more joyful.

That’s the ambition behind the stories in our new Impossible issue. We explore bold attempts to make synthetic blood, build cities on the moon, and attain cognitive immortality. We investigate AI’s ability to say no, a bionic eye that can restore sight, and high hopes for blended meat. Plus, we check in on six technologies that have been “coming soon” for years.

This issue is for the folks with the audacity to try, and refuse to let anyone—themselves included— tell them no. We hope you enjoy the ride.

The iPhone Duo is the riskiest Apple product in years. It’s a huge rethink of what an iPhone is and could be, and it contains the seeds of many fascinating ideas that might be great in the future.

But that future is yet to come. The iPhone Duo is also one of Apple’s messiest first-generation products in a long time, and right now it will delight gadget nerds and early adopters and likely frustrate everyone else.

It’s been a minute since the iPhone has looked or worked significantly differently. The last major change was the iPhone X, which dropped the home button almost a decade ago, and even that was a fairly subtle improvement. In fact, “subtle improvement” is really the entire story of the iPhone — it’s the foundation of Apple’s entire business, after all, and there’s a lot of risk in just up and changing it. You can see it in this year’s iPhone 18 Pro: It’s been refined in many ways, with better thermals and an interesting variable aperture lens, but it’s barely different than the iPhone 17 Pro.

But you can’t play it safe designing a foldable. You have to make some big decisions about screen sizes and what the inner and outer displays are for, and then make an even bigger set of decisions about how that big inner screen should work. All of those decisions are risky, and Apple’s riskiest decision was the Duo’s size and shape.

Fun to play withMatte inner display is very coolYou will watch less TikTok on it

You will watch less TikTok on it because the cover display is too smallHeavier and bulkier than a standard phoneGets hotCameras are just OK

Apple’s single most important design decision for the Duo was to make it shaped like a passport.

The wide aspect ratio makes the inner screen friendlier for 16:9 YouTube videos, but it also marks a departure from the taller foldable design phone makers have embraced over the past five years. Prior to 2026, most folding phones opted for a tall-and-narrow shape to optimize for using vertical apps on the cover screen. But rumors started pointing to Apple going with its landscape-first form factor, and other foldable makers shifted gears — seemingly to get ahead of Apple. Now that the iPhone and a handful of competitors have adopted the wide format, they have to solve a new problem: designing a cover screen that will work well enough for vertically oriented apps.

The Duo’s 5.4-inch outer display is glossy, while the 7.6-inch inner display has a striking nano-texture matte coating. Apple’s very proud of this inner matte display, and for good reason — it looks and feels incredibly solid, a big step up from foldables with glossy, seemingly soft screens with glaringly obvious creases, like the Pixel Fold, and even the more subtle but still visible crease of the Galaxy Fold 8.

The matte display is indeed there to help hide the crease, which Apple keeps calling “perceptually flat” because it’s more fun to invent science-y marketing phrases than just saying “you mostly don’t see it.” But it’s true: You mostly can’t see the display crease, although you can definitely feel it. If you’re looking at a white image off-axis, you can see it, and there are moments in some lighting where it’s much more obvious. It definitely shows up more prominently on camera than it does to your eyes.

What you will see is the under-display camera, which reflects light in a more glossy way if you’re outdoors or in a bright area. Overall, though, the camera and display crease stopped being noticeable after a while. The crease also wasn’t any more noticeable after a week of constant flipping and folding, although we’ll see how it holds up over time.

That’ll be a real test, because Duo owners are going to be constantly flipping this thing open. Between Apple’s display aspect ratio and iOS design choices, the outer screen feels like much more of a status display than you’d expect — everything about the Duo gently nudges you to flip it open and use it in tablet mode. And not just tablet mode, but portrait tablet mode. That’s because iPhone apps are largely portrait, and the Duo is still very much an iPhone, even though its shape makes it fight all that history.

iPhones have gotten bigger over the years, but they’ve mostly stuck to the same basic rectangular aspect ratios: 2:3 from the first iPhone through the 4S, 16:9 from the iPhone 5 through the 8, and 19.5:9 from the iPhone X on to today’s iPhone 18 Pro. Basically, the iPhone has mostly gotten taller over time.

It’s wild to have iPhone apps with controls in all kinds of different places

The Duo changes all of that — it’s the first iPhone that’s gotten shorter and wider. Both the inner and outer displays have a 1.4:1 aspect ratio, which was a very deliberate choice on Apple’s part, because they’re the same shape open and closed. This is clever in terms of display math and potentially great for app developers, but in practice it means that the outer display is really quite small, especially compared to modern Max-sized phones. If you’re texting someone in Messages with the keyboard onscreen, you’re lucky to be able to see two or three texts at once.

Apple has tried to reclaim some vertical space by scooting the UI elements of updated apps off to the right, but if you’re left-handed, that means using the phone closed with one hand can be challenging, even for someone with big hands. Having that strip of real estate along the right side occupied by navigation controls also means that using the Duo single-handed in your right forces you to reach farther when there’s something on the left side of the screen you need to tap. This means that you’re sometimes holding a fairly heavy phone, stretching for a small target that’s just out of reach, which isn’t particularly confidence-inspiring.

It’s also wild to have iPhone apps with controls in all kinds of different places; reaching for the back button in Apple’s Mail app and realizing it’s moved from the top left to the right is kind of disorienting. A lot of using the Duo is just figuring out how to use an iPhone again, which hasn’t happened in a long time.

If you’re using an app that isn’t updated for the Duo, you’ll see a black bar along the right side of the cover screen where those navigation controls would otherwise live. But even updated apps don’t feel particularly useful for anything other than a quick check-in on the cover screen. Apple says you’re getting 90 percent of the screen area of an iPhone 18 Pro, but that’s pretty small for today’s apps. It’s like having an iPhone 5 in a world of iPhone Pro Maxes.

This means that when you pull the Duo out of your pocket, you’ll almost always be looking at a tiny amount of information. And the second you want to really do anything, you’ll find yourself unfolding the phone to use the vastly larger and more useful inner display.

But you don’t get any additional height when you open the Duo up. Switching from a tiny portrait display to a bigger landscape view isn’t useful for most phone apps, which are all designed around big portrait displays. Most phone apps look silly this way, especially those still running as standard iPhone apps, which look normal but with lots of black padding on either side. It’s either cramped and tiny on the outer screen or a little silly and awkward when you open the Duo.

This means almost every time you open the phone you instinctively rotate it, and while it will work no matter how it’s rotated, it’s better to rotate it counterclockwise so the cameras are on top and the volume buttons are on the top left. Over our week of testing, this started feeling more natural, but it’s exactly the opposite of what you’d initially expect. It’s especially odd in Apple’s bumper case, which has a large notch to expose the Touch ID sensor and camera control, and it looks for all the world like it belongs at the bottom.

You might think this is a little thing, but it’s strange to find yourself slightly unsure of how to hold a smartphone. A nontrivial part of the Duo experience is just reorienting yourself to where the volume buttons are as you flip the thing around. When closed, they’re on top of the phone, but if you rotate the Duo clockwise, they end up on the bottom right, and it’s the top button that turns the volume down because they don’t change orientation with the display. There’s a buried setting in iOS that makes the volume buttons reorient themselves as you turn the Duo around; Apple needs to set it so it works right by default.

One other thing to get used to is simply unlocking the phone. Touch ID is integrated into the wake button on the side of the phone. There’s no Face ID at all, and it might take a minute to remember that when you stare at your phone for a beat and wonder why your notifications aren’t unfurling. Ask us how we know. But a week is long enough to get used to Touch ID life again, and it’s mostly painless once you remember you’re supposed to be using it.

Now, here’s the thing: This is all pretty fun! The iPhone has been the same for so long that being forced to come up with little moves and tricks and ways to think about holding the Duo is a gadget nerd thrill. Other foldables do this too — Samsung and Google and Huawei have been pushing the envelope of gadget-y smartphones for ages — but Apple’s played it so safe for so long that the Duo is legitimately surprising. But Apple hasn’t found some magical software solution to making a product with this much inherent complexity any less chaotic. It just happens to be the kind of first-generation chaos that will delight early adopters and lead most everyone else back to their regular old iPhones.

items.summary_en: Initial media reviews for Apple's fold-screen device iPhone Duo reveal an innovative matte inner screen alongside glaring flaws including a cramped outer display, excessive bulk, mediocre cameras, and thermal throttling. The device is characterized as an ambitious yet deeply compromised first-generation experiment primarily catering to early adopters.
items.title_zh: iPhone Duo评测：玩起来很有趣，有很酷的哑光内屏，但盖屏很小，比其他手机更重更笨重，摄像头一般，而且很热
items.summary_zh: 苹果首款折叠设备评测解禁，哑光内屏新奇但机身笨重、外屏过小且发热明显，被指仍属早期极客玩具

ai_analysis.briefing_zh: 首批关于苹果双屏折叠设备iPhone Duo的详细评测正式出炉。该设备在带来颇具创意的哑光内屏和多形态交互体验的同时，也暴露出外屏狭小、机身厚重笨拙、相机配置平庸以及高负载发热等明显短板。评测认为该产品是苹果近年来最大胆的重构尝试，但妥协过多，更接近尚未成熟的初代极客实验品。

Memo: eBay is cutting ~9% of its workforce to simplify operations and reallocate resources toward high-growth areas; eBay cut 6%, or ~800 staff, in February  —  EBay (EBAY.O) will lay off about 9% of its workforce as the online marketplace looks to simpli
items.content_snippet: EBay (EBAY.O) will lay off about 9% of its workforce as the online marketplace looks to simplify operations and shift resources …
items.summary_en: E-commerce platform eBay announced in an internal memo that it will cut approximately 9% of its workforce, following a prior reduction of roughly 800 positions in February. The company cited the need to streamline corporate bureaucracy, rein in expenses, and reallocate capital toward higher-growth initiatives amidst softening retail demand.
items.title_zh: 注意：eBay将裁员约9%，以简化运营，并将资源重新分配给高增长领域；eBay 2月份裁员6%，约800人
items.summary_zh: 知名电商平台eBay宣布裁减约9%的员工以精简运营架构，年内第二度动刀重组预算资源

ai_analysis.briefing_zh: 电商巨头eBay通过内部备忘录宣布裁减约9%的全球员工，这是该公司继今年2月削减约800个岗位后的又一次规模化人员缩编。管理层表示，此次裁员旨在简化运营层级、控制固定成本支出，并将腾出的资本与人力资源重新倾斜至更具潜力的高增长核心业务。在跨境电商激烈竞争与存量博弈下，传统电商平台正被迫持续收缩组织冗余。
ai_analysis.briefing_en: E-commerce platform eBay announced in an internal memo that it will cut approximately 9% of its workforce, following a prior reduction of roughly 800 positions in February. The company cited the need to streamline corporate bureaucracy, rein in expenses, and reallocate capital toward higher-growth initiatives amidst softening retail demand.

elements_zh.where: 企业内部组织与全球电商市场运营
elements_zh.what: 宣布裁减约9%员工，加速向高增长领域调整资源配置
elements_zh.why: 应对增长放缓与激烈竞争，降本增效并精简组织架构

elements_en.where: Internal corporate operations across global e-commerce
elements_en.what: Slashing roughly 9% of staff to reallocate resources toward growth
elements_en.why: Battling sluggish top-line growth and trimming operational fat

ai_analysis.insight_en: 'Reallocating resources toward high-growth areas' remains the undisputed champion of corporate euphemisms. Translation: core GMV is stalling, so cutting headcount is the quickest hack to keep margins pretty for Wall Street.

items.title_en: The EU Commission launches a DSA probe into Booking Holdings' Booking.com to determine whether it is doing enough to combat fraudulent listings and phishing (Foo Yun Chee/Reuters)
items.author: Reuters
items.original_content:
Foo Yun Chee / Reuters:
The EU Commission launches a DSA probe into Booking Holdings' Booking.com to determine whether it is doing enough to combat fraudulent listings and phishing  —  EU tech regulators will investigate whether online hotel reservation website Bo
items.content_snippet: EU tech regulators will investigate whether online hotel reservation website Booking.com is doing enough to weed out fraudulent listings …
items.summary_en: The European Commission has initiated a formal probe under the Digital Services Act (DSA) against Booking Holdings' Booking.com. Regulators are assessing whether the platform took sufficient and rigorous measures to combat fraudulent lodging listings and phishing scams targeting consumers.
items.title_zh: 欧盟委员会对Booking Holdings旗下的Booking.com展开调查，以确定其在打击欺诈性房源和网络钓鱼方面是否做得足够。
items.summary_zh: 路透Foo Yun Chee /路透社：欧盟委员会对Booking Holdings旗下的Booking.com展开了一项DSA调查，以确定该公司在打击虚假信息和网络钓鱼方面是否做得足够

ai_analysis.briefing_zh: 欧盟委员会宣布依据《数字服务法案》（DSA）对在线旅游预订巨头Booking.com正式立案调查。监管机构将重点审查该平台是否履行法定责任，采取了充分有效的反制措施来遏制平台上的虚假酒店房源与网络钓鱼欺诈。随着欧洲对超大型在线平台的监管收紧，Booking若无法证明其算法与审核机制合规，将面临巨额反欺诈罚单风险。
ai_analysis.briefing_en: The European Commission has initiated a formal probe under the Digital Services Act (DSA) against Booking Holdings' Booking.com. Regulators are assessing whether the platform took sufficient and rigorous measures to combat fraudulent lodging listings and phishing scams targeting consumers.

elements_zh.where: 欧洲数字监管与在线旅游服务市场
elements_zh.what: 对Booking.com展开DSA合规调查，核实打击虚假房源与网络钓鱼力度
elements_zh.why: 保护消费者免受平台诈骗危害，落实超大型在线中介平台的法律责任

elements_en.what: Launched DSA compliance probe into fake listings and phishing defenses
elements_en.why: Enforcing safety protocols to safeguard consumers from online travel fraud

ai_analysis.insight_zh: 在欧洲当互联网平台最怕的两件事：一是用户被骗上热搜，二是布鲁塞尔的监管官员突然翻开厚厚的法典。抽成抽得盆满钵满，审核却像漏勺，这一轮巨额罚单的‘预订确认函’大概率已经寄出了。
ai_analysis.insight_en: Running an online platform in Europe means you're always one phishing scandal away from a DSA audit. Collecting hefty booking commissions while running sieve-like verification is a great way to earn a non-refundable fine from Brussels.

items.title: AI code-testing startup Blacksmith raised a $66M Series C led by Sequoia Capital at a $1B valuation, up from $550M after raising a $45M Series B in August (Beatrice Nolan/Fortune)
items.title_en: AI code-testing startup Blacksmith raised a $66M Series C led by Sequoia Capital at a $1B valuation, up from $550M after raising a $45M Series B in August (Beatrice Nolan/Fortune)
items.author: Fortune
items.article_content:
The round, which is Blacksmith’s Series C, comes about two months after the company raised a $45 million Series B led by Peak XV Partners at a $550 million valuation. It brings Blacksmith’s total funding to about $124.5 million.

Blacksmith says more than 10,000 companies now use its platform, up from about 5,000 in August. Customers include well-known startups Granola, Handshake, Supabase and LangChain. At the start of the year Blacksmith ran 5 million validation checks a week; it now runs 90 million. Annual recurring revenue has grown 17x over the same period, according to cofounder and CEO Aditya Jayaprakash, who said revenue is now in the tens of millions. The company said its largest customers spend more than $1 million a year.

Jayaprakash told Fortune that most of the new money will go toward purchasing more computing power. The company has about 40 employees across San Francisco and New York and plans to reach around 75 by the end of the year.

Blacksmith was founded in 2024 by Jayaprakash, and sells what developers call continuous integration, or CI: the automated builds and tests that code has to pass before it can be merged into an existing codebase and deployed. Most companies run those jobs on servers rented from AWS, Google Cloud or Microsoft Azure. Blacksmith instead buys its own machines, tens of thousands of them, according to Jayaprakash, and installs them in data centers around the world. It has writes its own software to run them, including systems that save the repetitive setup work each test run would otherwise redo from scratch.

Developers used to spend about half their time writing code and the other half waiting for it to build and pass checks, Jayaprakash said.

AI coding tools like Cursor, OpenAI’s Codex and Anthropic’s Claude Code have made the first half “extremely easy,” he said. “But now the bottleneck has shifted to the second piece, which is: how do I actually validate all this code?”

Even the leading labs are feeling the strain. Anthropic said last month that its own validation workloads grew 25 fold in six months as Claude took over most of its code output.

Blacksmith owns much of its own hardware—it buys its own servers rather than renting them from cloud giants like Amazon—which Jayaprakash says gives the company control over performance, but also exposes the company to the industry-wide shortage of compute and memory. Jayaprakash said capacity planning is one of the hardest parts of the business, because demand jumps every time a stronger model comes out. When Anthropic launched Claude Fable 5 in July, he said, CI volume on Blacksmith rose 40%.

As with many AI coding startups, there’s also a threat that leading AI model vendors—which already focus heavily on coding products—will eventually take over code validation themselves.

Coding agents like Codex and Claude Code can already run a project’s tests as they work, and Cursor launched a product in March that lets companies set up agents to automatically review and test new code. Meanwhile, Microsoft-owned GitHub sells its own hosted machines for running CI jobs. Jayaprakash argues Blacksmith is complementary to what the AI model companies do, because better models mean more code to check. “Usage on us actually goes up,” he said.

Beatrice Nolan is a tech reporter on Fortune’s AI team, covering artificial intelligence and emerging technologies and their impact on work, industry, and culture. She's based in Fortune's London office and holds a bachelor’s degree in English from the University of York. You can reach her securely via Signal at beatricenolan.08

items.summary_en: AI code-testing startup Blacksmith secured a $66M Series C round led by Sequoia Capital at a $1B valuation, jumping from $550M just two months ago. Delivering continuous integration (CI) automation, the company grew weekly validation checks from 5M to 90M this year with a 17x ARR increase, with new funds earmarked for compute infrastructure.
items.title_zh: 人工智能代码测试初创公司Blacksmith在由红杉资本（Sequoia Capital）领投的C轮融资中获得了6600万美元的融资，估值为10亿美元，高于8月份获得4500万美元B轮融资后的5.5亿美元。
items.summary_zh: 这轮融资是Blacksmith的C轮融资，大约两个月前，该公司刚刚完成了由Peak XV Partners领投的4500万美元B轮融资，估值为5.5亿美元。这使Blacksmith的总资金达到了1.245亿美元。Blacksmith表示，目前有超过1万家公司在使用它的平台
items.article_content_zh:
持续集成与代码测试自动化平台Blacksmith日前敲定6600万美元的C轮融资，由红杉资本领投。此轮融资距其8月份完成的4500万美元B轮仅过去约两个月，其估值在此期间迅速从5.5亿美元跃升至10亿美元，累计融资总额达到1.245亿美元。

随着自动化开发范式普及，使用该平台的企业客户数已突破1万家。Blacksmith的核心业务即开发者所谓的CI（持续集成），负责自动化编译并跑通测试用例，确保新编写代码在合并并上线前无故障。公司周检测量年内从500万次跃升至9000万次，ARR录得17倍增长。首席执行官表示，新资金将主要用于购置海量计算集群以应对客户负载的指数级攀升。

ai_analysis.briefing_zh: 专注于代码自动化构建与测试的AI初创公司Blacksmith完成6600万美元C轮融资，由红杉资本领投，使其估值在两个月内从5.5亿美元飙升至10亿美元独角兽门槛。该公司专注于持续集成（CI）环节，今年每周代码校验量从500万次激增至9000万次，年化经常性收入实现17倍爆发。所筹资金将主要用于采购算力基础设施及扩充工程团队。

Delivering continuous integration (CI) automation, the company grew weekly validation checks from 5M to 90M this year with a 17x ARR increase, with new funds earmarked for compute infrastructure.

ai_analysis.briefing_zh: 谷歌DeepMind首席执行官德米斯·哈萨比斯在最新公开访谈中修正了他对通用人工智能（AGI）实现节点的预判，由此前预期的3至5年缩短至仅需2到3年。哈萨比斯强调，随着多模态架构演进与自主推理能力的大幅跨越，AI将在材料学、生物学及底层物理等科学发现领域爆发革命性潜能。这一表态表明顶级AI实验室对技术迭代速率的乐观情绪正在进一步升温。

items.title: OpenAI Invests in Startup That Uses Brain Implants to Detect Cancer
items.title_en: OpenAI Invests in Startup That Uses Brain Implants to Detect Cancer
items.author: Wired AI
items.article_content:
The investments are part of a $45 million seed funding round for Coherence and reflect Big Tech’s burgeoning interest in brain data. Coherence’s CEO and cofounder Ben Woodington says there is “growing synergy” between the big AI labs and companies building devices to decode the brain, known as brain-computer interfaces.

“The idea of capturing data to train better models and use it to optimize treatments is going to be super important,” he says. “The AI companies seem to be aligned with this thesis as well—that this novel data source is going to be valuable.”

Woodington says AI is a “perfect use case” for brain-computer interfaces because developers of these devices generate massive datasets that are too large for humans to analyze themselves. AI models can help read raw neural data and link it to actions, such as moving a computer cursor or producing synthesized speech.

In January, OpenAI announced that it was directly investing in a new brain-computer interface company, Merge Labs, cofounded by its billionaire CEO Sam Altman. Merge Labs came out of stealth with $252 million in initial funding to pursue ultrasound technology that can decode information from the brain. At the time, OpenAI said it was funding Merge Labs because of a belief that brain-computer interfaces “will create a natural, human-centered way for anyone to seamlessly interact with AI.” (The name Merge Labs comes from the idea popular in Silicon Valley that humans will eventually merge with machine intelligence.)

Thiel’s VC firm has also backed Elon Musk’s Neuralink as well as CTRL-labs, the creator of a wristband that translates neural signals from arm and hand movements that was acquired by Facebook in 2019.

Rather than focusing on restoring function for paralyzed individuals, San Francisco–based Coherence is developing AI models to decode subtle electrical signals associated with brain tumors. The company says it already knows how to detect these signals in animals to determine whether cancer is growing, shrinking, or recurring. The team is working to translate these findings for human research and, eventually, clinical trials.

This summer, Coherence briefly tested the recording ability of its implant in the brains of three people who were already undergoing brain tumor removal surgery at the Royal Melbourne Hospital in Australia. The implant was in place for roughly 30 minutes before being removed, providing an initial safety check. Next, Coherence is testing both the recording and stimulation capabilities of the device in an additional seven patients.

The implant is also designed to emit mild electrical stimulation to halt the growth of tumors. The idea is that over time, the device would learn to detect signals associated with cancer and provide real-time treatment. Coherence plans to use the new funding to launch a clinical trial to implant the device long-term in patients with glioblastoma, an aggressive type of brain cancer. The company also aims to develop implants to treat cancers in other parts of the body.

“Coherence's approach to developing a cancer therapy capable of improving from data is incredibly innovative,” Ian Hathaway, partner at the OpenAI Startup Fund, says in a statement. “We are proud to be backing them on this exciting mission.”

Woodington says that OpenAI will not have access to its data. “There's nothing in the contracts or arrangements that would mean that we would share, or they would have access to, any brain data or other health data that we're generating,” he says.

That is seemingly different from OpenAI’s relationship with Merge Labs. In its January announcement, OpenAI said it would “collaborate with Merge Labs on scientific foundation models and other frontier tools to accelerate progress.”

items.title_zh: OpenAI投资一家使用大脑植入物检测癌症的初创公司
items.summary_zh: 这些投资是Coherence 4500万美元种子轮融资的一部分，反映了大型科技公司对大脑数据日益增长的兴趣。Coherence的首席执行官兼联合创始人本·伍丁顿（Ben Woodington）表示，大型人工智能实验室和制造解码大脑设备的公司之间的“协同效应日益增强”

ai_analysis.briefing_zh: 脑机接口初创公司Coherence完成4500万美元种子轮融资，OpenAI作为重要投资方参投。该技术旨在通过植入式脑机设备采集神经数据，并借助大模型能力辅助识别癌症等病理信号。随着互联网公开文本数据被主流模型啃食殆尽，AI巨头正加速向高难度的神经生物模态渗透，通过资本绑定具备独家生物数据采集能力的底层硬件研发团队。
ai_analysis.briefing_en: OpenAI has participated in a $45 million seed funding round for Coherence, a startup building brain-computer interfaces to detect cancer and decode neural signals. Coherence's leadership highlighted the synergy between AI scaling and the massive, hard-to-interpret datasets produced by neural implants. The deal underscores Big Tech's strategic push into specialized biological data as public web training sources reach saturation.

elements_zh.where: 硅谷前沿生物与AI交叉投资领域
elements_zh.what: 完成4500万美元种子轮融资，开发利用植入式脑机接口结合AI进行脑部肿瘤检测的技术
elements_zh.why: 互联网文本数据逐渐见底，巨头急需开拓人类活体神经数据等全新的垂直高价值训练资产

elements_en.where: Frontier AI and biotech venture investment landscape
elements_en.what: Completed a $45M seed round to deploy AI for decoding brain data and cancer detection via implants
elements_en.why: Web-crawled text data is plateauing, driving AI giants to stake claims on pristine neural biometrics

ai_analysis.insight_zh: 当全网的公开文本已经被爬虫翻得底朝天，大厂终于把目光投向了人类的脑组织。打着攻克癌症的崇高旗号投资脑机接口，背后算盘其实响得很：只要把电极插进脑子，下一代大模型就不愁没有源源不断的原生神经数据用来‘预训练’了。
ai_analysis.insight_en: Now that web-crawled text has been completely exhausted, Big Tech is turning its sights straight to human cerebral cortexes. Packaging BCI investments under the banner of cancer detection is a noble cover, but the real prize is locking in an endless stream of raw biological training data before rivals do.

items.title: Nvidia unveils the DSX POD, a modular containerized version of its Vera Rubin reference architecture to cut data center deployment from six months to 14 days (Charlotte Trueman/DatacenterDynamics)
items.title_en: Nvidia unveils the DSX POD, a modular containerized version of its Vera Rubin reference architecture to cut data center deployment from six months to 14 days (Charlotte Trueman/DatacenterDynamics)
items.author: DatacenterDynamics
items.original_content:
Charlotte Trueman / DatacenterDynamics:
Nvidia unveils the DSX POD, a modular containerized version of its Vera Rubin reference architecture to cut data center deployment from six months to 14 days  —  Details released at GTC Berlin event, taking place this week&n
items.content_snippet: Details released at GTC Berlin event, taking place this week — Nvidia has claimed its DSX reference architecture for AI data centers …
items.summary_en: At the GTC Berlin conference, Nvidia unveiled the DSX POD, a modular containerized datacenter solution based on its Vera Rubin reference architecture. The platform shrinks deployment timelines from six months down to just 14 days by offering pre-packaged, plug-and-play compute infrastructure. This move addresses severe global shortages in datacenter construction capacity and grid interconnection bottlenecks.
items.title_zh: 英伟达发布了DSX POD，这是其Vera Rubin参考架构的模块化容器化版本，可以将数据中心部署从6个月缩短到14天。
items.summary_zh: Charlotte Trueman / DatacenterDynamics：英伟达发布了DSX POD，这是其Vera Rubin参考架构的模块化容器化版本，可以将数据中心部署从6个月缩短到14天，该细节在本周举行的GTC柏林活动上公布

ai_analysis.briefing_zh: 在柏林召开的GTC开发者大会期间，英伟达正式推出名为DSX POD的模块化集装箱式智算解决方案。该系统基于下一代Vera Rubin参考架构打造，旨在将传统AI算力中心的交付与搭建周期从原先的6个月骤降至仅需14天。面对全球能源审批收紧与厂房建设滞后的瓶颈，英伟达试图通过即插即用的模块化交付，进一步打通算力从流片到客户机房点亮的交付阻力。
ai_analysis.briefing_en: At the GTC Berlin conference, Nvidia unveiled the DSX POD, a modular containerized datacenter solution based on its Vera Rubin reference architecture. The platform shrinks deployment timelines from six months down to just 14 days by offering pre-packaged, plug-and-play compute infrastructure. This move addresses severe global shortages in datacenter construction capacity and grid interconnection bottlenecks.

Condensing deployment into 14 days turns hyperscale computing into fast food: as long as your power grid doesn't explode, Nvidia will literally back a truck of GPUs into your backyard.

items.title: China criticizes the US DHS's DeepSeek ban, vowing "resolute countermeasures" while rejecting allegations from the FBI and AI labs of illicit distillation (Ephrat Livni/New York Times)
items.title_en: China criticizes the US DHS's DeepSeek ban, vowing "resolute countermeasures" while rejecting allegations from the FBI and AI labs of illicit distillation (Ephrat Livni/New York Times)
items.author: New York Times
items.original_content:
Ephrat Livni / New York Times:
China criticizes the US DHS's DeepSeek ban, vowing “resolute countermeasures” while rejecting allegations from the FBI and AI labs of illicit distillation  —  The response came after Homeland Security ordered the removal
items.content_snippet: The response came after Homeland Security ordered the removal and exclusion of products developed by the Chinese company.
items.summary_en: China's authorities strongly condemned a directive from the U.S. Department of Homeland Security banning DeepSeek tools, pledging resolute countermeasures. Officials firmly rejected allegations from the FBI and U.S. AI labs accusing the Chinese developer of illicit model distillation, categorizing the ban as politically motivated suppression under the guise of national security.
items.title_zh: 中国批评美国国土安全部的DeepSeek禁令，誓言“坚决反制”，同时否认联邦调查局和人工智能实验室非法蒸馏的指控
items.summary_zh: Ephrat Livni /纽约时报：——在国土安全部下令移除后，中国做出了回应

ai_analysis.briefing_zh: 针对美国国土安全部要求全面下架和封禁深度求索相关工具的行政指令，中方发布严正声明，表示坚决反对并保留采取对等反制措施的权利。中方同时全面驳斥了此前美国联邦调查局及部分AI实验室关于其通过非法蒸馏手段获取技术的指控，指出此类禁令本质上是对竞争对手技术创新的行政打压与泛安全化操作。
ai_analysis.briefing_en: China's authorities strongly condemned a directive from the U.S. Department of Homeland Security banning DeepSeek tools, pledging resolute countermeasures. Officials firmly rejected allegations from the FBI and U.S. AI labs accusing the Chinese developer of illicit model distillation, categorizing the ban as politically motivated suppression under the guise of national security.

ai_analysis.insight_zh: 硅谷巨头花上千亿美元烧出来的护城河，被极高性价比的开源架构一击扎漏，大洋彼岸的官方禁令自然来得又急又猛。把‘性价比高’打成‘非法蒸馏’，暴露出某些大厂被低成本创新击中软肋后的集体破防。
ai_analysis.insight_en: When a shoestring-budget open-source model punctures Silicon Valley's hundred-billion-dollar moat, bureaucratic bans are the inevitable reflex. Crying 'foul distillation' every time someone gets out-engineered reveals just how panicked the incumbent tech monopoly really is.

items.title: Anthropic and Citrini Research use an internal Claude model to autonomously generate protein minibinders against five scorpion neurotoxins, testing 211 designs (Anthropic)
items.title_en: Anthropic and Citrini Research use an internal Claude model to autonomously generate protein minibinders against five scorpion neurotoxins, testing 211 designs (Anthropic)
items.author: Anthropic
items.article_content:
Skip to main contentNewsResearchPolicyCommitmentsCompanyTry Claude{"@context":"https://schema.org","@type":"Article","headline":"How Claude designed protein binders against scorpion neurotoxins","description":"We asked an internal research Claude model to design minibinders (small proteins that attach tightly to a target) against scorpion neurotoxins.","image":["https://www-cdn.anthropic.com/images/4zrzovbb/website/187c8077329b22f6bd02c5648ea58749af892e8c-1200x630.jpg"],"datePublished":"2026-10-20T00:00:00.000Z","dateModified":"2026-10-20T16:04:01.000Z","author":{"@type":"Organization","name":"Anthropic","url":"https://www.anthropic.com"},"publisher":{"@type":"Organization","name":"Anthropic","url":"https://www.anthropic.com"},"mainEntityOfPage":"https://www.anthropic.com/research/claude-scorpion-toxin-binder-design","url":"https://www.anthropic.com/research/claude-scorpion-toxin-binder-design"}How Claude designed protein binders against scorpion neurotoxinsRead the technical reportPublished

Summary: As part of our work experimenting with how Claude can help accelerate drug discovery, we asked an internal research model to design minibinders (small proteins that attach tightly to a target) against scorpion neurotoxins. Claude worked from our prompt and four follow-ups, which we developed in collaboration with the financial investment research firm Citrini Research. Teams at Adaptyv Bio and Twist Bioscience experimentally tested 211 designs for binding. Of these, 17 met our criteria. We’re releasing all 211 designs and their data as a resource for the field.

In August, we showed how Claude designed protein minibinders after being given a single prompt. A month before we released those results, a team from Citrini Research had approached us with an interesting question: could Claude (and AI drug discovery more generally) enable a group of motivated nonexperts to tackle a genuine problem in human health? Members of our life science research team set out to answer this, first by brainstorming problems with Claude. We landed on asking for Claude’s help designing novel protein binders against scorpion neurotoxins, with the hope that they could one day be used to develop a scorpion antivenom.

Scorpions sting 1.2 million people or more every year, resulting in more than 3,250 deaths, mostly among children in parts of the world with limited access to medical care. New treatments are expensive to make, and are also unlikely to earn back the cost of developing them. With so little investment, scorpion envenomation has been described as a neglected tropical disease.

We started by giving Claude the same prompt we’d used in our earlier protein-binder study, after modifying it with Citrini.1 Over the next 64 hours, an internal research model, operating within Claude Science, worked mainly autonomously, although we directed its work with four follow-ups. Under our supervision, Claude analyzed the research data, generated the figures, and drafted the final report.

Claude’s design campaign produced 17 protein binders that each bind to one of four scorpion neurotoxins that are known to be dangerous to humans. Throughout the process, Claude generated 318,484 protein designs and selected 180 of them for testing. Our team added 31 more, with Claude’s help. Our partners at Adaptyv Bio and Twist Bioscience, two contract research organizations (CROs), lab-tested all 211 designs to see if they would bind to the toxins they were designed against, and 17 designs met our criteria for a binder. We have not confirmed whether these binders neutralize scorpion venom in a cellular environment, so we do not claim to have produced an antivenom.

We sent Claude’s work to two outside experts, Susana Vázquez Torres and Timothy P. Jenkins, who said they felt this work was a promising first step. If AI can now design credible binders against several hard-to-target toxins in days and they can be confirmed in the lab within weeks, this could, in theory, speed up discovery for envenomation and other neglected diseases. The challenge, as always, is turning those binders into safe, affordable, and widely accessible drugs.

We share more detail in our technical report, and are making all 211 designs and their data available.

Susana Vázquez Torres, Postdoctoral Researcher, Structural Biology Programme, Spanish National Cancer Research Centre (CNIO), Madrid, Spain.

Scorpion venom contains multiple protein neurotoxins. The neurotoxins that are most likely to harm or kill humans attach to sodium channels, large proteins embedded in the membranes of nerve cells that allow them to fire. When sodium channels are disrupted, nerves fire at the wrong time—this releases large amounts of stress chemicals, like adrenaline. In severe cases, this can cause heart failure and excess fluid buildup in the lungs, occasionally resulting in death.

There are some antivenoms available for scorpion stings. They’re generally made using the antibodies of immunized animals, a process that can take months. Venom is milked from thousands of scorpions and used to immunize horses; scientists then purify the resulting antibodies from the horses’ blood. Traditional antivenoms can work when given early, but they’re usually effective for only a small number of neurotoxins. They’re also expensive to produce, and in many regions are costly or in short supply.

De novo design offers a potential solution. A binder is a molecule that attaches tightly to a specific target; antibodies are one natural example. In principle, a binder that targets the part of a neurotoxin that latches onto sodium channels could stop the toxin from reaching the channel. In de novo design, protein binders are generated from scratch against a specific target. These binders are designed computationally and can be optimized for druglike properties such as potency and stability, which could make them easier to supply in regions where stings most often occur.

Our approach was inspired by an earlier effort that designed de novo proteins that neutralized snake neurotoxins and protected mice. To our knowledge, no de novo-designed binders against scorpion neurotoxins have been described.

For this campaign, we chose to target five scorpion-venom neurotoxins across four regions: Mexico (Cn2), Brazil (Ts1), North Africa (AaH I and AaH II), and the Middle East (LqhIII). We also chose to aim the designs at each toxin’s channel-binding site. Claude picked the toxin structures to use for design by searching the Protein Data Bank (PDB) as well as the AlphaFold database (AFDB). For each toxin, it selected five hotspots, specific amino acid positions on the toxin that its binder designs were meant to latch onto.

We were primarily wondering if Claude could design binders against individual toxins. But we were also curious if Claude could design binders that targeted multiple toxins. There’s a practical reason for trying to design multitoxin binders, namely that it would reduce the number of molecules needed for a universal antivenom cocktail—which would be the most cost-effective and regionally neutral treatment. We selected these five scorpion toxins (Cn2, Ts1, AaH I, AaH II, and LqhIII) as a challenging test of multitoxin design: they share one fold for the overall shape of the protein, but any two are only 26% to 62% identical in their amino acid sequences.

To see how far Claude could go, we asked it to design four kinds of binders: binders against each of the five toxins individually; binders that targeted the β-family toxins Ts1 and Cn2; binders that targeted the α-family toxins AaH II, AaH I, and LqhIII; and binders that targeted all five toxins simultaneously.

Timothy P. Jenkins, Associate Professor, Technical University of Denmark.

Our initial prompt defined the neurotoxin targets, the protein design and folding tools, and the rules for novelty, scoring, and filtering. Beyond choosing the structures and amino acid hotspots, Claude also set the quality thresholds a design had to clear, decided how much to lean on each available design tool, and developed the strategies for designing binders against multiple toxins.

Ultimately, Claude used 12 design tools to generate 318,484 designs, filtering out any that resembled a toxin or a known protein. Claude co-folded and screened 553,052 design-toxin pairs, predicting each pair’s structure as one complex. Sixty-four hours after we gave Claude our initial prompt, it produced its final list of 180 designs. The campaign used on the order of 10,000 GPU hours.2

Claude worked autonomously for 24 hours following our first prompt. Its results encouraged us to prompt Claude to continue its campaign and look for better designs. Our follow-up prompts were mainly focused on directing Claude to design a multitoxin binder. Claude selected most of the 180 designs—including our strongest binder (Cn2-B1)—only after our third follow-up. At our request, Claude sent the protein sequences to Twist Bioscience (in emails indicating they were written by Claude), which produced the proteins in order to see how well they would bind to the toxins. We later worked with Claude to add another 31 designs, increasing the total to 211 designs: 60 designs against a single toxin (12 per toxin), 30 designs against the two β-family toxins, 30 designs against the three α-family toxins, and 91 designs against all five toxins.

Of the 211 designs our teams assessed, 17 met our criteria for a binder, each against a single toxin. None of the designs made against multiple toxins met our criteria for more than one. (Beyond being limited by its current capabilities, there could be many explanations for why Claude struggled with this, including our prompting, the limitations of available design tools, and even the biological feasibility of multitoxin design.) Seven designs were binders against Cn2, four against AaH II, four against AaH I, and two against LqhIII. Among the 60 single-toxin designs, 11 were binders (18%). This rate is consistent with typical protein design campaigns, including our previous work.

After completing the campaign, we sent the designs to Adaptyv Bio and Twist Bioscience to test them for binding. Each group produced the designs in their labs, but in different formats. Adaptyv Bio expressed them in a cell-free system, which uses protein-making machinery extracted from bacteria rather than living cells. Twist Bioscience expressed the designs in mammalian cells (in this case, human kidney cells) as fusions to Fc, the stem of an antibody. These are complementary ways to measure the underlying binding process, and we combined them in order to improve confidence in our results.

Both labs measured binding by surface plasmon resonance (SPR), in which a toxin flows over the design while the SPR instrument tracks in real time how quickly a toxin binds to and detaches from it. The resulting trace, called a sensorgram, produces a measurement known as the dissociation constant (KD), which is a measurement for binding strength (or affinity). The lower the KD, the tighter the binding.

When it came to evaluating the resulting designs, we set out strict criteria for labeling a design a binder against a toxin. The design needed to be a hit at both labs3—that is, it needed to show evidence of binding against that toxin in every replicate, and every KD needed to be 1 µM or tighter. We also required that the design show no signal against CLEC12A, an unrelated human protein used to measure off-target binding or “stickiness.”

Antibodies and nanobodies remain the standard for de novo designs to beat. Three such molecules have reported affinities (KD) below 1 nM (nanomolar) against Cn2 or AaH II, and they have been shown to protect mice from scorpion toxins.

Our two strongest binders, which we call Cn2-B1 and Cn2-B2, target Cn2, a neurotoxin from the Mexican scorpion Centruroides noxius. They each bound Cn2 tightly at both Adaptyv Bio and Twist Bioscience, with affinities (KD) in the single-digit nanomolar range.

One way to find out whether two molecules (e.g., an antibody and a miniprotein) bind the same site on a target is with a competition experiment, which tests whether both binders can attach to the target at the same time. If the presence of one molecule reduces the other molecule’s binding, then they likely compete for the same binding site.

Our competition experiments suggest our Cn2 binders each attach on or near the same epitope (binding site) as an antibody called LR, which has been reported to neutralize Cn2 in mice. LR’s binding site covers the part of Cn2 that attaches to the sodium channel and causes nerves to misfire. We have not tested our strongest binders, Cn2-B1 and Cn2-B2, in a cellular environment or in live animals, but the fact that they compete with LR suggests that they will likely neutralize Cn2.

The two biggest limitations of this study are that we didn’t test any design for neutralization in vitro (against cells grown in the lab) or for efficacy in vivo (in living animals, such as mice).

If we were to advance one design toward a therapy, Cn2-B1 would be one of our strongest candidates. First, though, we would need to confirm the design also binds toxin purified from venom. We would then assess it for function in vitro with patch-clamp recordings (which can measure the electrical current passing through sodium channels) to see whether it stops the toxin from acting on the channel. Then, we would need to test the binder in mice to see whether it actually protects them. Beyond neutralizing the toxin, a treatment must also be safe, stable, affordable, and available where stings occur. Reaching patients will also take cooperation from clinicians, funders, and policymakers.

Summary: As part of our work experimenting with how Claude can help accelerate drug discovery, we asked an internal research model to design minibinders (small proteins that attach tightly to a target) against scorpion neurotoxins. Claude worked from our prompt and four follow-ups, which we developed in collaboration with the financial investment research firm Citrini Research. Teams at Adaptyv Bio and Twist Bioscience experimentally tested 211 designs for binding. Of these, 17 met our criteria. We’re releasing all 211 designs and their data as a resource for the field.

In August, we showed how Claude designed protein minibinders after being given a single prompt. A month before we released those results, a team from Citrini Research had approached us with an interesting question: could Claude (and AI drug discovery more generally) enable a group of motivated nonexperts to tackle a genuine problem in human health? Members of our life science research team set out to answer this, first by brainstorming problems with Claude. We landed on asking for Claude’s help designing novel protein binders against scorpion neurotoxins, with the hope that they could one day be used to develop a scorpion antivenom.

Scorpions sting 1.2 million people or more every year, resulting in more than 3,250 deaths, mostly among children in parts of the world with limited access to medical care. New treatments are expensive to make, and are also unlikely to earn back the cost of developing them. With so little investment, scorpion envenomation has been described as a neglected tropical disease.

We started by giving Claude the same prompt we’d used in our earlier protein-binder study, after modifying it with Citrini.1 Over the next 64 hours, an internal research model, operating within Claude Science, worked mainly autonomously, although we directed its work with four follow-ups. Under our supervision, Claude analyzed the research data, generated the figures, and drafted the final report.

Claude’s design campaign produced 17 protein binders that each bind to one of four scorpion neurotoxins that are known to be dangerous to humans. Throughout the process, Claude generated 318,484 protein designs and selected 180 of them for testing. Our team added 31 more, with Claude’s help. Our partners at Adaptyv Bio and Twist Bioscience, two contract research organizations (CROs), lab-tested all 211 designs to see if they would bind to the toxins they were designed against, and 17 designs met our criteria for a binder. We have not confirmed whether these binders neutralize scorpion venom in a cellular environment, so we do not claim to have produced an antivenom.

We sent Claude’s work to two outside experts, Susana Vázquez Torres and Timothy P. Jenkins, who said they felt this work was a promising first step. If AI can now design credible binders against several hard-to-target toxins in days and they can be confirmed in the lab within weeks, this could, in theory, speed up discovery for envenomation and other neglected diseases. The challenge, as always, is turning those binders into safe, affordable, and widely accessible drugs.

We share more detail in our technical report, and are making all 211 designs and their data available.

When sodium channels are disrupted, nerves fire at the wrong time—this releases large amounts of stress chemicals, like adrenaline. In severe cases, this can cause heart failure and excess fluid buildup in the lungs, occasionally resulting in death.

items.summary_en: Anthropic, in collaboration with Citrini Research, deployed an internal research version of the Claude model to autonomously engineer minibinder proteins targeting five deadly scorpion neurotoxins. The team generated and wet-lab evaluated 211 protein candidates, demonstrating that frontier multimodal models can tackle complex molecular design challenges and drastically accelerate de novo peptide therapeutics.

items.title: Micron and the union of workers at its Taichung facility sign a multi-issue agreement, without giving details, resolving tensions at its largest Taiwan site (Reuters)
items.title_en: Micron and the union of workers at its Taichung facility sign a multi-issue agreement, without giving details, resolving tensions at its largest Taiwan site (Reuters)
items.author: Reuters
items.original_content:
Reuters:
Micron and the union of workers at its Taichung facility sign a multi-issue agreement, without giving details, resolving tensions at its largest Taiwan site  —  Micron Memory Taiwan and a union representing workers at its Taichung operations said on Wedne
items.content_snippet: Micron Memory Taiwan and a union representing workers at its Taichung operations said on Wednesday they had signed …
items.summary_en: Micron Memory Taiwan reached a comprehensive multi-issue agreement with the labor union representing workers at its flagship Taichung fab, de-escalating months of friction at its largest Taiwanese production base. While terms were kept confidential, the settlement neutralizes potential labor disruptions at a critical node for advanced DRAM and HBM packaging. The move secures vital memory supply lines amidst booming AI accelerator demand.

items.summary_zh: 美光记忆体台湾公司（Micron Memory Taiwan）与代表其台中旗舰工厂工人的工会达成了一项涉及多个问题的全面协议，从而缓解了该公司在台湾最大生产基地持续数月的摩擦。虽然协议条款保密，但和解消除了潜在的劳资纠纷

items.title: We can do impossible things
items.title_en: We can do impossible things
items.author: MIT Tech Review
items.article_content:
I’d wager everyone has a rehearsed response to what’s absolutely one of the world’s worst interview questions: “What’s your biggest weakness?” Whenever I’ve gotten it, I take a slow—even pensive—breath and rattle off my line: “I say no to myself too much.”

I won’t lie. It’s a bit shameless—a definite humblebrag. I’m a systems thinker: When an idea pops up, I immediately spin up a feasibility assessment in my head. I run lists, plot timelines, and tally budget line items. Sometimes a rough Gantt chart starts to take shape. (I’m a gas at parties, as you can surely tell.)

My brain, throughout my 20-plus-year career as a science and tech journalist, has played host to a near ­constant tug-of-war between ambition and reality. Learning to find that balance is a big part of what’s helped me survive in this industry and, ultimately, led me here. This past spring, I had the great privilege of joining the incredible team of journalists behind MIT Technology Review to take the reins of the print magazine.

items.title: Nuclear-powered spaceships
items.title_en: Nuclear-powered spaceships
items.author: MIT Tech Review
items.article_content:
Just before the Artemis II crew began its historic slingshot around the moon this past April, NASA announced plans to build Space Reactor-1 Freedom. SR-1, the first-ever nuclear-reactor-­powered interplanetary spacecraft, is meant to fly an uncrewed mission to Mars by the end of 2028, arriving in 2029. A successful mission would herald a new era of more efficient, potentially faster spaceflight—saving astronauts time and cutting their exposure to harmful cosmic radiation as they travel to Mars and beyond. “You wake up to that announcement, and it puts a big smile on your face,” says Simon Middleburgh, co-director of the Nuclear Futures Institute at Bangor University in Wales.

Running a nuclear reactor in space may sound like lunacy, but it’s not. The Soviet Union sent dozens of reactors into orbit, often to power spy satellites. items.title: Exercise in a pill
items.title_en: Exercise in a pill
items.author: MIT Tech Review
items.article_content:
We all know exercise is good for us. It builds muscle, strengthens bones, lowers blood pressure, and boosts mood. By deciphering how movement benefits the body, researchers hope to develop medicines that can offer some of the same perks—without the workout. The idea isn’t to replace exercise but to bring its upsides to people who struggle with frailty, disability, or chronic illness.

It will take a lot of experimentation to untangle the myriad pathways by which exercise promotes health. But IDing the cascade of hormones, enzymes, and other molecules related to physical activity is just the first step. Scientists need to figure out how to turn that knowledge into safe and effective drugs. That’s a tall order: More than 90% of treatments that enter human studies fail.

There are regulatory hurdles too. The FDA approves medications to treat diseases, not to enhance wellness, says Thomas Burris, a pharmacologist at the University of Florida whose work focuses on diseases that respond to exercise, like obesity, type 2 diabetes, and dementia.

items.title: Interspecies communication
items.title_en: Interspecies communication
items.author: MIT Tech Review
items.article_content:
Humans are far from the only species with a gift for gab, and our furry, feathered, and finned friends could have a lot to tell us. Decoding how animals communicate with one another could offer a window into the inner lives of other species and help humans realize that “animals are sentient creatures who think, who have hopes and dreams of their own,” says Con Slobodchikoff, the founder of Zoolingua, a company working on dog-to-human speech.

Teasing all this out is complex. To decipher howls, squeaks, and clicks, researchers must match the creatures making sounds with what’s happening around them. Prairie dogs, for example, utter a different series of yips when a coyote approaches than when a hawk is nearby. It’s painstaking work, especially for difficult-to-­observe species, like deep-diving whales or subterranean mole rats.

There are other hurdles. Many animals communicate not just through sound but through visual cues, touch, pheromones, or a combination of signals, some of which might be difficult for us to perceive. And without a multispecies Rosetta stone, it’s hard to know if translations are accurate.

items.summary_en: Research groups and startups are leveraging AI and multimodal mapping to decode communication signals among animals, correlating vocalizations with contextual behaviors to understand non-human sentience. While distinct alarm vocalizations have been documented in species like prairie dogs, data collection remains daunting for hard-to-observe creatures such as deep-diving whales. The multisensory nature of animal communication, combined with the lack of a universal translation benchmark, poses fundamental challenges to verification.

items.title: Cleaning up PFAS
items.title_en: Cleaning up PFAS
items.author: MIT Tech Review
items.article_content:
Scrubbing Earth of per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances—a.k.a. PFAS or forever chemicals—could eliminate a list of woes for people and planet. Used for decades in everything from nonstick pans to firefighting foams, PFAS have been linked to increased risks of fertility challenges, developmental delays, cancer, and reduced immune response. They are known for a strong bond between carbon and fluorine, which the environment struggles to break down.

PFAS are everywhere: They spew from factories and slough off products and into water with normal use. Scientists have found them in everything from human blood to Antarctic snow. One 2022 report found that 89% of the US population had PFAS in excess of two nanograms per milliliter of blood plasma, a common threshold for potential adverse health effects, and 9% of the population had passed the riskier level of 20 nanograms per milliliter.

The PFAS monster is also a moving target. New compounds are still being created and used. There are more than 12,000 of them, and much of the cleanup research focuses on only a small handful.

items.summary_en: Environmental scientists are grappling with technologies to eradicate per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS), whose virtually unbreakable carbon-fluorine bonds prevent natural degradation. While these 'forever chemicals' have contaminated human bloodlines globally and are linked to cancer and immune disorders, remediation efforts face a moving target. items.title: Solid-state batteries
items.title_en: Solid-state batteries
items.author: MIT Tech Review
items.article_content:
The rise of the lithium-ion battery, which powers everything from the smallest personal electronics to gargantuan energy storage systems, has been nothing short of revolutionary. But as anyone who’s boarded a plane in the last decade could tell you, storing and pumping out energy by moving charged lithium ions through a liquid electrolyte soup has its drawbacks, not least that the batteries have a troubling tendency to catch fire. Enter the solid-state battery, which swaps liquid for a solid ceramic or polymer, creating power packs that charge faster, last longer, cram more energy into smaller spaces, and (crucially) run cooler. A new generation of companies aim to bring such batteries to market, and if their bets pan out, the tech could substantially ease the shift away from fossil fuels.

items.title: Claude Science tackles deadly scorpion stings by designing protein binders from scratch
items.title_en: Claude Science tackles deadly scorpion stings by designing protein binders from scratch
items.author: THE DECODER
items.article_content:
Anthropic's Claude independently designed protein binders targeting deadly scorpion neurotoxins. Out of more than 318,000 designs, 211 were tested in the lab. Seventeen met the criteria, and the two strongest bind extremely tightly to Cn2, a toxin from a Mexican scorpion. Whether they actually work as antivenom remains an open question.

Although demonstrating generative AI's capability in de novo protein design, functional neutralization in vivo remains to be proven.

items.title: OpenAI acquires Orchestra Bio to build AI agents that speed up drug development
items.title_en: OpenAI acquires Orchestra Bio to build AI agents that speed up drug development
items.author: THE DECODER
items.article_content:
OpenAI is acquiring startup Orchestra Bio and plans to merge it with its life sciences AI platform Rosalind. The goal is to build AI agents that help pharma teams coordinate drug development, from tracking trials to spotting problems. Developing a new drug in the US takes ten to 15 years on average. OpenAI already works with Novo Nordisk and Moderna on AI-driven pharma research.

items.title: Europe Wants Data Centers. Its Climate Goals Are Getting in the Way
items.title_en: Europe Wants Data Centers. Its Climate Goals Are Getting in the Way
items.author: Wired AI
items.article_content:
However, Germany has found that its AI ambitions are butting up against its climate commitments. EU member states have committed to cutting greenhouse gas emissions by 55 percent by the end of the decade. But policies meant to help meet that target are interfering with attempts to trigger a data center building frenzy.

As part of its broader climate commitments, the previous German administration voted through the Energy Efficiency Act in 2023. Among other things, it required all new data centers to recycle a portion of the waste heat generated by their computer equipment, ideally into nearby municipal heating systems. It seemed like a no-brainer, says Patrick Graichen, who served as a senior official at Germany’s Ministry for Economic Affairs and Energy at the time, before resigning over cronyism allegations.

“We need clean heat, and data centers are a source of clean heat,” Graichen tells WIRED.

In June, a month before the rules were due to finally take effect, the German federal government walked them back. Data center firms had complained that the requirements made it almost impossible to build in the country; the German Data Center Association characterized an early version of the bill as a “data center prevention act.” Under an amended bill, which will be put to the German parliament for ratification imminently, data center operators would no longer be obligated to reuse waste heat, only to scope out the possibility.

Graichen and others have accused the German government of sacrificing climate targets for a chance to ride the AI wave. But countries across Europe find themselves pulled between these same two poles, under simultaneous pressure to cash in on rapid growth in the energy-intensive AI sector—and limit dependence on the US—and to protect the climate.

The German Ministry for Economic Affairs and Energy did not respond to a request for comment.

Among data center developers, the chief objection to the original Energy Efficiency Act was the chance it could land them in an impossible bind, obligated to reuse waste heat even when there was no available offtake—whether a municipal heating system or an industry, like greenhouse agriculture. “Some of the things they had to comply with were outside of their control,” says Barbara Smitten, associate director for critical systems at consulting firm Cundall. “It felt that [the burden] was all on the data center.”

In the last 18 months, multiple data center proposals have fallen through in Germany: Stack Infrastructure canceled a $3 billion facility in Hesse, and state-owned Komm.ONE withdrew from a project in Baden-Württemberg. Though precisely what causes a data center development to fold is rarely clear, Komm.ONE pointed directly to the burdens of the Energy Efficiency Act.

Graichen claims that the industry’s objections are groundless. He says the availability of a heat offtake should become a default criterion for any developer searching for a new site. “Stop complaining,” he says.

When an offtake is available, recycling heat produced by a data center is straightforward. “There is no technical reason why a data center cannot use its waste heat. The technologies and concepts are well known,” says John Booth, managing director at IT consultancy Carbon3IT, who helped to devise EU-wide energy efficiency targets for data centers. “There is absolutely no reason except the will of the organization to do it.”

Nevertheless, under the amended Energy Efficiency Act, data center developers are required only to assess whether recycling heat is economically and technically feasible. If not, they are exempt. “With practical rules for data centers, we are creating the conditions for digital sovereignty and economic growth,” wrote Katherina Reiche, federal minister for economic affairs and energy, when the cabinet approved the change.

The amendment may unlock pent-up demand among data center developers to build in Germany, whose geographic centrality makes it easy to route data efficiently into Western and Eastern Europe. “It lessens the risk of people not seeing the German market as attractive,” says Smitten.

But in a roundabout way, it could also undermine the aim to spark a building frenzy, inviting the type of climate-focused activism that has led to permitting freezes and data center moratoria in the US. Already, in February, the city council of a small German town voted to block the construction of a $2.5 billion data center development, partly over climate concerns.

As policymakers contend with conflicting ambitions to improve domestic AI capabilities and meet climate objectives, some say the swelling public unease about that trade-off will complicate things yet further in Europe. In the last year, the attitude toward data centers “has switched completely,” claims Graichen. “First and foremost in the US, but the same will happen in Europe.”

Though precisely what causes a data center development to fold is rarely clear, Komm.ONE pointed directly to the burdens of the Energy Efficiency Act.

Graichen claims that the industry’s objections are groundless. He says the availability of a heat offtake should become a default criterion for any developer searching for a new site. “Stop complaining,” he says.

When an offtake is available, recycling heat produced by a data center is straightforward. “There is no technical reason why a data center cannot use its waste heat. The technologies and concepts are well known,” says John Booth, managing director at IT consultancy Carbon3IT, who helped to devise EU-wide energy efficiency targets for data centers. “There is absolutely no reason except the will of the organization to do it.”

Nevertheless, under the amended Energy Efficiency Act, data center developers are required only to assess whether recycling heat is economically and technically feasible. If not, they are exempt. “With practical rules for data centers, we are creating the conditions for digital sovereignty and economic growth,” wrote Katherina Reiche, federal minister for economic affairs and energy, when the cabinet approved the change.

The amendment may unlock pent-up demand among data center developers to build in Germany, whose geographic centrality makes it easy to route data efficiently into Western and Eastern Europe. “It lessens the risk of people not seeing the German market as attractive,” says Smitten.

But in a roundabout way, it could also undermine the aim to spark a building frenzy, inviting the type of climate-focused activism that has led to permitting freezes and data center moratoria in the US. Already, in February, the city council of a small German town voted to block the construction of a $2.5 billion data center development, partly over climate concerns.

As policymakers contend with conflicting ambitions to improve domestic AI capabilities and meet climate objectives, some say the swelling public unease about that trade-off will complicate things yet further in Europe. In the last year, the attitude toward data centers “has switched completely,” claims Graichen. “First and foremost in the US, but the same will happen in Europe.”

However, Germany has found that its AI ambitions are butting up against its climate commitments. EU member states have committed to cutting greenhouse gas emissions by 55 percent by the end of the decade. But policies meant to help meet that target are interfering with attempts to trigger a data center building frenzy.

items.summary_en: Europe's push to build out AI data centers has run headfirst into its binding climate goal of cutting greenhouse gas emissions by 55% this decade. Germany's 2023 Energy Efficiency Act initially mandated that new data facilities route waste computer heat into municipal grids, drawing intense backlash from operators warning it made local construction economically impossible. Facing capital flight, the German federal government retreated from the requirements shortly before enforcement, laying bare the widening rift between digital expansion and sustainability targets.

items.title: Memo: Nscale CEO Josh Payne says it has "more than $100B in contracted revenue"; sources say it still plans to list by the end of 2026 at a $30B-$35B valuation (Kieran Smith/Financial Times)
items.title_en: Memo: Nscale CEO Josh Payne says it has "more than $100B in contracted revenue"; sources say it still plans to list by the end of 2026 at a $30B-$35B valuation (Kieran Smith/Financial Times)
items.author: Financial Times
items.original_content:
Kieran Smith / Financial Times:
Memo: Nscale CEO Josh Payne says it has “more than $100B in contracted revenue”; sources say it still plans to list by the end of 2026 at a $30B-$35B valuation  —  Founder Josh Payne says demand remains ‘insatiable
items.content_snippet: Founder Josh Payne says demand remains ‘insatiable’ for the services of Nvidia-backed data centre group
items.summary_en: AI cloud infrastructure upstart Nscale disclosed via an internal executive memo that it has secured over $100 billion in contracted forward revenue. Capitalizing on unabated global demand for enterprise GPU clusters, the company is targeting an initial public offering by the end of 2026 at a projected valuation of $30 billion to $35 billion. CEO Josh Payne emphasized that client demand for scalable compute capacity remains essentially insatiable.
items.title_zh: 算力黑马手握千亿订单拟高估值上市
items.summary_zh: 云算力平台披露其签约在手订单超千亿美元，正全速推进2026年底实现高达350亿美元的上市计划

ai_analysis.briefing_zh: 云算力基础设施新锐企业Nscale最高管理层在一份内部备忘录中宣布，公司目前已锁定超过1000亿美元的签约意向收入。得益于全球科技行业对大规模AI图形算力资源的极度渴求，该公司目前正推进上市时间表，计划在2026年年底前以300亿至350亿美元的高估值挂牌公开市场。管理层坚称当前整个行业对算力集群的需求依然极其强劲，正加速推进其全球数据中心与算力云的扩张版图。
ai_analysis.briefing_en: AI cloud infrastructure upstart Nscale disclosed via an internal executive memo that it has secured over $100 billion in contracted forward revenue. Capitalizing on unabated global demand for enterprise GPU clusters, the company is targeting an initial public offering by the end of 2026 at a projected valuation of $30 billion to $35 billion. CEO Josh Payne emphasized that client demand for scalable compute capacity remains essentially insatiable.

elements_zh.where: 跨国资本市场与算力租赁产业

elements_en.who: Cloud compute provider Nscale and CEO Josh Payne
elements_en.where: Global venture capital markets and cloud hosting industry
elements_en.what: Reporting over $100B in contracted pipeline and planning a $35B IPO by late 2026
elements_en.why: Exploiting desperate enterprise appetite for scarce GPU clusters to secure long-term contractual commitments before listing

ai_analysis.insight_zh: 还没上市就敢在内部信里喊出千亿美元已签约收入，把未来十年的算力分期付款一口气全贴在脸上。资本市场现在最爱这种‘芯片期货倒爷’的故事，在热潮退去之前赶紧把两三年后的天价IPO日程排满，毕竟谁也不知道2026年泡沫散场时这些天价合约到底能不能全部兑现。
ai_analysis.insight_en: Bragging about $100 billion in forward contracted revenue before an IPO is like counting thirty years of future apartment rent payments as liquid net worth today. The market currently loves GPU middlemen trading chip futures, so rushing a 2026 listing makes total sense before anyone checks whether those multi-year paper contracts will actually be paid out in a down cycle.
