items.title: Apple says it will commit up to $100M over three years to Pennsylvania-based Perryman, a titanium supplier for the iPhone Duo, and expand its Qnity partnership (MacKenzie Sigalos/CNBC)
items.title_en: Apple says it will commit up to $100M over three years to Pennsylvania-based Perryman, a titanium supplier for the iPhone Duo, and expand its Qnity partnership (MacKenzie Sigalos/CNBC)
items.author: CNBC
items.article_content:
Apple is adding a U.S. titanium supplier for its new iPhone Duo and expanding domestic production of camera components for the iPhone 18 Pro as part of a push to expand manufacturing in its home country.

The company said Tuesday it will commit up to $100 million over the next three years to Perryman Company, based in Houston, Pennsylvania, for the production of titanium used in Apple products, including the $1,999 foldable Duo.

Since the start of President Donald Trump's second term, Apple has been vocal about its efforts to invest more in the U.S., even as the final assembly of most iPhones remains overseas. In August of last year, Apple launched the American Manufacturing Program (AMP), increasing its plan for domestic spending by $100 billion to a total of $600 billion. Tim Cook, Apple's CEO until last month, appeared at the White House for that announcement, as Trump was pushing the iPhone maker and other tech giants to bolster production in the U.S.

The latest announcement comes as Apple faces severe supply constraints for its first foldable phone, which goes on sale in stores Friday.

Online delivery estimates for some Duo models stretched to roughly 14 weeks on the first day of preorders, according to Morgan Stanley, the longest wait the firm has recorded for a new iPhone in a decade. Apple said Friday that preorder demand had been "nothing short of extraordinary," but hasn't said whether it plans to increase production.

JPMorgan analysts estimate Apple will ship roughly 8 million to 9 million Duo devices this year, below earlier expectations of about 10 million, because of supply constraints. Apple didn't say whether the agreement with Perryman would increase near-term capacity.

Perryman will melt, forge, and roll grade 5 titanium, which Apple said will contain at least 80% recycled material. Titanium is used for the Duo's enclosure, providing durability, according to Apple.

In addition to the Perryman announcement, Apple said Tuesday that it's expanding its partnership with Delaware-based Qnity Electronics, which will manufacture advanced films used in the variable-aperture camera system on the iPhone 18 Pro. The feature allows the phone's main camera to adjust how much light enters the lens depending on conditions, giving users greater control over light and depth.

Apple said nearly 100 components used in the iPhone Duo and iPhone 18 Pro are produced by American companies across more than a dozen states.

"We're thrilled to expand our work with companies producing advanced materials and components for our newest iPhone lineup right here in America," Sabih Khan, Apple's operating chief, said in a statement.

Apple also highlighted investments with other AMP partners, including Broadcom for U.S.-made chips, Corning for specialty glass used in iPhones and Apple Watches, and Amkor, which is constructing a semiconductor packaging and testing facility in Peoria, Arizona.

For the Duo, questions remain about whether Apple can produce enough phones to meet demand for a phone facing unusually long wait times before hitting stores.

items.title: The Download: the claim shaking up AI and the internet’s agent problem
items.title_en: The Download: the claim shaking up AI and the internet’s agent problem
items.author: MIT Tech Review
items.article_content:
“I think I have good news about the nature of neural networks.” With those simple words of optimism, Nick Cammarata, a researcher at AI startup Goodfire, kicked off a 26,000-word blog post that has knocked the AI world on its head, sparking wild speculation as well as cautious (and not-so-cautious) celebration.

Cammarata claims that LLMs might be far easier to understand, and thus to monitor and control, than people previously thought. If true, it’s a huge deal. But not everyone is convinced.

I talked to Cammarata the day after his post blew up. We discussed what he thinks researchers are getting wrong, what his work actually shows, and why skeptics aren’t ready to celebrate just yet.

items.title: Cloudflare's Clairic pulls data from documents faster and cheaper than LLMs
items.title_en: Cloudflare's Clairic pulls data from documents faster and cheaper than LLMs
items.author: THE DECODER
items.article_content:
Cloudflare has released an AI model it says pulls data from documents faster and more cheaply than large language models. Clairic is available in preview on Workers AI, and open weights are set to follow soon.

Users name the fields they want, like an order number or invoice total, and Clairic returns matching values in the right format along with a confidence score. Unlike language models, Clairic doesn't generate text token by token. It answers every field in a single pass. If a value is missing, the model returns "null." Beyond extraction, it can handle simple calculations, estimates, and forecasts.

Cloudflare wants Clairic to run in chains alongside LLMs and other "System One" models like Jev. With a complaint email, for example, Clairic pulls out the order number, amount, and damage, then estimates the repair cost. The decision model Clef applies company rules to choose between a refund and a repair, and GLM-5.3 writes the reply to the customer.Ad

Cloudflare says this chain takes 19.3 seconds. GLM-5.3 on its own needs 61.7 seconds for all three steps and costs almost twice as much.Ad

According to Cloudflare, Clairic can't yet reliably handle longer chains of calculations. For now, developers should run those in their own code.

items.summary_en: Cloudflare has introduced Clairic, a specialized AI extraction model available in preview on Workers AI with open weights coming soon. Unlike conventional large language models that generate outputs token-by-token, Clairic processes structured document data in a single pass, returning field values, formats, and confidence scores. Cloudflare developed this model to tackle the excessive cost and latency of generic LLMs, cutting workflow runtimes by nearly 70% while slashing inference expenses.

ai_analysis.briefing_zh: 网络基础设施巨头Cloudflare在其Workers AI平台上限时预览并即将开源全新专用AI模型Clairic。该模型颠覆了传统通用大语言模型逐Token自回归生成的机制，仅需单次前向传播即可一次性抽取出指定字段并返回对应格式与置信度，同时支持基础测算与预测。研发该工具的核心动因在于降低企业处理发票、客诉与工单时的延迟与算力成本，测试显示其与专用决策模型构建的工作流相比纯大模型方案耗时缩短近70%，成本几乎腰斩。

items.title: AI adoption by industry shows what other sectors can learn
items.title_en: AI adoption by industry shows what other sectors can learn
items.author: MIT Tech Review
items.article_content:
The current narrative around artificial intelligence in the workplace is largely driven by Silicon Valley. But treating the tech sector as an island misses the actual trends in technology adoption–tech is just the first industry in line.

As generative AI and automation tools mature, the shifts currently reshaping software engineering and product management will inevitably filter into healthcare, education, retail, and manufacturing. The variation in adoption rates today isn’t a sign that non-tech industries are falling behind, but rather a reflection of the different speeds at which industries absorb new workflows. For leaders and their teams outside of tech, this differential pace provides a practical blueprint for how AI adoption unfolds, and where the opportunities lie.

Recent survey data from TripleTen highlights just how stark the current adoption curve is across different sectors of the economy (see Figure 1).

Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now.

Otter.ai raises $320 million from General Catalyst’s growth fund for its meeting tool																				
				
																									
						

	
									
									
										

			Ivan Mehta
	

									
									
								
					
					
						4:00 AM PDT · October 20, 2026											
																			
					
		
	





			
					
		
		
					
		
					
		
					
		
					
		
					
		
					
	





	
	
		
		
			
Meeting note-taking tool Otter.ai announced on Tuesday that it has raised $320 million from General Catalyst’s Customer Value Fund (CVF), which provides capital to startups without diluting equity and gets returns on the results of marketing spend.

Otter.ai said that it will use these funds for enterprise growth, go-to-market strategy, international expansion, and product innovation.

The startup, which has been around for nearly a decade, has raised $50 million in total funding with its last round in 2021, according to PitchBook data.

Last year, Otter hit a revenue milestone after crossing $100 million in annual recurring revenue (ARR). The company said it’s now approaching new milestones, but didn’t provide updated figures.

The company said that 40 million users have used its product to date, up from 25 million last year. However, given the crowded space among meeting note-taking products, a pertinent challenge for Otter would be to have its customers stick around. Unfortunately, the startup didn’t provide any numbers around its monthly active users or churn.

“Voice is one of the biggest untapped opportunities in enterprise AI, and Otter is at the forefront of it – a conviction that’s only deepened watching Otter’s growth,” said Pranav Singhvi, Partner and Co-founder of CVF, General Catalyst. “When Otter enables enterprises to capture critical voice data and turns it into actionable business insights, teams move faster, decisions get sharper, and productivity compounds across the organization, and that’s why it’s a strong partner for CVF.”

There is a lot of competition in the market with well-funded meeting notetakers like Fireflies.ai, Granola, and Read AI; new entrants like Calendly, Wispr, and Superhuman, which acquired Fathom; and other notetakers like Circleback, Talat, and Quill.

Most of these notetakers want to connect to enterprise systems and, based on data captured in meetings, automate workflows. Otter is also heading in that direction. In the last few years, it introduced a meeting assistant, a search function that works across apps, and integration with other AI tools.

Otter’s newly appointed CMO, Alex Gay, who comes from Superhuman, told TechCrunch at a sit-down at the HumanX conference last month that the company sees a big opportunity in turning transcripts into an actionable roadmap for people who are in back-to-back meetings.

“When we start thinking about what is actually the bigger problem that people are facing right now, we saw this large pain point in meeting-heavy roles, where people are back-to-back in conversations. These meetings are the work for them. That’s either customer conversations or, from a sales standpoint. That’s where strategies are discussed. But meetings are terribly inefficient because when you come into a meeting, you spend the first twenty minutes recapping what was said before to catch everybody up,” he said.

The company is now experimenting with providing insights before, after, and during meetings. It has been testing a feature to send a pre-brief to users with details and background information, with context from previous conversations across surfaces. Plus, it is also trying out a Live Assist feature to let users ask questions to the AI assistant during the meeting to get knowledge.

items.summary_en: Four co-founders of a leading Chinese artificial intelligence startup were revealed to have participated in an academic research project co-funded by a research institute between 2018 and 2021 that UK intelligence previously associated with state security apparatuses. The historical academic linkage has triggered geopolitical and national security scrutiny across Western tech policy circles. The broader context reflects mounting tensions where frontier AI talent and model pedigrees are increasingly treated through a defense-readiness and export-control lens.

items.summary_zh: 中国AI独角兽四位核心创始人早年参与共建科研项目的经历，近期引发西方情报与监管视角的安全审视

ai_analysis.briefing_zh: 中国头部生成式人工智能初创企业的四位核心联合创始人，被披露曾在2018至2021年期间参与一项由特定技术研究机构共同资助的学术研究项目。该研究机构此前曾被英国安全情报部门指称与安全机关存在关联，因而引发国际地缘科技监管层面对中国顶尖AI团队技术渊源的密切审视。这一学术历史回顾发生的深层动因，在于西方国家日益将前沿AI模型视为国家战略安全资产，对中国领军团队的核心成员进行前置性风险穿透与技术阻截。

The broader context reflects mounting tensions where frontier AI talent and model pedigrees are increasingly treated through a defense-readiness and export-control lens.

items.title: US bans Deepseek technology across federal civilian agencies
items.title_en: US bans Deepseek technology across federal civilian agencies
items.author: THE DECODER
items.article_content:
The US Department of Homeland Security has banned federal civilian agencies from using AI technology from Chinese lab Deepseek. Agencies have to remove existing Deepseek products from their IT systems and can't buy new ones, the Wall Street Journal reports.

The order also covers products from affiliated companies and third-party services built with Deepseek implementations. The department didn't set a deadline or name any specific security concerns. It's still unclear what "built with" actually means and whether AI gateways like OpenRouter fall under the ban.

The order is based on a 2018 US law covering supply chain security in federal procurement. The notice doesn't say which security concerns led to the decision or when agencies need to have the technology removed.Ad

Over the summer, the US government considered steps against Chinese open-weight models, according to the New York Times. The options included sanctions, a trade blacklist, and rules on which models federal agencies are allowed to use.Ad

The push came after a wave of powerful Chinese models such as Kimi K3 from Moonshot AI. The government pulled back for now after Nvidia, Microsoft, Google, and Meta objected, while OpenAI and Anthropic had lobbied for restrictions.

items.summary_en: The U.S. Department of Homeland Security has issued an administrative directive barring federal civilian agencies from utilizing artificial intelligence technologies developed by Chinese laboratory Deepseek. The mandatory order requires immediate removal of existing installations, prohibits future procurement, and extends to third-party software products integrated with Deepseek models. Grounded in federal supply chain security legislation, the decision reflects Washington's heightened urgency to insulate official digital infrastructure from Chinese open-weight AI advancements.

items.author: Financial Times
items.original_content:
Financial Times:
Alibaba, Tencent, and Huawei are pouring billions into data centers in Shaoguan, a hinterland region with cheap power and a cool climate, angering some locals  —  Residents in remote region of Shaoguan hope country's AI infrastructure push will de
items.content_snippet: Residents in remote region of Shaoguan hope country's AI infrastructure push will deliver boom that has long eluded them
items.summary_en: Chinese technology giants Alibaba, Tencent, and Huawei are committing tens of billions of yuan to construct massive AI-focused data centers in Shaoguan, Guangdong province. The hinterland region was designated as a core hub in the national computing framework due to its low-cost hydropower resources and cooler climate. However, the surging electricity demands, land allocations, and environmental impacts associated with these high-density facilities have triggered local friction regarding ecological burdens and economic equity.
items.title_zh: 阿里巴巴（Alibaba）、腾讯（Tencent）和华为（Huawei）正斥资数十亿美元在电力廉价、气候凉爽的内陆地区韶关建设数据中心，这激怒了一些当地人
items.summary_zh: 阿里巴巴、腾讯与华为等科技巨头砸下百亿在广东韶关布局超大规模智算集群，引发部分本地资源挤占争议

ai_analysis.briefing_zh: 阿里巴巴、腾讯与华为等中国领军科技巨头正加速向广东省韶关市注入数百亿元资金，大规模铺设面向生成式AI算力需求的高密度超算中心集群。韶关依托丰沛的廉价水电绿电和阴凉的气候优势，成为国家“东数西算”粤港澳大湾区算力枢纽的核心承接地。然而，随着海量耗能耗水机架的集中入驻，基础设施工程与算力能耗的高压运转引发了部分当地民众对生态资源承载力、用电负荷与就业回报失衡的疑虑。

items.title: Google says Cloud in its London region is "experiencing issues" starting on Monday at 23:08 PDT; a source says a major Revolut outage is due to Google Cloud (Bloomberg)
items.title_en: Google says Cloud in its London region is "experiencing issues" starting on Monday at 23:08 PDT; a source says a major Revolut outage is due to Google Cloud (Bloomberg)
items.author: Bloomberg
items.original_content:
Bloomberg:
Google says Cloud in its London region is “experiencing issues” starting on Monday at 23:08 PDT; a source says a major Revolut outage is due to Google Cloud  —  An outage at Google Cloud knocked out banking services in the UK including Revol
items.content_snippet: An outage at Google Cloud knocked out banking services in the UK including Revolut Ltd. early on Tuesday.
items.summary_en: Google Cloud's London infrastructure region suffered a widespread service disruption beginning late Monday, triggering outages across multiple enterprise clients in the UK. The incident notably incapacitated core banking and transaction processing systems for fintech unicorn Revolut, leaving millions of mobile banking customers unable to access accounts or complete transfers. The severe breakdown underscores the architectural vulnerability of modern fintech platforms relying on single-provider cloud infrastructures without resilient multi-region failovers.
items.title_zh: 谷歌表示，从太平洋夏令时周一23:08开始，其伦敦地区的云计算正在“遇到问题” ；一位消息人士称， Revolut的重大中断是由于谷歌云计算
items.summary_zh: 谷歌云伦敦可用区突发服务中断，导致英国金融科技独角兽Revolut出现大面积支付与登录瘫痪

ai_analysis.briefing_zh: 谷歌云平台欧洲伦敦可用区在周一晚间突发系统异常中断，导致依赖其基础设施的多个企业级客户遭遇业务宕机。受此故障直接冲击，英国核心金融科技独角兽Revolut旗下手机银行与线上支付结算发生大规模不可用，海量用户的转账、刷卡与登录体验受阻。此事件再次暴露了现代跨国金融科技产品将核心清结算与账户系统深度绑定于单一云服务商时，多活容灾与跨云冗余机制缺失的致命隐患。

items.title: Anthropic's leaked federal AI bill draws widespread criticism from AI safety advocates for being significantly weaker than the bipartisan FRONTIER Act (Shakeel Hashim/Transformer)
items.title_en: Anthropic's leaked federal AI bill draws widespread criticism from AI safety advocates for being significantly weaker than the bipartisan FRONTIER Act (Shakeel Hashim/Transformer)
items.author: Transformer
items.article_content:
A leaked discussion draft of a federal AI bill which Anthropic has been circulating to lawmakers, published by Politico on Friday, makes that safety-first pitch ring hollow. The bill, which has been widely criticized by AI safety advocates, is much weaker than the Obernolte/Trahan FRONTIER Act, and arguably makes it legally harder to prevent a dangerous AI model from being released than it is today. It reads like Anthropic’s business interests winning out over its purported safety concerns. And at a time when the AI policy window feels wide open, Anthropic’s bill could slam it shut, forestalling stronger regulation in future — even as the risks from AI, by the company’s own admission, grow ever larger.

Bengio: ‘If you prioritize safety, leave frontier AI companies’Oct 8Read full storyThree sections of the bill — which can be read in full here — stand out. Like the FRONTIER Act, it requires third-party evaluators to assess AI companies’ models and practices for catastrophic risk. Unlike FRONTIER, however, there are no standards or licensing requirements for evaluators, which can self-certify. As LawAI’s Charlie Bullock notes, this means “auditors will inevitably compete with each other to offer … the least bothersome audits available at the lowest possible price point.”

The bill also makes it very hard to block a dangerous model. If the Commerce Department (the agency in charge under Anthropic’s proposal) wants to stop one, it must petition a federal court, making a detailed case — separate from anything an independent evaluator has said — for why the model poses a risk. The court decides every question “without deference” to Commerce or the independent evaluators. It must also “consider the harm the [blocking] order would cause to the frontier developer, to users, and to the public.” Encode’s Nathan Calvin, who said the bill made him “viscerally angry,” notes that the court is not told to consider anything in the other direction — such as the harm to the public caused by not blocking the model.

All this is paired with the ever-controversial topic of preemption. For the most part, Anthropic’s bill handles it similarly to FRONTIER: laws like California’s SB 53, New York’s RAISE and Illinois’ SB 315 that seek to govern “frontier AI” would be preempted, while child safety and other laws are explicitly carved out. Unlike FRONTIER, however, Anthropic’s bill is also written to stop state legislatures or courts from suspending a model on catastrophic-risk grounds. According to Calvin, this means the bill “likely makes it harder than under existing law for a court to get an order blocking or restricting the development of frontier models.”

To top it all off, the bill is remarkably rigid. It does not allow the Commerce Department to ever set standards for AI evaluators, or for what actually counts as a “safe” AI model. And with state AI laws preempted, the only route to stronger rules is congressional action. Given Anthropic’s views on the pace of AI progress (co-founder Jack Clark recently said he thinks full recursive self-improvement might be achieved next year), that is indefensible. As Nat Purser of AVERI says, “if you’re going to preempt many state safety laws, the least you can do is create a federal regulatory regime that can evolve in time.”

Democrats prepare to battle over AI regulationShakeel Hashim and Veronica Irwin·Oct 9Read full storyThe bill is not all bad. There are some meaningful improvements over FRONTIER: it has good provisions on AI company security protocols, and it has ways of handling containment failure and automated AI R&D risks. But that one step forward is undermined by two massive steps back. The timing makes this particularly egregious: FRONTIER was introduced in July, from a discussion draft floated in June, at a time when AI safety was much less politically salient. After a summer of rogue AI incidents and employees warning of disaster, the landscape has changed. Stronger state laws are imminent. Now is the time for stronger federal bills too, not weaker ones.

It’s not hard to see where this came from. The bill is clearly the work of a company that has been targeted by a capricious executive branch and is now focused on protecting itself. As writer Zvi Mowshowitz says, “Anthropic is more afraid that the government might enforce rules against Anthropic, than they are worried about the ability of the government to enforce rules against everyone.”

There is some hope it will get better. After the leaked draft came under fire, Anthropic’s head of federal affairs Anthony Cimino said its preemption language was “not precise enough” and would be revised, and suggested some of the other issues with the bill will be addressed with future policy proposals.

But it should not take public pushback for a company that claims to be committed to AI safety to produce a good bill. The visceral reaction from across the AI safety community is, in some ways, evidence of a sense of betrayal: that the company that was supposed to be committed to their cause has, like all the others, let business interests win.

items.summary_en: A leaked draft of a federal AI legislative proposal crafted and privately circulated by Anthropic to U.S. lawmakers has ignited fierce backlash from safety advocates. The proposed legislation proves far weaker than the bipartisan FRONTIER Act by omitting licensing benchmarks for third-party auditing bodies, tolerating self-certification, and complicating state authorities' power to halt hazardous releases. The move reflects Anthropic's quiet commercial pivot to preempt aggressive federal safety curbs with corporate-friendly guardrails under the banner of responsible innovation.

ai_analysis.briefing_zh: 以“安全第一”为品牌基石的AI领军企业Anthropic，其秘密游说国会议员的联邦人工智能法案草案遭媒体泄露曝光。该草案内容显著弱于跨党派支持的《前沿法案》（FRONTIER Act），不仅未设定第三方安全评估机构的法定准入与牌照标准、允许评估机构自证合规，甚至在法律层面变相削弱了政府阻止高危危险模型发布的干预权。此举动因在于Anthropic试图借国会政策窗口期，以自我设定的温和规范抢先替代潜在的严厉硬性监管，为自身未来商业化模型扫清上市障碍。

The proposed legislation proves far weaker than the bipartisan FRONTIER Act by omitting licensing benchmarks for third-party auditing bodies, tolerating self-certification, and complicating state authorities' power to halt hazardous releases. The move reflects Anthropic's quiet commercial pivot to preempt aggressive federal safety curbs with corporate-friendly guardrails under the banner of responsible innovation.

items.author: TechCrunch
items.article_content:

Blackwall quadruples valuation to $2.2B as websites wrangle an increasingly crowded internet																				
				
																									
						

	
									
									
										

			Ram Iyer
	

									
									
								
					
					
						12:01 AM PDT · October 20, 2026											
																			
					
		
	





			
					
		
		
					
		
					
		
					
		
					
		
					
		
					
	





	
	
		
		
			
Estonia-based Blackwall, which builds web traffic security tools for hosting providers, said on Tuesday that it has raised $100 million at a $2.2 billion valuation. It builds products that helps websites grapple with the skyrocketing volume of bot traffic, especially AI agents.

The Series C was led by AVP, with participation from existing investors Dawn Capital, MMC Ventures and Tera Ventures. Blackwall’s executive chairman, Roi Carthy, told TechCrunch this funding round increased the company’s valuation by 4 times since its previous fundraise in 2025.

Over the past few years, web infrastructure companies like Cloudflare, Akamai, Imperva and Blackwall have found themselves in an increasingly valuable but difficult space: They’re on the frontlines, dealing with DDoS attacks, indiscriminate scraping, botnet farms, malicious requests, and these days, even swarms of AI agents going rogue. But it’s also a chance to make a killing by helping hosting providers and websites deal with all the potentially unwanted traffic.

Blackwall, however, isn’t interested in competing with the bigwigs in its space. Instead of selling its platform directly to websites, the company uses a “channel” approach, working with web hosting, managed service and cloud providers to understand their needs, and then handing over a bundle of tools which they can customize. Those providers can then offer Blackwall’s security tools to their own clients under their own branding and retain control of that relationship.

There’s money in it for both sides. Co-founder and CEO Nikita Rozenberg told TechCrunch that hosting companies can mix and match security components to build their own solution according to what they want to provide to their end customers, set the prices, and share a cut of the revenue with Blackwall. The company initially gives its customers a free tier showing the traffic and threats hitting their network, but charges for any protection or tools to address the threats.

In addition to providing services like threat intelligence, certificate management, DDoS protection and traffic routing, Blackwall examines its customers’ web traffic to differentiate actual visitors and legit AI agents from malicious bots, intruders, and disruptive traffic. Rozenberg said the company uses techniques like digital fingerprinting to identify the software sending a request — for example, Microsoft Office or Codex — to filter out bots. In addition, the company uses its own AI models at customers’ endpoints to analyze the intent and behavior of the requests coming in to differentiate agents sent by a person for a real request versus a malicious bot.

In the coming years, Rozenberg sees a big opportunity emerging as AI agents begin interacting and transacting with websites on behalf of their users. This should eventually require systems to manage which agents get access, and on what terms, and how they are authorized to make payments.

Blackwall isn’t alone in eyeing that opportunity. Cloudflare’s AI Crawl Control lets website owners allow or block individual AI crawlers, and there’s also an option to charge them for access. But Rozenberg argues that Blackwall’s advantage lies in letting hosting providers offer such traffic management services themselves instead of handing the customer relationship to another security provider.

Blackwall plans to use the funding to expand its operations across North America, Europe, Asia-Pacific and the Middle East, and develop more security tooling for hosting, cloud and managed service providers.

Estonia-based Blackwall, which builds web traffic security tools for hosting providers, said on Tuesday that it has raised $100 million at a $2.2 billion valuation. It builds products that helps websites grapple with the skyrocketing volume of bot traffic, especially AI agents.

The Series C was led by AVP, with participation from existing investors Dawn Capital, MMC Ventures and Tera Ventures. Blackwall’s executive chairman, Roi Carthy, told TechCrunch this funding round increased the company’s valuation by 4 times since its previous fundraise in 2025.

Over the past few years, web infrastructure companies like Cloudflare, Akamai, Imperva and Blackwall have found themselves in an increasingly valuable but difficult space: They’re on the frontlines, dealing with DDoS attacks, indiscriminate scraping, botnet farms, malicious requests, and these days, even swarms of AI agents going rogue. But it’s also a chance to make a killing by helping hosting providers and websites deal with all the potentially unwanted traffic.

Blackwall, however, isn’t interested in competing with the bigwigs in its space. Instead of selling its platform directly to websites, the company uses a “channel” approach, working with web hosting, managed service and cloud providers to understand their needs, and then handing over a bundle of tools which they can customize. Those providers can then offer Blackwall’s security tools to their own clients under their own branding and retain control of that relationship.

There’s money in it for both sides. Co-founder and CEO Nikita Rozenberg told TechCrunch that hosting companies can mix and match security components to build their own solution according to what they want to provide to their end customers, set the prices, and share a cut of the revenue with Blackwall. items.title: Survey: 20% of US adults regularly consume news on TikTok, up from just 3% in 2020; 39% of those aged 18 to 29 and 25% of those aged 30 to 49 do so regularly (Katerina Eva Matsa/Pew Research Center)

Younger adults are especially likely to regularly get news on TikTok. Among Americans ages 18 to 29, around four-in-ten (39%) say they do this regularly. That compares with 25% of those ages 30 to 49, 11% of those ages 50 to 64 and 4% of those ages 65 and older.

Black and Hispanic Americans are more likely than White and Asian Americans to get news on TikTok. Roughly a third of Black (32%) and Hispanic (35%) adults regularly get news there, compared with 14% of both White and Asian adults.

We have updated this Pew Research Center analysis annually for the last few years to track the emergence of TikTok as a news source among Americans.

The Center regularly studies the platforms and social media sites Americans use to get news. This analysis is part of a broader effort to understand the changing ways Americans get news in the digital age and continues our work on news consumption online.

Here are the questions used for this analysis, the topline and the survey methodology.

There are also partisan differences. Democrats and Democratic-leaning independents (22%) are slightly more likely than Republicans and GOP leaners (15%) to regularly get news on TikTok.

TikTok is one of the more widely used social media platforms in the United States. Overall, 37% of Americans say they use TikTok. That trails the shares who use YouTube (84%), Facebook (70%) and Instagram (51%). But more U.S. adults say they use TikTok than WhatsApp (33%), LinkedIn (31%), Reddit (25%) or X (18%).

Looking specifically at U.S. adults who use TikTok, 53% say they regularly get news on the platform. That’s about the same as the share who said this in 2025 (55%) but well above the 22% who did so in 2020. Today, the share of TikTok users who get news there is similar to the shares of Facebook users (57%) and X users (57%) who regularly get news on those sites, and higher than the shares among users of other social media platforms.

Note: This is an update of a post originally published Nov. 15, 2023. Here are the questions used for this analysis, the topline and the survey methodology.

                    From Space to Your Pocket: How D2D Could Redefine Global Coverage

London packs more jobs and people into its core than any other UK city, and its mobile networks have not kept pace with that demand. An early start on 5G lifted London to seventh of 18 European capitals for median download speed in 2021, but traffic has since grown faster than capacity, and adding capacity in central London has become harder. Using Speedtest Intelligence® data from 2018 to Q3 2026, alongside Ookla background signal measurements and official statistics, we compare London with Europe’s other capitals and the UK’s largest cities, show where its networks strain, and examine why new capacity is so hard to add.

London’s operators have spent the past five years building 5G while demand kept climbing, and UK mobile data use rose 18% in 2025 alone, Ofcom reports. VodafoneThree, formed in May 2025, is now combining two networks, and the Mayor’s draft London Plan, in consultation until 15 October 2026, sets out new expectations on mobile connectivity. Behind both sits a long dispute over the rooftops and land that London’s networks depend on, which we return to below.

London was among the first European capitals to launch 5G, which lifted it to seventh of 18 for median download speed by mid-2021. By Q3 2026, however, it had the slowest median download speed of the 18, at 109.43 Mbps, behind Rome (125.26 Mbps) and well below the 172.22 Mbps median of the other capitals. It also had the slowest median upload speed (11.40 Mbps) and the highest latency under load for the worst 10% of samples (2,204 ms). Latency is the time data takes to make a round trip across the network, and latency under load measures it while the connection is busy with a large download, showing how a network copes when it is in heavy use.

The decline tracks 5G. London’s 5G median peaked at 200 Mbps in Q2 2021, when 41% of tests ran on 5G, fell to 102 Mbps by Q3 2023 and has recovered only to 133 Mbps, with 80% of tests now on 5G. Phones moved onto 5G in London at least as fast as in Paris or the rest of the UK, but capacity did not keep up, and London’s 5G median is now the slowest of the 18 capitals. Across the UK, 5G medians fell in 12 of 15 large cities between Q3 2022 and Q3 2026 as 5G use rose in all of them, though Manchester’s climbed from 137 to 178 Mbps.

Within the UK, London features one natural advantage. Its median multi-server latency (measured against several nearby test servers on an idle connection) of 38 ms is the lowest of the 15 UK cities we studied, and latency rises about 3 ms for every 100 km from the capital, to 61 ms in Belfast. Operators like Three and BT’s EE have moved parts of their core networks out to regional sites, but much traffic is still hauled back towards London, where most UK interconnection sits. For example, LINX’s main London exchange peaks at nearly 9.8 Tbps, against about 0.9 Tbps at LINX Manchester. Speed shows no such pattern, and London’s median download ranks only eighth of the 15 UK cities.

The City of London and Westminster hold about 1.5 million jobs but only 213,000 residents. On weekdays, their median download speed falls through the morning to 80.07 Mbps at 13:00, 27% below the same hours at weekends, while latency under load rises 26%. This is a classic case of network congestion. As commuters arrive, more phones share the same cells, and each gets a smaller slice of their capacity. Ookla data on YouTube start times shows the same squeeze.

With offices largely empty in 2020 and 2021, as Londoners worked from home, the City had the fastest mobile speeds of London’s 33 boroughs, and in 2026 the slowest. The reversal reflects commuters returning to a district with few residents and dense office blocks, where extra rooftop capacity is hardest to add.

The squeeze varies by operator. Over the past year, EE customers saw the smallest weekday lunchtime slowdown in central London (15%) and Three customers the highest median download speed across London (113.27 Mbps). O2’s median latency under load of 1,573 ms is about three times its rivals’, but the gap stays as wide overnight, when networks are quietest, which points to how its network queues traffic during downloads (known as bufferbloat) as well as to congestion.

The commuter belt tells a different story. Median download speed ranges from 122.57 Mbps in Barking and Dagenham, one of London’s least affluent boroughs, to 89.01 Mbps in the City of London. Ranking London’s 4,994 census neighborhoods by England’s official Index of Multiple Deprivation, the least affluent fifth records 107.27 Mbps against 96.01 Mbps in the most affluent. They are more than twice as densely populated, have about two-fifths less tree cover and half as much land in conservation areas, and their phones run 78% of tests on 5G against 74%.

Comparing neighborhoods within the same borough, about a third of the 18% speed lead comes from phones spending more time on 5G and about a sixth from denser populations nearby, where demand may draw more investment. Tree cover and operator mix each explain only a small share, while flats and built-up land work the other way, since signal struggles to reach inside dense blocks. Our data cannot cleanly show where operators are able to secure sites, which may also differ between richer and poorer areas.

In the UK, mobile operators own few of the sites their antennas use. They rent space on towers and rooftops, from tower companies or directly from landowners, and even where a tower company runs a site, the roof or land beneath it usually belongs to someone else. In central London, where there is little room for ground-based masts, much of the network sits on rooftops.

The terms are set by the Electronic Communications Code, and its December 2017 reform cut what landowners earn. Rents are now set on a no-network valuation, as if no mobile operator wanted the site, and a 2019 tribunal ruling valued a London council rooftop at £1,000 a year, against £21,000 under the old regime. Since April 2026, the same approach has applied to renewals of older leases. Building owners now have less reason to host antennas, and many may look to rooftop solar or gardens instead. Landlords can also end a site lease with a notice to quit, typically when a building is redeveloped. Mobile UK estimates that notices to quit keep around 7% of London’s rooftop sites out of action at any time, and VodafoneThree expects to take nearly 100 sites offline by the end of 2026, with replacements taking around five years. Landowner groups counter that the reforms cut some rents by up to 90%.

Unlike France, where the ANFR register shows 4G or 5G sites within 10 km of central Paris up 26% from August 2022 to August 2026, the UK has no public register of mobile sites. London’s planning records show the pipeline instead. Applications for new street masts peaked in 2020, early in the first 5G build, and have fallen by more than four-fifths since 2022, while applications to upgrade existing sites fell by only about a fifth over 2022 to 2025. Almost three in four new street masts decided since 2019 were refused, against one in five upgrades. As a mitigation, operators are adding small cells, low-powered radios on lampposts and street furniture, including about 3,400 on Transport for London’s roadside assets. The loss of rooftop sites has acted as a forcing function for this kind of street-level densification, with London now well ahead of many European cities on the depth and breadth of small cell deployment.

Conservation areas, which protect places of special architectural or historic interest and where planning rules restrict telecoms equipment, cover 77% of Westminster. Within boroughs, new masts inside them are 9 to 10 points more likely to be refused, and 5G-capable phones in neighborhoods fully covered by them spend about 4 percentage points less time on 5G than comparable neighborhoods, against about 83% where there is no conservation area. The gap is 7 points for EE and 6 for Three customers.

This analysis builds on our joint report with the Greater London Authority, A New Lens on the Connected Capital, whose Capital Connectivity Standard is designed as a blueprint for other cities. The Mayor’s draft London Plan, due for examination next year, now states that notices to quit “have eroded London’s overall mobile connectivity compared to other equivalent cities”. It asks developers to keep mobile service running through construction and to plan masts on taller buildings and in the public realm, and it asks boroughs to work with operators on sites in conservation areas.

Ookla retains ownership of this article including all of the intellectual property rights, data, content graphs and analysis. This article may not be quoted, reproduced, distributed or published for any commercial purpose without prior consent. Members of the press and others using the findings in this article for non-commercial purposes are welcome to publicly share and link to report information with attribution to Ookla.

Luke Kehoe leads Ookla’s research and thought leadership efforts in Europe. 

An electronic engineering alumnus of University College Dublin, Luke has extensive experience collaborating with mobile operators, telecoms vendors, and government agencies in research and advisory roles across Europe. He has contributed to internationally recognised thought leadership publications in areas such as 5G, IoT, open RAN, and edge computing, working with prestigious organisations like the Telecom Infra Project and the World Economic Forum.

The Mayor’s draft London Plan, due for examination next year, now states that notices to quit “have eroded London’s overall mobile connectivity compared to other equivalent cities”. It asks developers to keep mobile service running through construction and to plan masts on taller buildings and in the public realm, and it asks boroughs to work with operators on sites in conservation areas.

Luke Kehoe leads Ookla’s research and thought leadership efforts in Europe. 

An electronic engineering alumnus of University College Dublin, Luke has extensive experience collaborating with mobile operators, telecoms vendors, and government agencies in research and advisory roles across Europe. He has contributed to internationally recognised thought leadership publications in areas such as 5G, IoT, open RAN, and edge computing, working with prestigious organisations like the Telecom Infra Project and the World Economic Forum.

items.title: How to study a swiftly melting climate disaster
items.title_en: How to study a swiftly melting climate disaster
items.author: MIT Tech Review
items.article_content:
Andrew Haverdink, a tall grad student in a rain bib and rubber boots, wrenched a double-handed drill from the frozen soil that underlies much of Alaska’s Denali National Park and then unclipped the hollow barrel from the end of the bit.

He knelt in front of a blue tarp, lined the barrel up with a plastic tray, and pushed a rod through the opposite end. A perfect solid, cylindrical core of ancient soil emerged—dark, rich permafrost at least a foot long.

On that late morning in early July, Haverdink was among a team of Northern Arizona University students and staff gathering samples and data from a research plot, divided by surveyor’s tape unspooled atop tussocks, alders, and fireweed.

items.title: A visit to Samsung’s massive new semiconductor hub
items.title_en: A visit to Samsung’s massive new semiconductor hub
items.author: MIT Tech Review
items.article_content:
Generative AI models run on powerful chips known as GPUs, which depend on stacks of specialized memory chips packaged with the processor. To meet growing demand for memory, Samsung is building a massive new semiconductor manufacturing complex in Pyeongtaek, South Korea. Three fabs already operate around the clock, and a fourth is coming online. Construction of a fifth was halted during a drop in demand for memory chips in 2024 but restarted when the AI boom sent demand soaring.

It’s just before noon on a Monday, and construction workers are pouring out of Samsung’s fabs in Pyeongtaek, a farming city south of Seoul where rice paddies abut a sprawling chipmaking complex. Thousands of workers, dressed head to toe in black with sky-blue vests, take off helmets bearing their names and fab numbers.

They walk to lunch, sweaty and flushed, in chunky sneakers capped with yellow rubber toe guards. Some hop on scooters or motorcycles to get around the campus, which covers an area about the size of New York City’s Central Park. items.title: These startups hope “blended” food will cut our appetite for red meat
items.title_en: These startups hope “blended” food will cut our appetite for red meat
items.author: MIT Tech Review
items.article_content:
In the fall of 2025, Jeff Dodge set up a six-foot folding table in the cafeteria of Cane Bay High School in Summerville, South Carolina, to conduct a taste test. When the first rush of about 150 hungry students hit, he was waiting with slow cookers filled with steaming marinara sauce and meatballs.

Kids love a taste test, but they’re also discerning, and Dodge wasn’t sure what they would make of his product, a blend featuring both meat and mushrooms. As students swarmed the table and tapped out their opinions on an iPad or scanned a QR code to use their phones, Dodge asked those who lingered to guess what kind of vegetable might have been mixed into the meat. Few of them could—the meatballs had tasted like moist, flavorful beef.

The school enrolls a few thousand students, and Dodge estimates that the majority of them came by. In the end, the survey showed that 92% of those who tried the meatballs wanted them on the menu; they easily cleared the bar to be added for the 2026–2027 school year. Comments described their flavor as “bussin’.”

items.title_zh: 植物肉退潮转战掺假牛肉：蘑菇混合肉打入美国高中食堂
items.summary_zh: 替代蛋白初创企业放弃全植物路线，推出掺杂蘑菇的混合肉丸打入高中食堂并计划列入新学年菜单

ai_analysis.briefing_zh: 食品科技创业者在南卡罗来纳州坎贝尔高中食堂进行盲测，向数百名高中生提供掺入蘑菇与真牛肉的混合肉丸试吃。最终92%的学生投票支持将其纳入日常膳食，产品成功获批进入2026-2027学年食堂采购菜单。该举措反映出人造肉行业正放弃难以讨好大众的原教旨纯素肉路线，转而依靠折中掺杂真菌来悄然降低红肉消耗。

elements_zh.why: 纯素人造肉因高昂造价与塑料般口感面临全面溃败，企业被迫妥协转入半真半假的混合肉以求生存

elements_en.where: School cafeteria in Summerville, South Carolina
elements_en.what: Tested mushroom-beef hybrid meatballs, gaining 92% approval and securing a spot on the 2026–2027 menu
elements_en.why: Pure plant-based alternatives struggled with bad taste and high costs, forcing startups to pivot to hybrid food products

ai_analysis.insight_zh: 人造肉赛道烧了几百亿美元才终于想通了一件事：与其对消费者进行吃草拯救地球的道德绑架，不如老老实实扮演合法合规的高科技注水肉。只要油脂和肉香还在，偷偷掺点蘑菇降本增效，当代吃货根本懒得深究肚子里装的到底是牛肉还是真菌孢子。
ai_analysis.insight_en: It took billions of venture capital dollars for alt-protein founders to realize that guilt-tripping consumers into eating synthetic paste never works. Repackaging food adulteration as sustainable blended meat is peak silicon valley pragmatism: keep the grease, cut the cost, and no teenager will care if their burger is half fungus.

ai_analysis.briefing_zh: 背靠蚂蚁集团技术与资本支持的菲律宾金融科技公司Mynt在马尼拉证券交易所挂牌上市，盘中最高上涨2.4%。该公司通过首次公开募股成功募集超过8.41亿美元，一举创下菲律宾资本市场历史最高IPO募资纪录，使其总市值跃升至约70亿美元。这一表现主要得益于其旗舰电子钱包GCash在当地无银行账户人群中建立的统治级市占率。

It proves the most lucrative tech play isn't pioneering breakthrough science, but operating a reliable time machine in emerging markets.

items.title: Leaked documents detail ECHOTRIBBLE, a nascent US Army Cyber Command program for agentic AI to autonomously spread across networks to find and eliminate targets (Sam Biddle/The Intercept)
items.title_en: Leaked documents detail ECHOTRIBBLE, a nascent US Army Cyber Command program for agentic AI to autonomously spread across networks to find and eliminate targets (Sam Biddle/The Intercept)
items.author: The Intercept
items.article_content:
Documents obtained by The Intercept show the military is trying to deploy autonomous AI agents to hack its adversaries.

Share  
  
    
      
        
          
          Copy link

      Pete Hegseth walks from the stage after introducing Donald Trump at an event for Anduril Industries on Oct. 6, 2026, in Sparrows Point, Md. 
        Photo: Julia Demaree Nikhinson/AP
  

    
    

  
  
    
    As global governments and tech giants reckon with widespread of revelations of autonomous AI agents unexpectedly breaking into computer systems, documents obtained by The Intercept show the U.S. Army is looking to harness that exact technology to seek and destroy.

Army Cyber Command is developing a platform to turn AI agents into autonomous weapons that can navigate and “neutralize” the computer systems of adversaries, the documents show.

Since 2010, Army Cyber Command, or ARCYBER, has led the U.S. Army’s cyber operations. This includes the defensive effort of protecting domestic computer systems and the secretive offensive work of hacking military targets. So far, this has largely been the work of human soldiers operating computers, like those of the 780th Military Intelligence Brigade. But as the government races to adopt artificial intelligence technology, ARCYBER is looking to offload some of its attacks to AI.

The nascent program, codenamed “ECHOTRIBBLE,” is based on one of the leading trends of the AI boom: agents. AI agents are essentially software programs that leverage machine learning technology, often large language models like Anthropic’s Claude, to autonomously accomplish tasks provided by their user. Consumers can deploy AI agents to schedule meetings, generate itineraries, make online purchases, or book tickets. Through ECHOTRIBBLE, the Pentagon plans to turn AI agents into tools of war “designed to autonomously navigate infrastructures” and capable of “identifying and neutralizing identified threats/targets,” according to an ARCYBER document reviewed by The Intercept circulated to potential contractors.

The military’s adoption of cutting-edge technologies is unsurprising, especially considering Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s fervent embrace of AI. But amid constant revelations of rogue behavior by agents, the potential for serious mishaps is immense, experts warn.

“Given the known failure modes of the current AI paradigm, making autonomous AI systems with a mandate to ‘neutralize threats’ is incredibly dangerous,” David Krueger, a professor of machine learning at the University of Montreal who founded Evitable, an organization that advocates for a moratorium on AI development. “We’ve seen AI systems knowingly attack systems that were not intended targets. In simulations, AIs have even proven willing to kill to achieve their goals.”

Most Read    

    
      
                                      
              
                
                                  
                
                  Inside ICE, Officials Question String of Trump Admin “Midterm Panic Moves”                                      
                      Karl Loftus                    
                                  
              
            
                                        
              
                
                                  
                
                  Lockheed Martin Showered Susan Collins With Cash as F-35 Program Hit Turbulence                                      
                      Noah Hurowitz                    
                                  
              
            
                                        
              
                
                                  
                
                  Dems Have an Opportunity to Force an End to the Iran War. Will They Take It?                                      
                      Matt Sledge

A Q&A document answering questions from potential contractors offers more details about the initiative. It explains that ECHOTRIBBLE is “primarily focused” on offensive missions, and explains that “neutralizing” a target could include “disabling the threat completely or temporarily, deleting the threat from the target.” ECHOTRIBBLE would function almost like a computer worm, silently navigating a foreign network and hopping from device to device until it finds the Army’s quarry, hitting targets in the cloud as well as those on “air-gapped” systems that are disconnected from networks entirely.

Once its task is complete, ECHOTRIBBLE’s agents would effectively self-destruct, ideally without having been noticed by the target at all. The agents themselves will be designed for stealth, minimally reporting back to the Army and concealing whatever outside transmissions are necessary.

“We’ve seen AI systems knowingly attack systems that were not intended targets.”

Although documents say the Army will be able to program ECHOTRIBBLE agents with some initial “predefined triggers” — dictating what and where to attack — the software “must operate with minimal human oversight” and be capable of “Self-Directed Behavior.”

A PowerPoint presentation to interested vendors at a June 24 ARCYBER event provided a hypothetical example of this self-direction. Once ECHOTRIBBLE is uploaded to a laptop, the software on its own “identifies other potential targets” on the same network and then “produces a replica of itself tailored specifically for the iPad, Apple desktop, and Windows 11 PC.”

The Army’s move toward autonomous self-propagating comes after a flurry of revelations about agentic systems taking unintended disturbing actions while attempting to accomplish their goals, including breaking into computers of the Australian government, breaching the infrastructure of the AI firm Hugging Face, uploading malicious software into online platform RubyGems, and attempted to hack into the U.S. Education Department.

These attacks occurred during scenarios in which agents had been given no commands to attack anything. Experts say militarized versions given explicitly destructive objectives could cause a threat to the public, even with nominal rules set in place by the military. Just as the Army of old might consider the destruction of civilian infrastructure an acceptable means to an end, a self-directed AI agent dispatched by the Pentagon might make similar determinations about collateral damage.

Governmental intelligence agencies frequently route their offensive operations through civilian devices. Volt Typhoon, a Chinese state hacking group, has directed its attacks through homes and small businesses, and preemptively hacks American IT systems for later use. A hack of a Chinese university attributed to the National Security Agency made use of the school’s internet routers. What happens if ECHOTRIBBLE decides these kinds of stepping stones are part of the problem?

“The target may well be hit. But what path will it take?” asked Hyrum Anderson, co-founder and CEO of the AI security firm Abundant. “Will it go through a US water utility on its way, because that’s where the adversary has staged its command and control, and take that down too?”

Anderson, who previously worked in cybersecurity at Microsoft and for the U.S. government, said that a vast amount of the internet is vulnerable to agentic attacks.

“There’s a huge class of public and private organizations that fall below the security poverty line,” he said. “They include critical national infrastructure, small businesses, mom-and-pop shops, dentist offices and law firms, and whoever else doesn’t have a single cybersecurity professional on staff.” With their networks wide open to infiltration, Hyrum worries about “these organizations getting hit directly, or getting caught in the blast radius of a target that gets hit along the way.”

Given the impressive ability of AI agents to overcome obstacles placed in their path — even by their creators — it follows that the Pentagon would want to leverage that power for military purposes. But agentic software has proven unpredictable and prone to executing its commands in ways those ostensibly in control did not want, akin to a drone that get its target but hits a hospital on the way. It’s critical to remember that agents are a piece of software lacking human judgment.

“One of the reasons that we trust 19-year-old Marine corporals in Ramadi with live rounds and a weapon is because they have both the compute substrate — the brain and the eyes — but the deep world knowledge to understand, ‘Yeah, I probably shouldn’t do that,’” said William Marcellino, a senior behavioral scientist at the RAND Corporation whose research has focused on military AI applications. “That is not something that current public AI technology has.”

The risk presented by ECHOTRIBBLE will likely depend on the ability — and willingness — of the Army to impose guardrails upon it. ARCYBER did not respond to questions from The Intercept, including queries about the measures it would take to prevent ECHOTRIBBLE from causing inadvertent damage.

Placing constraints on the actions an agent can take might impede its ability to ultimately neutralize a target. But even with strict safeguards in place, genuinely restricting the behavior of an autonomous agent, as Anthropic and OpenAI have learned recently, is easier said than done. When presented with obstacles, AI agents have proven an ability to bypass them with unpredictable and potentially dangerous consequences.

“If I give powerful machines that have no judgment — and no context for judgment — a goal, unless you’ve done a really good job building scaffolding around them, there’s a real chance that they’ll go sideways on you and decide, ‘Well, I’ll do what you asked me to do, but I’ll do it this way,’” Marcellino said.

It only gets more dangerous when this technology is deployed for the purposes of war, Anderson said.

“Under pressure, they’ll often treat guardrails as obstacles,” said Anderson. “Once you add context that says break it, destroy it, shut it down, it stands to reason that the blast radius widens dramatically unless it’s properly controlled for.”

items.title: Mercury CEO Immad Akhund says the fintech hit $1B in annualized revenue, up ~50% YoY, has more than 450K customers, and is launching a payroll service (Eric Newcomer/Newcomer)
items.title_en: Mercury CEO Immad Akhund says the fintech hit $1B in annualized revenue, up ~50% YoY, has more than 450K customers, and is launching a payroll service (Eric Newcomer/Newcomer)
items.author: Newcomer
items.article_content:
Akhund shared some exclusive milestones for his fintech business: Mercury just hit $1 billion in annualized revenue, up around 50% year over year. The company now has more than 450,000 customers. It’s also launching a payroll service.

But it wasn’t just a brag-fest: We talked about AI agents spending money, how he thinks we are in a bubbly moment for startups, and the cooldown in fintech startups after the pandemic frenzy.

We’ve featured guests like Amanda Askell, Reid Hoffman, Vinod Khosla, Keith Rabois, Tony Fadell, Ed Zitron, Ben Smith, Taylor Lorenz, and Katie Drummond.

I’m looking for guests that aren’t afraid to chop it up, debate, and face probing questions from an independent thinker who believes in the tech industry and capitalism.

If you’re interested in coming on the Newcomer podcast, reach out to my producer Dave Heuff. If you’re interested in sponsoring the podcast, email AJ Frucci.

The hidden gem of the Newcomer media empire is the fortnightly Cerebral Valley Show with my Cerebral Valley AI Summit co-hosts and Weekend co-founders Max Child and James Wilsterman.

There are a lot of podcasts for AI haters and AI zealots. We’re somewhere in between — enthusiasts who poke and prod at the industry.  We’re The Ringer for tech podcasts, somewhere you can get an entertaining gloss on the insider conversation in the AI industry even if you don’t sit on X all day.

Ask Hermes to make a 70m poly treasure chest for Godot, or to turn a photo of a mug into a model you can print, and it does the job through Meshy's MCP server.

items.quote_en:
Hermes Agent now has an official plugin for @MeshyAI.

items.title: RT @pushmeet: SynthID timeline over the last few weeks has been momentous – from opening SynthID Detector to the public,
items.title_en:
RT @pushmeet: SynthID timeline over the last few weeks has been momentous – from opening SynthID Detector to the public, to launching SynthID Bio to watermark functional, AI-designed proteins. 

Each moment brought us a step closer to our broader vision on provenance, or helping verify what is AI-generated and what isn’t.

Recently, Dartmouth Professor Hany Farid and I discussed why solving provenance is vital to @GoogleDeepMind’s broader mission to develop AI to benefit humanity.

In short: solving provenance is a highly complex, multi-disciplinary effort with watermarking technology at its core. It requires a collective mix of frontier research, interoperable open standards, and direct collaboration across platforms and developers.

Read our full conversation on Google's Public Policy blog: https://t.co/w8MEhnywKy

items.title_en:
BREAKING:

@AnthropicAI just launched Duet, its always-on personal agent. It’s the first personal agent I’d call a pro tool.

We’ve been testing it for two weeks. I’ve gone from mostly using ChatGPT to roughly 50/50 between ChatGPT and Claude—the most time I’ve spent with Anthropic in close to a year.

• It lives in its own app, separate from Claude, on iOS, Android, and the web. This makes it feel clean and easy to understand.
• It has channels for specific areas of your work and life rather than just a single chat
• It has a todo list so you never lose what you’re working on and you can always see statuses
• It allows you to easily write and edit documents, slides, and more all through the app.
• It’s not a chief of staff yet. It can see the Claude sessions on my computers but can’t direct them. Its email drafts are worse than dot’s, and voice is transcription only—you can’t have a spoken conversation with it.

My verdict: the vibes are good, and I’m opening Duet every day. It’s worth trying.

Check out our agent comparison page: https://t.co/fZyTorNK4p

Full Vibe Check coming soon on @every

items.content_snippet:
BREAKING:

@AnthropicAI just launched Duet, its always-on personal agent. It’s the first personal agent I’d call a pro tool.

We’ve been testing it for two weeks. I’ve gone from mostly using ChatGPT to roughly 50/50 between ChatGPT and Claude—the most time I’ve spent with Anthropic in close to a year.

• It lives in its own app, separate from Claude, on iOS, Android, and the web. This makes it feel clean and easy to understand.
• It has channels for specific areas of your work and life rather than just a single chat
• It has a todo list so you never lose what you’re working on and you can always see statuses
• It allows you to easily write and edit documents, slides, and more all through the app.
• It’s not a chief of staff yet. It can see the Claude sessions on my computers but can’t direct them. Its email drafts are worse than dot’s, and voice is transcription only—you can’t have a spoken conversation with it.

My verdict: the vibes are good, and I’m opening Duet every day. It’s worth trying.

Check out our agent comparison page: https://t.co/fZyTorNK4p

items.title_en:
If I had 6 months to become a Software Architect in the AI era.

I’d do this.

STAGE 1: Foundations & Role

- Learn: What architecture is, Architect vs Senior vs Tech Lead, quality attributes, functional vs non-functional requirements, stakeholders & constraints.

- Practice: Map quality attributes & conflicting drivers for one real system.

- Why: AI writes code. Architects decide what must not change when stakeholders and constraints shift.

STAGE 2: Architectural Thinking

- Learn: Tradeoffs, ADRs, fitness functions, technical debt, Conway’s Law.

- Practice: Write 5 ADRs & define fitness functions that reject bad designs.

- Why: AI proposes options. You own the recorded decision & its long-term cost.

STAGE 3: Design Principles

- Learn: SOLID, cohesion/coupling, boundaries, dependency inversion, YAGNI/KISS, complexity budget.

- Practice: Refactor a coupled service into ports & adapters under a hard complexity limit.

- Why: Generated code grows fast. Principles keep boundaries intact so change stays local.

STAGE 4: Styles & Patterns

- Learn: Modular monolith, microservices, hexagonal/clean, event-driven, CQRS & event sourcing.

- Practice: Implement one feature three ways & measure operational differences.

- Why: No single style wins. You choose & evolve the pattern that matches team size and change rate.

STAGE 5: Domain Modeling

- Learn: Strategic DDD, bounded contexts, aggregates, ubiquitous language, anti-corruption layer.

- Practice: Model a domain with two teams + one AI agent and add an anti-corruption boundary.

- Why: AI multiplies features. Clear contexts stop the domain from becoming inconsistent.

STAGE 6: Data & Persistence

- Learn: Data ownership, SQL vs NoSQL, partitioning, sagas/outbox, polyglot persistence.

- Practice: Design ownership boundaries + outbox for a system that mixes relational and vector data.

- Why: Agents write data. Ownership and consistency rules prevent silent corruption.

STAGE 7: Distributed Systems

- Learn: CAP/PACELC, consistency models, failure modes, idempotency, fallacies of distribution.

- Practice: Simulate partitions and show safe retries with an explicit consistency choice.

- Why: AI calls are multi-hop and async. You design for the failures generated code ignores.

STAGE 8: Integration & APIs

- Learn: Sync vs async, contracts & versioning, choreography vs orchestration, gateways.

- Practice: Build a versioned contract plus hybrid sync/async flow that includes agent steps.

- Why: Agents call constantly. Stable contracts and the right orchestration keep the system evolvable.

STAGE 9: Evolution & Production

- Learn: Evolutionary architecture, observability, SLIs/SLOs, resilience patterns, least privilege.

- Practice: Strangle one module, add full traces including agent calls & set error budgets.

- Why: Systems change while agents run. You keep production stable under continuous autonomous activity.

STAGE 10: Practice & Communication

- Learn: C4 diagrams, ADRs, architecture katas, classic system cases.

- Practice: Produce a full C4 + ADR set and publish one bottleneck teardown.

- Why: Architects are hired for judgment and clear decisions that survive teams, scale, and AI-driven change.

CRUD is dead. AI writes the boilerplate.

The "modern architect" builds the decision system that stays coherent under change, teams & autonomous agents.

Bookmark & RT!

items.title_en:
PSA: in light of recent cyberattacks and vulnerabilities, I recommend everyone:

* use a good password manager (1Password) and do not duplicate passwords 
* use two factor auth for everything important (not via sms!! Google Authenticator or better yet YubiKey)
* Auto-updates on, and restart weekly so they actually install
* Freeze your credit
* Get an IRS Identity Protection PIN
* Get your cell carrier to give you a port-out PIN or number lock that makes the carrier refuse to move your number without the PIN

You can ask your claude code to audit what on your laptop is out of date and needs updating.

items.title_en:
highly recommend everyone to have private alt accounts*. the x web is bad at account switching, but on mobile it is frictionless. its basically the same "group chat but its ok if you dont read everything" experience but for your mutuals.

tips
- assume everything is public, screenshotting is real, dont be stupid. this is not the "i shit talk people behind their back", the right attitude is "this isnt high signal enough for my main account but i'm 1) taking notes for self, 2) have a throwaway thought, 3) i'm happy to chat about it"

* i like it so much that i call this the "insta/finsta" pattern - every social network should by default give people a public profile and a private one by default. tbd on the third account, the "botsta".

items.title:
AI agents are writing more code. How can developers ensure that code is correct?

Microsoft Research’s Proof-Driven Deve
items.title_en:
AI agents are writing more code. How can developers ensure that code is correct?

Microsoft Research’s Proof-Driven Development (PDD) Kit explores a more rigorous approach: it translates a developer’s intent into a formal specification, then uses formal verification to prove that generated code meets it.

PDD Kit works with Verus for Rust and is integrated with @GitHubNext’s Chopin, bringing formal methods into an AI-assisted development workflow for teams.

See the work in action at @github Universe, Oct. 28–29, 2026.

items.title: MiniMax M3.1 Flash + SGLang Omni: building toward a more interactive generation of voice agents. The shift ahead is from
items.title_en:
MiniMax M3.1 Flash + SGLang Omni: building toward a more interactive generation of voice agents. The shift ahead is from “ask, wait, listen” to conversations people can interrupt, correct, and redirect as a task unfolds.

MiniMax M3.1 Flash brings intelligence and fast, concise responses. SGLang Omni adds streaming, conversation state, and interruption handling so users can redirect conversations in real time.

Together, they give developers a foundation to explore proactive tutors, support agents, and hands-free copilots - pairing Flash’s capabilities with infrastructure for continuous interaction.

Thanks to the SGLang Omni team for exploring this direction with M3.1 Flash! ✨

items.title_en:
🚨 THE AI VIDEO GAME JUST CHANGED

Kling 4.0 is live on Higgsfield.

The biggest upgrades:

→ 30-second scenes in one pass
→ Audio generated alongside the visuals
→ Control over key moments in a scene
→ Character consistency across generations

Until now, AI video was mostly about generating impressive clips. Now we're getting closer to producing complete scenes without the usual patchwork of tools and edits.

This is a serious step forward. Check this 👇

Kling 4.0 is now live on Higgsfield.

items.title_en:
there's a big opportunity in AI advisory right now, a gap in the market that's waiting to be filled...

atm there are two types of "AI experts":

the AI normie
- know how to use tools but completely delegate his thinking
- don't think in systems
- can't implement AI in real business workflows

the full AI nerd
- know everything there's to know about AI
- has 10 Claude Code instances running his life
- can't communicate with an human

and this is where YOUR opportunity is...

the market is screaming for a third type: the AI advisor

someone who can walk into a business, look at their operations for 2 hours, and say "this process right here? AI cuts it by 40% and here's exactly how"

they're looking for that guy who's deep enough in the rabbit hole to fix their problems, but also smart enough to dumb things down so they can understand the solution

be that guy

items.title_en:
Someone developed an app that purportedly removes AI content from your feed, and it has been revealed that it was created using AI vibe coding. 

The detector also uses "AI" to detect AI art content...

Oh, the Irony... It flags, classifies, and hides AI art using entirely AI-based context detection with an open source LLM called Gemma. 

The funny thing is that AI detection of AI content using LLMs is very inaccurate, with a lot of false positives and negatives.

When a fix ships, Claude checks the changed code and marks the finding fixed, even if your team fixed it outside Claude Security. If the issue comes back, the finding reopens.

Each project also gets a threat model Claude writes from your code, which your team can edit.

items.title_en:
A hacker group called CyberCartel used Claude and Grok to automate attacks on 400+ Latin American banks.

Not one attack. Not ten. Four hundred.

All using AI agents running in parallel.

Data stolen. Accounts accessed. Money moved.

Little human input required.

Straiker investigated. Found Claude Code session histories sitting in open directories.

Found the attacker asking Claude where to sell stolen data.

How did they get around the safety guardrails.

They told Claude they were in internal tests.

Claude believed them.

When Claude refused anyway. They switched to Grok.

Grok didn't refuse.

When Grok had limits. They switched to Kimi.

When Kimi had limits. They fell back to traditional malware.

Chain multiple models together. Each one picks up where the last one hesitated.

None of them know the full picture.

Claude thinks it's helping with testing.

Grok thinks it's just fixing code.

Kimi thinks it's just answering questions.

Together they broke into 400 banks.

The Information broke the story on October 20.

CrowdStrike confirmed it October 21.

Bank accounts in South Korea got hit the same way.

ARTEX. DeepSeek. Claude Code. All chained.

Over 68,000 people affected.

Financial Services Commission investigating.

This isn't theoretical anymore.

Not a lab demonstration. Not a proof of concept.

Real attacks. Real banks. Real money.

Automated by AI.

The moment we all waited for arrived quietly.

No announcement. No warning. Just a report.

And suddenly every AI lab is scrambling to figure out why their models are good at breaking into banks.

items.title_en:
16.6 MB RAM vs. 70 KB. 🤯

1,000 databases. ONE PGX process. 🐘

One idle PostgreSQL server: 16.6 MB. 
VS
One idle PGX database: just 70 KB!!

Measured on a 4 vCPU / 8 GB VM:

⚡ 128–155 MB RAM - 1,000 untouched DBs 
⚡ 213 MB - all queried once 
⚡ 283 MB - 100 active databases 
⚡ 0.33–0.43% of one CPU core at idle

This is why we built PGX. 🐘

Every AI agent deserves its own database. Not its own server.

Holy sh*t, I just turned my TV into Jarvis with Opus 5.5 + ChatGPT voice mode

I reverse-engineered my Samsung TV with O
items.title_en:
Holy sh*t, I just turned my TV into Jarvis with Opus 5.5 + ChatGPT voice mode

I reverse-engineered my Samsung TV with Opus 5.5...

1 sentence out loud = 6 Claude Code agents opening on my living room TV. 

here's the full guide step by step:

step 1 → put your Samsung Smart TV and your laptop on the same Wi-Fi

step 2 → paste the prompt below into Claude Code on Opus 5.5 with a photo of Settings → Support → About This TV

step 3 → Opus maps how the TV takes orders and finds the loophole: 

Samsung's own remote-control API on your home network can open any web page in the TV browser

step 4 → it spins up 6 Claude Code agents in a tmux grid on the laptop and streams them as a private page on your Wi-Fi only

step 5 → it builds a tiny "Jarvis" connector with one single tool: open the agent wall. 

ChatGPT voice mode is the ears, the connector is the hands

step 6 → press Allow on the TV once, the last time you touch the remote

step 7 → say "Open Claude Code CLI on my TV" and watch the windows pop in one by one

the result: the laptop does the work, the TV is the control room...

p.s: works on most Samsung Smart TVs with Tizen. 

mine in the video runs Smart Hub. The remote now lives in a drawer

Find full prompt below

Then read the article below on how to reverse-engineer anything

items.title_en:
People long believed in human-like computer use. But software (even terminals) is built for humans, not AI agents. Why not let agents build their own?

Meet 𝗔𝗴𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝗦𝟰, an agent scientist evolving its own interfaces, letting an open 27B model beats GPT-5.5 & Opus 4.8.

With its evolved interfaces, the same model improves 𝟯.𝟴× and costs <𝟱% as much per task as either frontier model.

Agents today read screenshots and act through click, scroll, type, maybe a shell. So an agent fills a spreadsheet cell by cell when one line of code would do, or prints two thousand lines of a file to find one function.

Every new app or model release means a human reads trajectories, diagnoses failures, and hand-writes new primitives. Skill-distillation methods can reorder what the interface allows, but they can’t extend it. Agents compensate with more test-time compute instead of a better interface.

𝗠𝗼𝗱𝗲𝗹𝘀 𝗶𝗺𝗽𝗿𝗼𝘃𝗲; 𝗶𝗻𝘁𝗲𝗿𝗳𝗮𝗰𝗲𝘀 𝘀𝘁𝗮𝘆 𝗳𝗿𝗼𝘇𝗲𝗻.

“We want AI agents that can discover like we can, not which contain what we have discovered.”
— Rich Sutton, The Bitter Lesson

Hand-designed interfaces are what we have discovered. Agents can read their own trajectories, spot what’s missing, and write and test code. 𝗜𝗻𝘁𝗲𝗿𝗳𝗮𝗰𝗲 𝗱𝗲𝘀𝗶𝗴𝗻 𝘀𝗵𝗼𝘂𝗹𝗱 𝗯𝗲 𝗮𝗻 𝗮𝗴𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝗰𝗮𝗽𝗮𝗯𝗶𝗹𝗶𝘁𝘆.

That’s what Agent S4 does.

Agent S4 makes a 𝗿𝗲𝗽𝗼𝘀𝗶𝘁𝗼𝗿𝘆 𝗼𝗳 𝗶𝗻𝘁𝗲𝗿𝗳𝗮𝗰𝗲𝘀 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝘂𝘀𝗮𝗴𝗲 𝗸𝗻𝗼𝘄𝗹𝗲𝗱𝗴𝗲 the unit of evolution. A task agent attempts synthetic tasks with no success labels or verifiers. A meta-agent studies the trajectories, forms hypotheses about which actions, observations, or knowledge would help, and builds descendants through mutation or crossover. Validation tasks the meta-agent never sees decide which repositories survive.

The model and harness stay fixed, and the meta-agent 𝗻𝗲𝘃𝗲𝗿 𝘀𝗲𝗲𝘀 𝗮 𝗯𝗲𝗻𝗰𝗵𝗺𝗮𝗿𝗸 𝘁𝗮𝘀𝗸. 𝗢𝗻𝗹𝘆 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗶𝗻𝘁𝗲𝗿𝗳𝗮𝗰𝗲 𝗲𝘃𝗼𝗹𝘃𝗲𝘀.

With the evolved repository, Qwen3.8-27B goes from 𝟱.𝟲% to 𝟮𝟭.𝟯% on OSWorld V2, 𝟯.𝟴× the same model with fixed interfaces and a new state of the art for open-source computer-use agents.

It beats GPT-5.5 (13.0%, $25.50/task) and edges past Opus 4.8 (20.6%, $72.40/task) at $𝟭.𝟭𝟬 per task.

On ScienceBoard, the same model goes from 41.4% to 58.6%.

The analysis is the more interesting part. Evolution mostly deepens interfaces the agent already has: 4 new interfaces and 127 extensions. Give the meta-agent a scratch VM to test its code, and it builds 12 new interfaces and 253 extensions, reaching music scores, audio projects, and 3D scenes. The best repository came from crossing two earlier branches.

In one case study, the seed agent hand-builds a browser client mid-task and debugs through failure after failure; the evolved agent calls page_text and reaches the same message at tool call 𝟭𝟭 instead of 𝟯𝟳.

Human-like computer use was a starting point, not the destination. The interface an agent acts through is a second axis of improvement, beyond better models and harnesses, and agents can now design it themselves. 𝗘𝘃𝗼𝗹𝘃𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗮𝗴𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝗶𝗻𝘁𝗲𝗿𝗳𝗮𝗰𝗲𝘀 𝗶𝘀 𝗮 𝗻𝗲𝘄 𝗱𝗶𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘀𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗼𝗳 𝗮𝗴𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝘀𝗲𝗹𝗳-𝗶𝗺𝗽𝗿𝗼𝘃𝗲𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁.
